sections.title: Wiring methods — general rules
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 300 is the rulebook that sits over every wiring method in this chapter. Whichever cable or raceway you pick later — NM, MC, EMT, PVC — these general rules still apply: protect the wiring from damage, give underground runs enough cover, support what you install, and leave enough free wire at every box to make a proper joint. Read this article first, then go to the article for the specific method.
• Protection (300.4): cable and raceway through framing stays 1-1/4 in back from the nearest edge of the wood, or gets a steel plate at least 1/16 in thick.
• Cover (300.5): underground wiring is buried to Table 300.5 — in open ground, 24 in of cover over a direct-burial cable, 18 in over PVC raceway, 6 in over rigid metal conduit.
• Support (300.11): every method is secured and supported at the spacing its own article sets; wiring never hangs off other raceways, pipes or ceiling wires.
• Free conductor (300.14): at least 6 in of free conductor at every outlet, junction and switch point, and 3 in out of the opening where the box opening is under 8 in.
• A box at every point (300.15): conduit, tubing and cable methods get a box or conduit body at each splice, outlet, switch, junction, termination and pull point.
sections.on_the_job: Before you choose a method, ask three questions: Where does it run (dry, damp, wet, underground, exposed)? What can hit it? How will it be supported? The answers pick the method and trigger the 300 rules. On a Florida house, one 20 A circuit shows all three at once: NM stapled through the stud bays inside (300.4 setback, plates where a hole lands close), a PVC run out to the pool equipment buried with 18 in of cover (300.5), and 6 in of free conductor folded into the box at the disconnect (300.14).
sections.figure_idea: Cross-section of a house wall, slab and yard showing one circuit as NM in the wall, EMT on the surface and UF underground, with callouts to 300.4, 300.5 and 300.11.

nec2023_change.change: Cables pulled into a raceway now fall under the general fill limit too, not only individual conductors. Too many cables trap heat and get skinned on the pull. Cables are now named in 300.17: a raceway can only hold as many conductors or cables as heat and a clean pull allow.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 300.17 Raceway fill now counts cables

nec2023_change.change: New 300.26 sorts remote-control and signaling circuits into three groups and points each to its rules: Article 724, Article 725, or the general wiring rules of Article 300. Circuits that aren't power-limited are wired like any power circuit, using the general rules of Article 300 and Chapter 3 wiring methods.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 300.26 Sorting control and signal circuits

nec2023_change.change: Enclosures, other than fences and walls, are now on the corrosion lists. Any thread not cut at the factory counts as field-cut and needs conductive compound where corrosion protection is needed. Enclosures, except fences and walls around equipment, now join raceways, boxes and fittings in needing materials fit for the location.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 300.6 Corrosion protection for enclosures

sections.why_it_exists: These rules exist because most wiring damage does not happen on the day of the install. It happens later: a drywall screw finds a cable, a shovel finds a shallow run, a device gets changed on wires too short to remake the joint. Article 300 puts distance, steel, depth and slack between the wiring and the people who will dig, drill and remodel around it for the next fifty years.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating Article 300 as fine print that the method article overrides. It does not. A perfectly legal NM run still fails when the bored hole sits 1/2 in from the stud edge with no plate: 300.4 applies on top of Article 334, not instead of it.
inspection_fails: Bored hole 1/2 in from the stud edge, no steel plate (300.4(A)(1)).
UF cable buried at 10 in in open ground; Table 300.5 wants 24 in of cover.
Conductors cut to 3 in at a device box; 300.14 wants 6 in free.
Splice floating in a wall cavity with no box (300.15).
Cable draped over the ceiling grid, tied to a sprinkler pipe (300.11).

page_quiz.question: A bored hole leaves 3/4 in between the hole edge and the stud face, with no plate. Legal?
choices: Yes, if the cable is centered
No — it needs 1-1/4 in or a 1/16 in steel plate
No — holes must sit 2 in back
page_quiz.explain_plain: 300.4(A)(1) measures from the edge of the hole: 1-1/4 in minimum, or protect the cable with a steel plate at least 1/16 in thick.

page_quiz.question: How much free conductor at a switch box whose opening is under 8 in?
choices: 6 in, sticking 3 in out of the opening
page_quiz.explain_plain: 300.14 wants at least 6 in of free conductor, and 3 in out of the opening where the opening is under 8 in in any direction.

page_quiz.question: A direct-burial cable in open ground needs how much cover?
page_quiz.explain_plain: Table 300.5 wants 24 in over a direct-burial cable in open ground; PVC raceway takes 18 in and rigid metal conduit 6 in.

sections.title: All conductors of a circuit run together
sections.plain_explanation:
Every conductor of a circuit — the ungrounded conductors, the grounded (neutral) conductor, and the equipment grounding conductor — is installed in the same raceway, cable, trench, or cord.
• Ungrounded (hot) conductors: in the same run as the rest of the circuit.
• Grounded (neutral) conductor: in the same run.
• Equipment grounding conductor: in the same run.
The rule keeps the circuit's magnetic fields canceling each other (conductors run separately heat surrounding metal and behave unpredictably), and it guarantees the ground path travels with the circuit it protects. The exceptions are narrow — conductors in parallel sets, and a few underground and existing-installation arrangements this section names — and even they require the conductors to be grouped so each raceway or cable carries a complete, balanced set.
sections.on_the_job: The field failure is the borrowed ground or the lone neutral: a ground pulled from a different cable, or one circuit's neutral run in another conduit. On a multiwire branch circuit the shared neutral stays in the same cable as both hots, start to finish. If the conductors did not arrive together, they do not splice together — re-pull the run.
sections.figure_idea: One conduit with hot, neutral, and ground entering together (correct), and a second conduit carrying only a stray ground borrowed from another run (crossed out).
sections.why_it_exists: Current that goes out by one path and returns by another makes a loop, and that loop induces voltage and heat in every piece of metal it circles. A ground borrowed from somewhere else may not be there — or may not carry this circuit's fault — on the one day it is needed. Run together, the fields cancel and the fault path is the one you can see and test.
inspection_fails: An equipment ground for a circuit pulled from a different cable because the run's own ground was cut short.
One circuit's neutral run in a separate conduit from its hot conductors.
Hot conductors in one raceway and the neutral in another on a long commercial run.
A parallel set grouped by phase — all of one phase in one raceway, the next phase in another — instead of a complete set in each raceway.
sections.exam_trap: A parallel feeder can run all the phase A conductors in one conduit and all the phase B conductors in another — same total copper, easier pull. Wrong. Each raceway of a parallel set carries a complete, balanced set: one conductor of each phase, the neutral where one is used, and the equipment grounding conductor.

page_quiz.question: Under 300.3(B), the equipment grounding conductor of a circuit must be installed:
choices: In any raceway that is convenient
In the same raceway or cable as the circuit conductors
Directly in the earth beside the run
page_quiz.explain_plain: All conductors of a circuit — ungrounded, grounded and equipment grounding — are installed in the same raceway, cable, trench or cord.

choices: Yes, if both conduits are the same size
No — the neutral runs with its circuit
page_quiz.explain_plain: The grounded conductor is part of the circuit and must be installed with its ungrounded conductors, not borrowed or routed separately.

page_quiz.question: Conductors are installed in parallel in two raceways. Each raceway must contain:
choices: A complete, balanced set of the circuit
page_quiz.explain_plain: Even under the parallel exception, each raceway or cable carries a complete set — one of each phase, the neutral where used, and the grounding conductor — so the fields cancel.

sections.title: Protecting wiring from physical damage
sections.plain_explanation:
This is the nail-and-screw section. Where cable or raceway passes through or runs alongside wood or metal framing, it has to sit far enough back from the face of the framing that drywall screws and nails miss it — or be shielded by a steel plate.
• Through wood framing (300.4(A)(1)): bore the hole so the edge of the hole is at least 1-1/4 in from the nearest edge of the wood. If that cannot be kept, protect the cable with a steel plate at least 1/16 in thick.
• Through metal framing (300.4(B)): a bushing or listed grommet covers all metal edges and is fastened in the opening before the cable is installed. Where nails or screws threaten NM cable or ENT, add a steel sleeve, plate or clip at least 1/16 in thick.
• Parallel to framing (300.4(D)): keep the nearest surface of the cable or raceway at least 1-1/4 in from the framing edge wherever nails or screws are likely — or plate it. Rigid metal conduit, IMC, rigid nonmetallic conduit and EMT need no plate; the raceway is its own protection.
• Under metal-corrugated roof decking (300.4(E)): keep cables, raceways and boxes at least 1-1/2 in below the lowest surface of the decking, and never run them concealed inside the decking itself. The fastener here is the roofing screw.
sections.on_the_job: Center your holes, keep the 1-1/4 in setback in 300.4(A)(1), and plate anything that ends up closer. Kick plates / nail plates are not extras — if the cable is in the strike zone, the plate goes on before drywall, every time. On a Marion County rough-in, walk every stud bay before insulation: any hole that ends up closer than 1-1/4 in to a face gets its plate the same day, not on the punch list.
sections.sharma_note: Kick plates are always in Sharma takeoffs — stock them on every rough-in truck, do not treat them as an optional add-on.
sections.figure_idea: Front view of a stud bay: a centered bored hole marked 1-1/4 in minimum from each face, and beside it a shallow hole covered by a 1/16 in steel nail plate.

nec2023_change.change: The exceptions to 300.4(E) were reworked. Exception No. 1: rigid metal conduit and intermediate metal conduit, with listed steel or malleable iron fittings and boxes, shall not be required to comply with 300.4(E). Exception No. 2: the 1-1/2 in spacing is not required where metal-corrugated sheet roof decking is covered with a minimum thickness 2 in concrete slab, measured from the top of the corrugated roofing.
nec2023_change.source: Carosella/NFPA-based 2023 NEC change workbook: 300.4(E) Ex. No. 1 and 2 Cables, Raceways, or Boxes Installed in or Under Metal-Corrugated Roof

sections.why_it_exists: Drywall screws, trim nails and roofing screws are driven blind — the installer cannot see the cable behind the surface. A screw through a conductor may not trip anything today; it leaves a nicked, arcing fault inside a closed wall. Setbacks keep copper out of the strike zone, and the 1/16 in plate is thick enough to stop or deflect the fastener when the setback cannot be had.
inspection_fails: Bored hole 3/4 in from the stud face, cable pulled, no nail plate (300.4(A)(1)).
NM cable through a punched steel stud with no grommet — jacket sliced on the raw edge (300.4(B)(1)).
Cable run tight along the stud edge in the screw zone, unplated (300.4(D)).
Raceway strapped hard against metal roof decking, inside the 1-1/2 in roofing-screw zone (300.4(E)).
sections.exam_trap: The trap: measuring the 1-1/4 in to the center of the bored hole. The rule measures from the edge of the hole to the nearest edge of the wood. A hole that looks centered in a shallow stud can still be too close on one face — check both faces before you pull.

sections.title: Bored holes in wood framing
sections.plain_explanation:
A hole bored through a wood stud or joist for cable or raceway must be drilled so the edge of the hole is at least 1-1/4 in from the nearest edge of the wood. If that distance cannot be kept, the cable must be protected by a steel plate at least 1/16 in thick, of a suitable length and width, installed to protect the wiring.
The measurement runs from the edge of the hole to the nearest edge of the wood — never from the center of the hole. Check both faces of the member: on a stud drilled slightly off line, one face can pass while the other fails. Where the setback cannot be held, the plate is the fix: steel, at least 1/16 in thick, long and wide enough to shield the cable where it passes the framing. The same 1/16 in plate protects cable in metal framing under 300.4(B)(2).
sections.on_the_job: Drill in the middle third of the stud width where you can. Check both faces — a hole can be legal from the front and too close from the back on a shallow stud. Plate first, then pull cable, so the plate is not forgotten. Worked case on a 2×4 (3-1/2 in deep): a 7/8 in hole drilled dead center leaves 1-5/16 in from the hole edge to each face — legal, no plate. Step up to a 1-3/8 in hole for a fat cable and the same centered hole leaves only 1-1/16 in — that hole gets a steel plate before the cable is pulled.
sections.figure_idea: Close-up of a 2x4 stud with a centered hole, dimension arrows showing 1-1/4 in from hole edge to stud face.
sections.why_it_exists: Drywall goes up with screws, cabinets and trim go up with nails, and nobody can see the cable behind the board. The 1-1/4 in setback puts the wiring deeper than the fasteners reach; the plate is armor for the spots where the framing is too shallow to buy that depth.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is measuring from the center of the hole. A hole centered 1-1/4 in from the face, drilled with a 1 in bit, leaves only 3/4 in from the hole's edge — the rule measures edge to edge, and that run needs a plate.
inspection_fails: Bored hole with its edge 7/8 in from the stud face, no steel plate (300.4(A)(1)).
Plate installed but narrower than the cable run it is supposed to shield.
Hole drilled off-center: 1-3/8 in from the front face, 15/16 in from the back, no plate.

page_quiz.question: The 1-1/4 in of 300.4(A)(1) is measured from:
choices: The edge of the hole to the nearest edge of the wood
page_quiz.explain_plain: The rule measures edge to edge: the edge of the bored hole to the nearest edge of the wood member.

page_quiz.question: A hole's edge ends up 1 in from the stud face. The fix is:
choices: A steel plate at least 1/16 in thick
page_quiz.explain_plain: Where the 1-1/4 in cannot be kept, 300.4(A)(1) calls for a steel plate at least 1/16 in thick protecting the wiring.

page_quiz.question: A centered 1-3/8 in hole in a 2×4 (3-1/2 in deep) leaves how much wood at each face?
page_quiz.explain_plain: (3-1/2 − 1-3/8) ÷ 2 = 1-1/16 in — under 1-1/4 in, so that hole needs a plate.

sections.title: Cables through metal framing — bushings and plates
sections.plain_explanation:
Metal studs change the protection hardware:
• Through a hole: where a cable passes through a hole in a metal framing member, it is protected by a bushing or a listed grommet. Under 300.4(B)(1) the bushing or grommet must cover all metal edges and be securely fastened in the opening before the cable is installed.
• Where nails or screws are likely to penetrate: protect NM cable or ENT in metal framing with a steel sleeve, steel plate or steel clip at least 1/16 in thick (300.4(B)(2)).
A raw punched steel edge will saw through a cable jacket under vibration and thermal movement — the bushing is not optional trim.
sections.on_the_job: Stock grommets on the truck for steel-stud work and snap them in as you lay out the holes, not after the cable is pulled — a grommet forced over a pulled cable usually ends up in a pocket instead. Walk the run before insulation: every hole, every cable, one bushing. On a steel-stud tenant job, make that walk a two-man pass: one man with the grommet pouch, one with the cable, and nobody pulls the next stud bay until the last one is bushed and checked.
sections.figure_idea: Steel stud with three holes: a bare punched hole with cable through it (crossed out), a hole with a snap-in grommet, and a slotted run protected by a 1/16 in plate.
sections.why_it_exists: A punched steel-stud hole is a knife edge with a cable resting on it. Building vibration and thermal movement work the jacket against that edge until the insulation is cut and the conductor faults to the stud — inside a closed wall. The steel plate rule covers the second attack: the drywall screw headed for the same cable.
inspection_fails: NM cable through a punched steel-stud hole with no bushing or listed grommet (300.4(B)(1)).
Grommet loose in the opening, not fastened in place, cable resting on the bare steel edge (300.4(B)(1)).
Cable in metal framing where drywall screws will land, with no 1/16 in steel sleeve, plate or clip (300.4(B)(2)).
sections.exam_trap: The trap is trusting the grommet to do both jobs: "A listed grommet is in the hole, so the cable is protected." The grommet covers the edge, but where nails or screws are likely to penetrate, 300.4(B)(2) wants steel — a sleeve, plate or clip at least 1/16 in thick.

sections.title: Cables and raceways parallel to framing members and furring strips
sections.plain_explanation: This is the along-the-framing companion to the bored-hole rule. In exposed or concealed work, where a cable or raceway runs parallel to a framing member — a joist, rafter or stud — or parallel to furring strips, it has to be installed and supported so the nearest outside surface of the cable or raceway is at least 1-1/4 in from the nearest edge of the framing member or furring strip, wherever nails or screws are likely to penetrate. Where that distance cannot be kept, the cable or raceway must be protected from nail or screw penetration by a steel plate, sleeve or equivalent at least 1/16 in thick; a listed and marked thinner steel plate that provides equal or better protection is also permitted. Steel plates are not required for rigid metal conduit, IMC, rigid nonmetallic conduit or EMT — the raceway is its own protection — and for concealed work in finished buildings, cables may be fished between access points where supporting them is impracticable.
sections.on_the_job: Running down a stud bay in a wood-frame house in Ocala, the NM drops are held on cable stackers so the nearest surface of the cable stays 1-1/4 in off the stud edge the drywall screws will come through. One stretch has to pass a furring strip tight to the edge — that stretch gets a 1/16 in steel plate before the wall closes. If a stretch of the run has to hug the edge, plate that stretch; finding it after the screw does is a callback and a patch.
sections.figure_idea: Side view of a stud bay: a cable running vertically along a stud, held 1-1/4 in from the stud's nearest edge by a cable stacker, with a second run tight to the edge covered by a 1/16 in steel plate.
sections.why_it_exists: Drywall screws and trim nails are driven blind, and they go in along framing edges — exactly where a parallel cable wants to lie. A cable held 1-1/4 in off the edge sits outside the fastener path; one hugging the edge is a short circuit waiting for the finisher. The steel plate is the fallback for the stretches where the distance cannot be kept.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: "The 1-1/4 in rule is only for bored holes." 300.4(A)(1) covers holes; this section, 300.4(D), covers cables and raceways running parallel to framing members and furring strips — same distance, different run. The second trap is plating everything: rigid metal conduit, IMC, rigid nonmetallic conduit and EMT are their own protection and need no plate.
inspection_fails: NM stapled tight along the stud edge, right in line with the drywall screws.
Parallel run 1/2 in from the edge of a furring strip, with no steel plate.
Plate thinner than 1/16 in, not listed or marked, used as the protection.
Cable crossing to the edge of the framing at a doorway with no plate before the wall closed.

page_quiz.question: Which of these needs no steel plate under 300.4(D)?
page_quiz.explain_plain: Steel plates are not required for rigid metal conduit, IMC, rigid nonmetallic conduit or EMT — the raceway is its own protection.

No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.

sections.title: Protecting large conductors where they enter enclosures
sections.plain_explanation:
Where raceways contain insulated circuit conductors 4 AWG and larger, and those conductors enter a cabinet, a box, an enclosure or a raceway, the conductors have to be protected from abrasion at the entry (300.4(G)). The protection is one of the following:
• An identified fitting providing a smoothly rounded insulating surface — the classic insulating bushing.
• A listed metal fitting that has smoothly rounded edges.
• Separation from the fitting or raceway using an identified insulating material that is securely fastened in place.
• Threaded hubs or bosses that are an integral part of the enclosure or raceway and provide a smoothly rounded or flared entry.
Two limits ride along: a bushing made wholly of insulating material may not be used to secure a fitting or raceway, and the insulating fitting or material must carry a temperature rating at least equal to the insulation rating of the conductors it protects. Big conductors are stiff, heavy and expensive; a sharp knockout edge plus one hard pull is insulation damage you cannot see after the cover goes on.
sections.on_the_job: Fit the insulating bushing before the pull, not after you see the scrape. On service and feeder entries, check every entry edge with a fingertip before conductors go in. On a 200 A Orlando service change, the 4/0 conductors entering the new Siemens meter-main through a threaded nipple got insulating bushings on every entry first — and the fingertip check found one burred knockout edge that would have skinned a conductor on the pull.
sections.figure_idea: Service conductor entering a meter enclosure through a listed fitting with a smooth rounded insulating surface, sharp-edge version crossed out beside it.

nec2023_change.change: Bushings for 4 AWG and larger now have to be on before the pull. Under metal roof decking, a concrete exception was added, and the rigid and intermediate metal conduit pass now depends on fittings. Where conductors 4 AWG or bigger enter a box or enclosure, the bushing or other protection now goes on before they're pulled (300.4(G)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 300.4 Protection from physical damage

sections.edition_note:
NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 300.4: Bushings for 4 AWG and larger now have to be on before the pull. Under metal roof decking, a concrete exception was added, and the rigid and intermediate metal conduit pass now depends on fittings. Where conductors 4 AWG or bigger enter a box or enclosure, the bushing or other protection now goes on before they're pulled (300.4(G)).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: The edge of a knockout, a locknut corner or a threaded raceway end is a knife under pulling tension. A 4/0 conductor dragged across it shaves its own insulation, and the damage hides inside the enclosure. The fault shows up later — under load, as a ground fault or an arc inside the gear. The smooth, rounded surface spreads the contact so the insulation survives the pull.
inspection_fails: 4/0 feeder conductors entering a panel over a bare threaded nipple — no bushing or fitting at the entry (300.4(G)).
Insulation shaved bright at a knockout edge on 2 AWG conductors; tape wrapped over the damage instead of listed protection (300.4(G)).
All-plastic bushing used as the means of securing the raceway to the enclosure (300.4(G)).
Entry protected with an insulating fitting rated below the temperature rating of the conductors' insulation (300.4(G)).
sections.exam_trap: The trap: 'Only 1/0 and larger needs a bushing' — or 'any metal bushing counts.' The trigger is 4 AWG and larger, and a plain metal bushing with a sharp inner edge is not on the list: the metal fitting must be listed with smoothly rounded edges, or the surface the conductor bears on must be insulating.

tables.caption: What counts as entry protection (300.4(G))
rows: Identified fitting with a smoothly rounded insulating surface
Listed metal fitting with smoothly rounded edges
Identified insulating material, securely fastened, separating conductors from the fitting
Integral threaded hub or boss with a smooth, flared entry
Plain locknut against a sharp knockout edge

figures.alt: Two enclosure entries side by side: on the left a large conductor passes through an insulating bushing with a smooth rounded surface and a green check; on the right a conductor drags over a sharp knockout edge with its insulation nicked, marked with a red X.
figures.caption: The fitting must give big conductors a smooth, rounded surface to bear on.

page_quiz.question: What is the smallest conductor size that triggers 300.4(G)?
page_quiz.explain_plain: 300.4(G) starts at 4 AWG and larger insulated circuit conductors entering a cabinet, box, enclosure or raceway.

page_quiz.question: Which entry protection is permitted for 4/0 conductors?
choices: A listed metal fitting with smoothly rounded edges
An all-plastic bushing used to secure the raceway
page_quiz.explain_plain: A listed metal fitting with smoothly rounded edges is one of the four permitted methods in 300.4(G). Tape is not a method, and an all-insulating bushing may not be used to secure the raceway.

page_quiz.question: The insulating fitting's temperature rating must be at least what?
choices: The insulation temperature rating of the installed conductors
page_quiz.explain_plain: 300.4(G) requires the insulating fitting or insulating material to have a temperature rating not less than the insulation temperature rating of the installed conductors.

rich_sources.claim: 300.4(G) in the 2020 NEC: conductors 4 AWG and larger entering a cabinet, box, enclosure or raceway are protected by (1) a fitting providing a smoothly rounded insulating surface, (2) a listed metal fitting with smoothly rounded edges, (3) separation using an identified insulating material securely fastened in place, or (4) integral threaded hubs or bosses providing a smoothly rounded or flared entry
rich_sources.source: Mike Holt, NEC Questions and Answers based on the 2020 NEC (May 2021)

sections.title: Underground wiring — cover, protection and sealing
sections.plain_explanation: Underground runs have to be in a wiring method approved for burial and buried deep enough that digging, traffic and frost do not reach them. Cover is measured from the top of the cable or raceway to finished grade, and the required depth depends on the method and what is above it — a yard, a driveway and a slab are not the same row of the table. Risers coming out of the ground need protection from damage. Under 300.5(G), a raceway through which moisture could contact energized live parts has to be sealed or plugged at either or both ends, with a sealant identified for use with the cable or conductor insulation; the separate seal for a raceway that passes between different temperatures, where condensation is known to be a problem, is in 300.7(A), not in this section. Direct-buried splices and taps are permitted without a splice box only when made under 110.14(B), and wire connectors or splicing means used for direct burial must be listed for that use.
sections.on_the_job: The rows Sharma digs to most (Table 300.5, cover over the top of the cable or raceway): in open ground — direct-burial cable 24 in, nonmetallic raceway (PVC) 18 in, rigid metal conduit 6 in. Under a one- or two-family dwelling driveway or outdoor parking area used only for the dwelling, all three methods are 18 in. Under streets, roads, alleys, driveways and parking lots (the commercial row), 24 in for every method. The 12 in figure is only the separate column for a residential branch circuit of 120 V, 20 A or less with GFCI protection — it is not the depth for PVC in general. Slabs and building interiors have their own rows: check the row for the actual location before you trench, and never carry one depth to every location.
sections.figure_idea: Trench cross-section with four parallel runs at 24, 18, 12 and 6 in, each labeled with its method, and a tape measure to finished grade.
sections.florida_note: NEC 300.5(D)(3) itself requires a warning ribbon — that part is code, not local preference — but only for underground service conductors that are not encased in concrete and are buried 18 in or more below grade: their location must be identified by a warning ribbon placed in the trench at least 12 in above the underground installation. The NEC does not impose that ribbon rule on ordinary feeders and branch circuits. Local AHJs may add bedding or tape requirements beyond it — confirm at permit, and do not assume the table is the whole job.

nec2023_change.change: EMT now has its own burial depths in Table 300.5(A), and the underground damage protection rules, warning ribbon included, now apply to conductors in raceways as well as direct-buried ones. EMT now has a spot in Column 3 of Table 300.5(A): 18 inches of cover in general, 24 inches under streets and roads.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 300.5 Underground EMT and warning ribbon

sections.why_it_exists: Buried wiring sits out of sight for decades, and its enemies are shovels, car tires, settling soil and water. Cover puts dirt between the run and the next person digging. Sealing keeps the moisture that does get into a raceway from traveling inside and reaching live parts in the building.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is answering '18 in' for everything because that is the PVC row in open ground — or worse, '12 in,' which is only the GFCI-protected 120 V residential branch-circuit column. Under a commercial driveway every method is 24 in, and in open ground direct-burial cable is 24 in while rigid metal conduit is only 6 in. The answer is always a row and a column, never one number.
inspection_fails: PVC feeder buried at 12 in in open ground — that depth belongs only to the GFCI-protected 120 V, 20 A residential branch-circuit column (Table 300.5).
Raceway entering the building unsealed where moisture can contact live parts (300.5(G)).
Direct-buried splice made with connectors not listed for direct burial (110.14(B)).
Underground service conductors buried 18 in or more with no warning ribbon placed 12 in above them (300.5(D)(3)).

tables.caption: Table 300.5 — the cover Sharma digs to most
tables.note: The 12 in depth is a separate column: residential branch circuits only, 120 V, 20 A max, GFCI-protected.

figures.alt: Trench cross-section in open ground showing three runs at their Table 300.5 cover depths: direct-burial cable at 24 inches, PVC raceway at 18 inches and rigid metal conduit at 6 inches, each dimensioned from finished grade, with the 12 inch GFCI branch-circuit column called out separately.
figures.caption: Cover is a row and a column — never one depth for every job.

page_quiz.question: In open ground, a PVC raceway needs how much cover?
page_quiz.explain_plain: Table 300.5, general row: nonmetallic raceway 18 in. Direct-burial cable is 24 in and rigid metal conduit is 6 in.

page_quiz.question: Under a commercial parking lot, the cover for every wiring method is:
page_quiz.explain_plain: The streets, roads, driveways and parking lots row is 24 in for every method in the table.

page_quiz.question: A raceway that could let moisture contact energized live parts must be:
choices: Sealed or plugged at either or both ends with an identified sealant
Left open so it can drain
page_quiz.explain_plain: 300.5(G): seal or plug the raceway at either or both ends, with a sealant identified for use with the cable or conductor insulation.

sections.edition_note:
NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 300.5: EMT now has its own burial depths in Table 300.5(A), and the underground damage protection rules, warning ribbon included, now apply to conductors in raceways as well as direct-buried ones. EMT now has a spot in Column 3 of Table 300.5(A): 18 inches of cover in general, 24 inches under streets and roads.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

sections.title: Sealing raceways that pass between different temperatures
sections.plain_explanation: Where part of a raceway sits at a much lower temperature than another part — a run from a warm building into a cold-storage room is the textbook case — the warmer air inside the raceway circulates into the cold part and its moisture condenses there, wetting conductors that were installed dry. This section requires the raceway to be filled with an approved sealing material at the temperature boundary, to stop that air circulation. It is a condensation seal, not a waterproofing seal: the separate rule for sealing a raceway so moisture cannot reach live parts is 300.5(G), and explosionproof sealing fittings are a hazardous-location subject in Article 501, not this section. 300.7(A) does not say which side gets sealed; it requires the raceway or sleeve to be filled with an approved material to prevent circulation of warm air to a colder section. It also applies where a raceway passes from the interior to the exterior of a building, and sealants must be identified for use with the cable or conductor insulation, bare conductors, shields or other components. 300.7(B): expansion, expansion-deflection or deflection fittings are required where thermal expansion or contraction is expected.
sections.on_the_job: The Florida case is any conduit that leaves a hot attic or a sun-baked exterior wall and enters an air-conditioned space or a walk-in cooler: put the duct seal in the run where the temperature changes, before the conductors are pulled or as the section's method directs. A run that drips at the panel in August is usually this rule, missed.
sections.figure_idea: A conduit crossing a wall from a sunlit exterior into a cooler interior, with a seal drawn inside the conduit at the wall line and condensation drops shown on the unsealed version beside it.
sections.why_it_exists: A raceway is a pipe for air as well as wire. Warm air holds moisture; when that air drifts into a cold section and cools, the water falls out on the conductors and terminations. The seal breaks the chimney: no circulation, no condensation cycle, no corroded lugs or nuisance faults in a cooler that was wired dry.
inspection_fails: No duct seal where a conduit leaves a hot attic and enters a walk-in cooler — 300.7(A).
Sealant not identified for use with the conductor insulation installed.
Long sun-exposed run with no expansion or expansion-deflection fitting where movement is expected — 300.7(B).
Panel dripping water in August: unsealed raceway from a sun-baked exterior wall into the air-conditioned space.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer calls the 300.7 seal 'waterproofing' and reaches for an explosionproof sealing fitting. Both are the wrong subjects: keeping moisture from reaching live parts is 300.5(G), and explosionproof seals belong to Article 501 hazardous locations. 300.7(A) is a condensation seal — fill the raceway with an approved material at the temperature boundary to stop the air circulation.

tables.caption: Three seals that are not the same seal
rows: Warm air circulating to a colder section
Flame and gas passage in classified locations

figures.alt: Two wall crossings side by side: a conduit sealed with approved material at the temperature boundary with the warm air stopped, and an unsealed conduit with condensation drops forming on the cooled side.
figures.caption: Seal at the boundary — not at the box, not at the far end.

page_quiz.question: A conduit runs from a hot attic into a walk-in cooler and drips water at the box. What was missed?
choices: A 300.7(A) seal at the temperature boundary
page_quiz.explain_plain: Where a raceway passes between very different temperatures, 300.7(A) requires it to be filled with an approved material to stop warm air circulating into the cold section and condensing.

page_quiz.question: The 300.7(A) seal exists to:
choices: Keep rain out of the raceway
Stop the circulation of warm air to a colder section
page_quiz.explain_plain: It is a condensation seal: it prevents circulation of warm air to a colder section of the raceway. It is not the 300.5(G) moisture seal or an Article 501 explosionproof seal.

page_quiz.question: A long raceway run is expected to expand and contract with temperature swings. 300.7(B) requires:
page_quiz.explain_plain: 300.7(B): expansion, expansion-deflection or deflection fittings are required where thermal expansion or contraction is expected.

sections.title: Securing and supporting — general
sections.plain_explanation:
Raceways, cables and enclosures must be secured in place and supported at the intervals their own article requires — 300.11 is the general rule, and each wiring method's article carries its own numbers (see the table).
• Nothing hangs off something else's support. Raceways and cables may not be used to support other raceways, cables or equipment unless the rule for that method specifically allows it.
• Cable may not rest on, or be tied to, the ceiling grid or its support wires. In a fire-rated ceiling assembly the support must be independent of the ceiling, so the wiring does not come down when the ceiling does.
• One narrow 2020 exception: Class 2 control cable may be supported by the raceway that carries power to the equipment that cable controls — and only that equipment.
When in doubt, support it yourself: your own strap, on structure, at the spacing in the method's article.
sections.on_the_job: When in doubt, support it yourself: your own strap, on structure, at the spacing in the method's article (334.30 for NM, 330.30 for MC, 358.30 for EMT, 352.30 for PVC). Never lay cable on a ceiling tile or tie it to a sprinkler pipe. On a Winter Park bakery build-out, Sharma's 3/4 in EMT home runs took straps within 3 ft of the panel and every box, then at least every 10 ft. The write-up on that job was the thermostat cable another trade zip-tied to our EMT: their cable, our raceway, one violation under 300.11.
sections.edition_note:
NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 300.11: Class 3 control cable can now be supported by the power raceway for the equipment it controls. In 2020, only Class 2 cable got that allowance. A raceway carrying power to equipment can hold up Class 2 or 3 control cable that serves only that same equipment (300.11(C)(2)).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: A run that is not supported sags onto sharp edges, pulls sideways on terminations and works its connections loose over years of thermal cycling. In a fire, the ceiling grid is expected to fail — anything tied to it falls into the egress path and onto firefighters. Supporting from structure keeps the electrical system where it was inspected, for the life of the building.
inspection_fails: MC cable draped across the ceiling grid, resting on tiles — supported by nothing (300.11, 330.30).
NM stapled at 7 ft intervals in the attic — 4-1/2 ft is the maximum spacing (334.30).
EMT with no strap within 3 ft of the box it enters (358.30).
Low-voltage cable zip-tied to a sprinkler pipe for support.
Cable tied to ceiling support wires above a fire-rated corridor ceiling — support must be independent.
sections.exam_trap: The tempting wrong answer: “The ceiling wires hold the ceiling, so they can hold the cable.” Ceiling support wires hold tiles, not wiring. Above a fire-rated ceiling, cable support must be independent of the ceiling assembly — and everywhere else, cable still may not rest on the grid or hang from its wires.

tables.caption: Support numbers live in each method's article
tables.note: PVC spacing grows with conduit size — see Table 352.30.

figures.alt: Top panel: an EMT run strapped to structure within 3 feet of a box and at 10 foot intervals. Bottom panel: a ceiling section where one cable hangs from an independent support wire to structure with a green check, and another cable tied to a ceiling grid wire with a red X.
figures.caption: Support from structure: strap spacing on the run, independent wires at the ceiling.

page_quiz.question: EMT must be fastened within ___ of each box and supported at intervals not exceeding ___.
page_quiz.explain_plain: 358.30: securely fastened within 3 ft of each box or termination, and supported at intervals not exceeding 10 ft.

page_quiz.question: NM cable support intervals may not exceed:
page_quiz.explain_plain: 334.30: NM is secured and supported at intervals not exceeding 4-1/2 ft, and within 12 in of every box, cabinet and fitting.

page_quiz.question: Above a fire-rated ceiling, wiring must be supported:
page_quiz.explain_plain: 300.11 requires support independent of the fire-rated ceiling assembly, so the wiring stays up when the ceiling comes down.

nec2023_change.change: Class 3 control cable can now be supported by the power raceway for the equipment it controls. In 2020, only Class 2 cable got that allowance. A raceway carrying power to equipment can hold up Class 2 or 3 control cable that serves only that same equipment (300.11(C)(2)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 300.11 Raceways supporting control cables

sections.title: Free conductor length at boxes
sections.plain_explanation:
At every outlet, junction and switch point, leave at least 6 in of free conductor, measured from where the conductor comes out of its raceway or cable sheath.
• At least 6 in of free conductor at the point, measured from where it emerges from the raceway or sheath.
• Where the box opening is smaller than 8 in in any direction, the conductors also have to stick out of the opening by at least 3 in, so devices can be made up and folded back without fighting short wires.
• Conductors that pass straight through a box without a splice or termination are not counted by this rule.
The rule applies at switch points too — a switch loop made up short is the same violation as a short receptacle tail.
sections.on_the_job: Strip and make up with the full 6 in in hand. If you are short, the fix is a bigger pull or a re-pull — not a wire nut buried with 2 in stubs. Leave the same working length on the spare conductors you cap off.
sections.figure_idea: Side view of a single-gang box with 6 in of conductor looped out, and a 3 in dimension from the box opening.

nec2023_change.change: It's settled: the 6 inches of free conductor at a box can be spliced or unspliced, so a short conductor can be pieced out with a pigtail. The 6 inches of free conductor at each outlet, junction or switch point can now be spliced or unspliced.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 300.14 6 inches of free conductor

sections.why_it_exists: Short conductors are a slow failure: devices get made up under tension, splices sit at the edge of the box where they chafe, and the next electrician cannot re-make a connection without re-pulling the whole run. The extra length is working room and service life, not waste — it is what lets a device be pulled out, tested and replaced years later.
inspection_fails: Wire nuts made up on 2 in stubs at a receptacle — no working length to fold the device back.
Conductors cut flush at the cable sheath, so nothing reaches out of the box opening.
A switch loop with tails too short to pull the switch out of the box for testing.
Spare conductors in a junction box snipped short instead of capped at full length.
sections.exam_trap: Measure the 6 in from the back of the box, or from the connector. Wrong start point, short wires. The measurement starts where the conductor emerges from its raceway or cable sheath. And the 3 in past the opening does not replace the 6 in — on a small box you owe both.

tables.caption: The two measurements in 300.14
rows: Where the conductor leaves the raceway or sheath
The box opening, where the opening is under 8 in in any direction
A conductor passing straight through, no splice or termination

figures.alt: Side view of a single-gang box in a wall: conductors leave the cable sheath inside the box, loop out of the opening, with a 6 in dimension from the sheath exit to the conductor end and a 3 in dimension past the box opening.
figures.caption: Free conductor: 6 in to work with, 3 in out of the opening.

page_quiz.question: How much free conductor is required at each outlet, junction and switch point?
page_quiz.explain_plain: At least 6 in, measured from where the conductor emerges from its raceway or cable sheath.

page_quiz.question: The box opening is 4 in wide. How far must the conductors extend past the opening?
choices: They only need to reach the opening
page_quiz.explain_plain: Where the opening is smaller than 8 in in any direction, at least 3 in must extend out of the opening — on top of the 6 in of free conductor.

page_quiz.question: A conductor passes straight through a junction box with no splice or termination. Does 300.14 set its length?
choices: No — pass-through conductors are not counted by this rule
Yes — it must loop once in the box
page_quiz.explain_plain: Conductors that pass through a box without a splice or termination are not counted by 300.14.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 300.14: It's settled: the 6 inches of free conductor at a box can be spliced or unspliced, so a short conductor can be pieced out with a pigtail. The 6 inches of free conductor at each outlet, junction or switch point can now be spliced or unspliced.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

sections.title: A box or fitting at each splice, outlet and junction
sections.plain_explanation:
Where the wiring method is conduit, tubing, Type AC cable, Type MC cable, Type MI cable, nonmetallic-sheathed cable or another cable method, a box or conduit body has to be installed at each of these points — unless one of the exceptions in 300.15(A) through (L) permits otherwise for that case:
• each conductor splice point
• each outlet point, switch point and junction point
• each termination point and pull point
A fitting identified for the use may be used in place of a box or conduit body where conductors are not spliced or terminated inside the fitting, and that fitting has to stay accessible after installation unless it is listed for concealed installation. Boxes themselves have to stay accessible under 314.29, without tearing the building apart. A joint made in open air, in a wall cavity, or inside a raceway run, with no exception behind it, is not a joint the next electrician — or an inspector — can ever find.
sections.on_the_job: Plan box locations while the walls are open. If a splice has to exist, it gets a box with a cover that stays reachable after finishes go on. On a Sharma rough-in, a home run that comes up short of the panel does not get spliced inside the stud bay and buried — it gets a junction box where it can be reached, or the run is re-pulled. The box costs minutes; the buried splice costs a failed inspection and a callback.

nec2023_change.change: A change from one wiring method to another, like MC cable to EMT, is now on the list of spots requiring a box, conduit body or fitting. A box, conduit body or identified fitting is now required where one wiring method changes to another, such as MC cable to EMT.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 300.15 Boxes at wiring method changes

sections.why_it_exists: Splices are where circuits fail first: a loose connection in open air arcs against framing and nobody can find it later. The box gives the splice a listed, contained home and keeps it reachable for the life of the building. A buried joint passes rough-in because nobody sees it, then hides a fault for thirty years of service calls.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: "an identified fitting can always stand in for a box." Only where no conductors are spliced or terminated inside it — a fitting used as a splice point is not the exception, it is the violation. And a box that gets buried behind tile still fails: accessibility under 314.29 is part of the rule.
inspection_fails: Splice buried in a wall cavity with no box — found at trim, when the circuit is dead and the wall is closed.
Junction box drywalled over with no access — a box that cannot be reached fails 314.29.
Conductors spliced inside a plain fitting that is neither a box nor a conduit body.
Fitting used in place of a box where conductors are terminated inside it — the identified-fitting allowance ends where splices and terminations begin.

tables.caption: Points that require a box, conduit body or fitting
rows: An identified fitting may serve instead

figures.alt: Wall run with a junction box at a splice point, an outlet box and a switch box on one conduit run, and below it a buried splice inside a wall cavity crossed out in red.
figures.caption: Every splice, outlet, switch, junction, termination and pull point gets a box.

page_quiz.question: A fitting identified for the use may be used in place of a box at a point where:
choices: No conductors are spliced or terminated inside it
It will be buried in concrete
The wiring method is NM cable
page_quiz.explain_plain: The fitting allowance in 300.15 holds only where conductors are not spliced or terminated inside the fitting.

page_quiz.question: A junction box is installed for a splice, then drywalled over with no access. The result:
choices: Fine, if the splice is taped
Fails — boxes must remain accessible without removing building finish
Fails only if the circuit is over 20 A
page_quiz.explain_plain: 300.15 puts the box in; 314.29 keeps it accessible. A buried box is a buried splice with extra steps.

page_quiz.question: Which of these does NOT, by itself, require a box or conduit body under 300.15?
choices: Conductors passing straight through a raceway with no splice, outlet or junction
page_quiz.explain_plain: The box list in 300.15 is splice, outlet, switch, junction, termination and pull points. A straight pass-through is none of them.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 300.15: A change from one wiring method to another, like MC cable to EMT, is now on the list of spots requiring a box, conduit body or fitting. A box, conduit body or identified fitting is now required where one wiring method changes to another, such as MC cable to EMT.

sections.title: Finish the raceway before the wire goes in
sections.plain_explanation:
A raceway system is installed complete — runs finished, boxes set, fittings in place — before the conductors are pulled into it (300.18(A)).
• Cut ends are reamed or otherwise finished so no sharp edge waits inside to skin insulation during the pull. The reaming rule itself lives in the wiring-method articles — 344.28 for rigid metal conduit, 358.28 for EMT — not in 300.18.
• Exception: short sections of raceway used only to protect conductors or cable assemblies from physical damage do not have to be installed complete before the conductors or cables are installed (300.18(A) Exception).
• The everyday nipple between two enclosures still follows its own fill rules — 60 percent for a nipple 24 in or shorter (Chapter 9, Table 1).
Pulling wire into a half-built run and 'finishing around it' damages insulation where nobody can see it.
sections.on_the_job: Walk the run with a flashlight before the pull: every coupling tight, every end reamed, bushings on. The time to find a burr is before 200 ft of THHN is sitting in the pipe. On a tenant rough-in, that walk is the foreman's last check before the pull crew starts: the run that is short one coupling gets finished empty, not threaded.
sections.figure_idea: Conduit run in two states: complete with reamed ends and bushings, wire spool staged (ready); versus a gap in the run with wire already threaded through it (crossed out).
sections.why_it_exists: The pull is the roughest hour of a conductor's life. A burr, a missing coupling or a sharp box edge skins insulation under pulling tension, and the damage hides inside the finished run until it becomes a ground fault or an arc. A complete, reamed raceway is the only one that cannot hurt the wire.
inspection_fails: Conductors already pulled into an incomplete run, with a coupling being added around the installed wire (300.18(A)).
EMT cut end left unreamed; conductor insulation skinned during the pull (358.28).
Wire threaded through a gap in the run to save time, raceway finished around the conductors afterward (300.18(A)).
sections.exam_trap: The trap: "300.18 requires reaming." It does not — 300.18 requires the complete raceway before conductors. Reaming lives in the wiring-method articles, 344.28 and 358.28. The exam pairs the two ideas and credits the answer that keeps each rule in its own section.

figures.alt: The same conduit run in two states: complete with tight couplings, reamed ends and bushings with the wire spool staged beside it, versus a run with a gap in the middle and wire already threaded through it, crossed out.
figures.caption: Complete, reamed and bushed first — then the wire goes in.

page_quiz.question: Conductors may be pulled into a raceway when:
choices: Half the run is up, to save a trip
The raceway system is installed complete
The wire is needed to hold the couplings in line
It is the last day of rough-in
page_quiz.explain_plain: 300.18(A) requires the raceway system to be installed complete before conductors are installed in it.

page_quiz.question: The exception to 'complete before conductors' covers:
choices: Short sections used only to protect conductors or cables from physical damage
page_quiz.explain_plain: Short sections of raceway used solely for physical protection do not have to be installed complete first.

page_quiz.question: The requirement to ream cut EMT ends is found in:
page_quiz.explain_plain: Reaming EMT is 358.28; rigid metal conduit is 344.28. Section 300.18 covers the complete raceway, not reaming.

sections.title: Firestopping penetrations of rated construction
sections.plain_explanation:
Where wiring passes through a fire-rated floor, wall or ceiling, the opening around it has to be firestopped with an approved system so fire and smoke do not travel through the penetration. The electrical work does not end at the conduit — the annular space around it is part of the rated assembly's performance.
• The system is matched to the assembly: the construction type and fire rating, the penetrating item — conduit, cable, tray — and the size of the opening all come from the system's listing.
• Ordinary expanding foam from the truck is not a firestop system unless it is listed as one for that assembly and penetration.
• Every penetration counts. One unsealed conduit is a hole in the rating of the whole wall.
sections.on_the_job: On commercial and multi-family work, plan the firestop with the run: listed system for the assembly, the raceway type and the opening size, installed before the wall is signed off. Photograph it — the next inspector cannot see inside a closed wall either. A typical Sharma multifamily punch item: a bank of six conduits through a rated demising wall between units, each penetration sealed with the system listed for that wall — not one tube of generic red caulk spread over all six.
sections.figure_idea: Rated wall section with a conduit penetration sealed by a red listed firestop system, callout 'system matched to assembly — not generic foam'.
sections.florida_note: Firestop systems are assembly-specific; Florida inspectors on rated multi-family and commercial work check them by listing, not by color.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: Rated walls and floors buy time — time for people to get out and for firefighters to work. Fire and smoke hunt for the holes, and a conduit penetration is a ready-made chimney between floors and units. Firestopping restores the barrier at the one place the trades had to break it.
inspection_fails: Conduit through a rated demising wall sealed with ordinary expanding foam — not a listed firestop system (300.21).
Annular space left open around a conduit bank penetrating a rated floor (300.21).
Firestop system listed for a concrete floor installed in a wood-frame wall assembly (300.21).
Penetration stuffed with insulation scraps and smeared with caulk — no system at all (300.21).
sections.exam_trap: The trap: 'If it is red, it is firestop.' Color is not a listing. Generic foam or caulk fails even in red. The right answer is always a listed, approved system matched to the assembly, the penetrating item and the opening size.

page_quiz.question: What makes a firestop acceptable at a penetration of a rated wall?
choices: A listed, approved system matched to the assembly, the penetrating item and the opening
page_quiz.explain_plain: 300.21 requires openings around penetrations to be firestopped with an approved method that maintains the fire resistance rating — and the system is listed for a specific assembly and penetration.

page_quiz.question: Ordinary expanding foam around a conduit in a rated wall is:
choices: Acceptable only if listed as a firestop system for that assembly and penetration

Filled with any leftover material on site
Sealed only where the inspector can see it
page_quiz.explain_plain: 300.21 treats the opening around the penetration as part of the assembly. An open annulus lets fire and smoke straight through the rating.

sections.title: Wiring in ducts, plenums and other air-handling spaces
sections.plain_explanation:
Spaces made for moving environmental air — ducts, plenums and the space above a ceiling used as a return-air plenum — restrict what wiring may run there and how, because anything burning or smoldering in that space feeds the whole building's air. The section splits the spaces three ways:
• Ducts for dust, loose stock or vapor removal (300.22(A)): no wiring system of any type inside.
• Ducts or plenums specifically fabricated to transport environmental air (300.22(B)): equipment only where it is necessary for direct action on, or sensing of, the contained air. The wiring methods are Type MI cable; Type MC cable with a smooth or corrugated impervious metal sheath and no overall nonmetallic covering; EMT; flexible metallic tubing; IMC; and RMC without a nonmetallic covering. Flexible metal conduit up to 4 ft may connect physically adjustable equipment.
• Other spaces used for environmental air (300.22(C)) — the space above a suspended ceiling or below a raised floor that carries return air: metal raceways such as EMT, IMC, RMC and flexible metal conduit, Type AC cable, Type MC cable without a nonmetallic cover, and, where accessible, surface metal raceway or metal wireway with metal covers. Equipment needs a metal enclosure, or a nonmetallic enclosure listed for the use.
• NM cable is on neither list. It does not go into a plenum ceiling.
sections.on_the_job: The field trap is the plenum ceiling that looks like an ordinary ceiling: before you run a method through a ceiling space on commercial work, ask whether that space is a return-air plenum. If it is, the method list shrinks — when in doubt, ask the AHJ before rough-in, not at inspection. On a Sharma tenant fit-out, the lighting home runs above that ceiling go in EMT or jacket-free MC. The NM whip that passes in a house fails here.
sections.figure_idea: Reflected ceiling plan with the return-air plenum shaded and two wiring methods shown: one allowed routing tagged, one barred routing crossed out.
sections.why_it_exists: Return air touches every room the system serves. A fault that smolders in a plenum ceiling is blown building-wide as smoke long before flames show anywhere. Metal wiring methods and listed enclosures keep fuel out of the airstream, and the fabricated-duct list is the shortest because that wiring sits directly in the air path.
inspection_fails: NM cable run above a return-air plenum ceiling — NM is not a 300.22(C) wiring method.
Jacketed MC cable installed in a fabricated duct — 300.22(B) requires an impervious metal sheath with no overall nonmetallic covering.
Equipment inside a fabricated duct that neither acts on nor senses the contained air.
Cable in a plenum space secured with ordinary cable ties not listed for use in the space.
Nonmetallic junction box, not listed for air-handling use, installed in a plenum ceiling (300.22(C)).
sections.exam_trap: Two wrong answers mirror each other. One treats the space above a suspended ceiling like a fabricated duct and applies only the short 300.22(B) list — that space is a 300.22(C) other space, with its own wider list. The other says NM cable is fine above any ceiling — NM is on neither list, so it fails in both spaces.

page_quiz.explain_plain: 300.22(C)(1) permits metal raceways, Type AC and jacket-free Type MC. NM cable is not on the list.

page_quiz.question: Inside a fabricated supply-air duct, a damper motor that acts directly on the contained air may be wired with:

page_quiz.explain_plain: The 300.22(B) list is the short one: MI, impervious-sheath MC without a jacket, EMT, FMT, IMC and RMC. AC cable is a (C)-space method, not a fabricated-duct method.

sections.title: Wiring in exit enclosures
sections.plain_explanation:
Exit enclosures — the protected stair towers and exit passageways people escape through — may contain only the wiring that serves the exit enclosure itself. The 2020 text: where an exit enclosure is required to be separated from the building, only electrical wiring methods serving equipment permitted by the authority having jurisdiction in the exit enclosure shall be installed within the exit enclosure. Ordinary branch circuits passing through a stair tower on their way somewhere else do not belong there — not even pulled inside a shared conduit.
• What belongs: the tower's own lighting and exit signs, and equipment the AHJ permits there — fire alarm devices, security and public address systems, and fire department emergency communications are the examples the Life Safety Code annex gives.
• A panelboard or junction box for other floors does not become permitted because the tower is convenient space; it takes the AHJ's documented permission.
• This section was new in the 2020 NEC, which is why older study material and older habits do not mention it. Its informational note points to NFPA 101, Life Safety Code, 7.1.3.2.1(10)(b).
sections.on_the_job: On multi-family and commercial work, route around the stair tower by default. If a run must enter it, stop and check what it serves before it goes in. The tempting shortcut on a Florida mid-rise is the tower shaft for a water-heater or corridor circuit — that is exactly the run 300.25 removes. The tower keeps its own lighting and exit-sign circuits; everything else goes around, even when around is longer. If the design truly needs equipment in the tower, get the AHJ's permission documented before rough-in, not at final.
sections.figure_idea: Building section of a stair tower with a foreign branch circuit shown re-routed around the enclosure and only the tower's own lighting circuit inside.

nec2023_change.change: A new exception lets the egress light outside a stair tower's exterior door run off the wiring inside the stair. The rule itself now hinges on the building code's fire-resistance rating. New exception: the egress light over the stair's exterior exit door can be fed from the stair's own wiring.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 300.25 Exit stair towers

sections.why_it_exists: The stair tower is the one part of the building that must stay usable while everything else is on fire. Foreign wiring brings foreign fuel, extra penetrations through the rated walls, and a chance for a fault in a through-circuit to start a fire inside the escape route itself. Keeping the tower's wiring to the tower's own equipment keeps the protected path protected for its full rating.
inspection_fails: Corridor or water-heater branch circuit piped straight through the stair tower (300.25).
Panelboard for other floors mounted in the exit enclosure without AHJ permission.
Foreign conductors sharing a conduit that passes through the tower.
Junction box in the tower serving loads outside it.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is 'the circuit is in EMT, so it may pass through.' 300.25 is not about the wiring method — it is about what the wiring serves, and a foreign branch circuit in conduit is still foreign. The second trap is age: the section was new in 2020, so a 2017-based answer that ignores it is wrong.

sections.title: Conductors for general wiring
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 310 is about the conductors themselves: what they are made of, how they are insulated, and — most used of all — how much current they may carry. The ampacity work lives in 310.12 for dwelling services and feeders, 310.15 for correction and adjustment, and Table 310.16 for the ampacity values themselves. Termination temperature limits live back in 110.14(C) in Chapter 1; this article hands you the number, Chapter 1 tells you which column you may actually use.
• The metals: copper fills the left of Table 310.16; aluminum and copper-clad aluminum share the right-hand columns. CCA reads the aluminum values, never the copper ones.
• Dwelling services and feeders (310.12): a single-phase dwelling service, or a feeder carrying the whole dwelling load, rated 100 A through 400 A, may be sized at 83 percent of the rating — a 200 A service takes 2/0 copper or 4/0 aluminum.
• Correction and adjustment (310.15): ambient heat over 30 °C, and more than three current-carrying conductors in one raceway, both cut the ampacity before the breaker is picked.
• The cap (240.4(D)): whatever the table allows, copper 14, 12 and 10 AWG stop at 15, 20 and 30 A breakers; aluminum and CCA 12 and 10 AWG stop at 15 and 25 A.
sections.on_the_job: Start every sizing question here in this order: load, then Table 310.16 column allowed by the terminations, then correction/adjustment in 310.15, then the small-conductor caps in 240.4(D) from Chapter 2. Worked Sharma example: a 200 A house service. The dwelling rule (310.12) sizes the service conductors at 83 percent, so 2/0 copper THHN — 175 A in the 75 °C column — carries the 200 A service. Run that same 2/0 as a partial-load feeder to a garage subpanel and the 83 percent gift disappears: full Table 310.16 value, no shortcut.
sections.figure_idea: Flowchart with four boxes: Load -> Table 310.16 -> 310.15 correction/adjustment -> 240.4(D) cap.

nec2023_change.change: Parallel conductor rules were rewritten for clarity, supply-side bonding jumpers joined the list of conductors that must match, and both temperature correction and adjustment now clearly apply. Supply-side bonding jumpers run in parallel now have to match each other in length, material, size, insulation and termination (310.10(G)(2)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 310.10 Parallel conductors

sections.why_it_exists: A conductor is a heater that happens to carry current. Push it past its ampacity and the insulation ages, cracks, and finally fails against a stud or a box wall. Article 310 matches the wire to the load and to the place it runs through, so the insulation outlives the building.
sections.exam_trap: The exam trap is reading the 90 °C column as the answer. THHN 12 AWG shows 30 A there, but the terminations cap the usable value at the 60 or 75 °C column, and 240.4(D) caps the breaker at 20 A. The 90 °C column is only the starting point for derating.
inspection_fails: 12 AWG copper on a 30 A breaker — 'the 90 °C column says 30 A' (the 240.4(D) cap is 20 A).
CCA sized out of the copper columns of Table 310.16.
The 310.12 83 percent rule used on a partial-load feeder to a subpanel.
Four current-carrying conductors in one raceway with no 310.15 adjustment.

page_quiz.question: A 200 A single-phase dwelling service, copper, carrying the whole load. Smallest service conductor under 310.12?
page_quiz.explain_plain: Table 310.12 allows 2/0 copper for a 200 A dwelling service at 83 percent of the rating.

page_quiz.question: 12 AWG THHN copper, 75 °C terminations, no derating needed. Largest breaker?
page_quiz.explain_plain: The 75 °C ampacity is 25 A, but 240.4(D) caps 12 AWG copper at a 20 A breaker.

page_quiz.question: A CCA conductor takes its ampacity from which Table 310.16 columns?
page_quiz.explain_plain: Copper-clad aluminum shares the aluminum columns of Table 310.16; it is never sized as copper.

figures.alt: Flowchart of the four gates for sizing a conductor: the load, Table 310.16 with the column the terminations allow, correction and adjustment in 310.15, and the 240.4(D) breaker cap, with a worked strip showing 12 AWG THHN capped at a 20 A breaker and a 200 A dwelling service on 2/0 copper.

sections.title: Conductor minimums — size, material, stranding
sections.plain_explanation: This section sets the floor for building wire. The smallest conductor for branch circuits and feeders is 14 AWG copper or 12 AWG aluminum or copper-clad aluminum — which is why there is no 14 AWG CCA branch-circuit wire in 2020 work. Conductors are copper, aluminum, or copper-clad aluminum, and the material decides which ampacity column and which termination rules apply. Conductors 8 AWG and larger installed in raceways are stranded. Smaller conductors and special circuits (fixture wires, control and signaling circuits, and the other cases other articles govern) follow their own articles — this floor is for general wiring.
sections.on_the_job: Ordering rule that follows from this page: a '14 AWG' line on a takeoff means copper. If the job is CCA, the smallest branch-circuit reel on the truck is 12 AWG — and per S-10 it lands on a 15A breaker, not a 20A.
sections.sharma_note: S-10: copper by default; CCA one size up. This section is where the 'no 14 AWG CCA' rule lives.
sections.figure_idea: Three reels labeled by material with their minimum branch-circuit sizes: copper 14 AWG, aluminum 12 AWG, CCA 12 AWG.

nec2023_change.change: Copper-clad aluminum got its own material rule in 310.3(B): an AA-8000 series aluminum core wrapped in copper that makes up 10 percent or more of the cross-section. Copper-clad aluminum (CCA) now has its own item in 310.3(B): the aluminum core has to be AA-8000 series alloy.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 310.3 Copper-clad aluminum conductors

sections.why_it_exists: Wire that is too small for its breaker overheats in the wall, and the wrong metal on the wrong lug loosens as it heats and cools. The floor in 310.3 keeps the smallest branch-circuit conductor big enough for its overcurrent device and its terminations — and it is written by material, because copper, aluminum and CCA do not carry current the same way at the same size. The material also decides the termination rules and the ampacity column, so a size that is legal in copper is not automatically legal in aluminum or CCA.
inspection_fails: 14 AWG CCA pulled for a branch circuit — CCA starts at 12 AWG (310.3).
12 AWG aluminum or CCA landed on a 20 A breaker — it is capped at 15 A (240.4(D)).
Solid 8 AWG installed in a raceway — 8 AWG and larger in raceways must be stranded.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is '14 AWG is the minimum, whatever the metal.' In 2020 work there is no 14 AWG CCA branch-circuit conductor: the minimum is 14 AWG copper or 12 AWG aluminum or CCA. The follow-up trap is landing 12 AWG CCA on a 20 A breaker because '12 is 20 A' — under S-10 and 240.4(D) it is a 15 A conductor.

page_quiz.explain_plain: 310.3 requires conductors 8 AWG and larger in raceways to be stranded.

sections.title: The dwelling 83% rule for services and whole-load feeders
sections.plain_explanation:
For a single-phase dwelling service rated 100A through 400A that carries the entire load of the house, the service conductors may be sized at 83% of the service rating instead of at full Table 310.16 ampacity. The same allowance covers a feeder that carries the entire dwelling load — the classic case is the feeder from an outside meter-main to the inside main panel.
• The rule covers a one-family dwelling, or an individual dwelling unit of a two-family or multifamily dwelling.
• It does not apply to a partial-load feeder — a feeder to a garage subpanel is sized at full value.
• Table 310.12 may be used directly only where no adjustment or correction factors are required. Where factors are required, size from Table 310.16 with the factors applied — and the result may not be smaller than the 83% minimum.
• Feeders are not required to be larger than the service conductors (310.12(B), (C)).
The full Table 310.12 is in the tables below: the service or whole-load feeder rating, then the conductor it permits.
sections.on_the_job: The pair Sharma uses daily: a 200A house service is 2/0 copper or 4/0 aluminum where this rule applies; a 150A service is 1 AWG copper or 2/0 aluminum. A feeder to a garage subpanel carries only part of the load, so it is sized at full value from Table 310.16 — no 83%.
sections.figure_idea: One-line of a house: meter-main outside, main panel inside, the feeder between them labeled 'whole load — 83% can apply'; a second feeder to a garage labeled 'partial load — full size'.
sections.why_it_exists: A whole house never runs everything at once — cooking, cooling, laundry and water heating cycle on and off. Decades of demand data sit behind the 83%: a whole dwelling load is predictable in a way a single feeder is not. That is why the discount exists only where the conductor carries the entire load, where the diversity is real.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer sizes the garage subpanel feeder at 83% because 'it is a dwelling feeder.' The rule follows the load, not the building: only a service or feeder carrying the entire dwelling load gets 83%. A partial-load feeder is full size from Table 310.16.
inspection_fails: 83% sizing used on a partial-load feeder to a garage subpanel.
Table 310.12 used where derating factors apply, without the Table 310.16 check.
83% applied to a service under 100A or over 400A.
83% applied to a three-phase or commercial service.

sections.title: Ampacity correction (temperature) and adjustment (bundling)
sections.plain_explanation:
Table 310.16 assumes no more than three current-carrying conductors together and a 30°C (86°F) surrounding temperature. When reality is hotter, or more conductors share a raceway or cable, the ampacity goes down: an ambient correction factor for temperature, and an adjustment factor for the count of current-carrying conductors — 80% for 4 to 6, 70% for 7 to 9, 50% for 10 to 20, 45% for 21 to 30, 40% for 31 to 40, and 35% for 41 or more. Equipment grounding conductors do not count, and a neutral carrying only unbalanced load usually does not count either. You may start the math from the insulation rating (the 90°C column for THHN, say) as long as the final number stays under the termination column and the method's own limit.
Ambient correction factors (Table 310.15(B)(1)), above the 30°C base:
• At 31–35°C — 0.91 (60°C), 0.94 (75°C), 0.96 (90°C)
• At 36–40°C — 0.82 / 0.88 / 0.91
• At 41–45°C — 0.71 / 0.82 / 0.87
• At 46–50°C — 0.58 / 0.75 / 0.82
• At 51–55°C — 0.41 / 0.67 / 0.76
• At 56–60°C — 60°C column: — (no longer corrects) / 0.58 / 0.71
• At 61–65°C — — / 0.47 / 0.65
• At 66–70°C — — / 0.33 / 0.58
Where both apply, the factors multiply — count and temperature together.
2020 rooftop rule: raceways or cables exposed to sunlight on or above rooftops and less than 7/8 in. above the roof add 33°C (60°F) to the outdoor ambient (310.15(B)(2)); Type XHHW-2 is exempt.
sections.on_the_job: Count honestly on a home-run bundle: three 12/2 NM cables bundled over 24 in are six current-carrying conductors, not three circuits at full ampacity. Hot Florida attics are the ambient case Sharma hits most — see the attic tip AH-07. Worked example: 12 AWG THHN starts at 30 A in the 90°C column. In a 50°C attic the correction is 0.82, giving 24.6 A — still enough for its 20 A breaker. Run as NM cable, the same conductor is capped at its 60°C table value of 20 A before the 240.4(D) cap is even reached, so a single attic circuit rarely changes; a bundle of home runs, where the count factor stacks on the temperature factor, is where the answer moves.
sections.figure_idea: Bar chart: one raceway at 3, 6 and 9 current-carrying conductors with the 100%, 80% and 70% factors marked.
sections.florida_note: Florida attics routinely run far above 30°C in summer; that is a design condition here, not an edge case.

nec2023_change.change: Raceways and cables in direct sun now escape the 60°F rooftop adder once they sit 3/4 inch above the roof, down from 7/8 inch. The ambient correction tables were also renumbered. Raceways or cables in direct sunlight less than 3/4 inch above a roof get 60°F added to the outdoor temperature (310.15(B)(2)).

sections.why_it_exists: A conductor heats from the current it carries. In a 50°C attic it starts halfway toward its insulation limit before any load flows, and bundled conductors heat each other. Correction and adjustment put the margin back before the insulation cooks.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is applying only one factor: derating for the hot attic but forgetting the bundle, or counting the conductors but using the room-temperature factor. Where both conditions exist, the factors multiply. The second trap counts the equipment ground as current-carrying — it never counts.
inspection_fails: Home runs bundled over 24 in with no adjustment factor applied (310.15(C)(1)).
Ampacity figured at a 30°C ambient for a run through a Florida attic (Table 310.15(B)(1)).
Rooftop raceway in direct sun, less than 7/8 in above the roof, with no 33°C (60°F) adder (310.15(B)(2)).
Derated ampacity allowed to exceed the termination column value at the breaker (110.14(C)).
