sections.title: Table 310.16 — how to read the ampacity table
sections.plain_explanation:
Table 310.16 gives the allowable ampacity of insulated conductors rated up to 2000 V, with not more than three current-carrying conductors in a raceway, cable or earth, at an ambient of 30 °C (86 °F). Read it in four steps:
• Size and metal. Copper is on the left. Aluminum and copper-clad aluminum share the right-hand columns.
• Temperature column: 60, 75 or 90 °C. The insulation sets the highest column you may start from. The terminations set the column you finish in (110.14(C)): circuits of 100 A or less, or 14 through 1 AWG, use 60 °C unless the equipment is listed and marked for 75 °C; over 100 A or larger than 1 AWG, 75 °C.
• Correct and adjust. Hotter than 30 °C, or more than three current-carrying conductors? Apply 310.15(B) and 310.15(C)(1), normally starting from the 90 °C value.
• Check the breaker cap. 240.4(D) limits small conductors whatever the table says: copper 14, 12 and 10 AWG at 15, 20 and 30 A; aluminum or CCA 12 and 10 AWG at 15 and 25 A.
sections.on_the_job: A Sharma home run: two 20 A circuits of 12 AWG THHN copper in one EMT through a 104 °F mechanical space, so four current-carrying conductors. 30 A (90 °C) × 0.91 × 0.80 = 21.8 A. That is above the 20 A breaker and below the 25 A 75 °C value, so the 20 A breaker stands. The same circuit in NM cable is held to the 60 °C result (20 A) by 334.80. On a commercial tenant job, a 100 A feeder on 3 AWG copper THHN works with 75 °C lugs (100 A) but not at 60 °C (85 A), so read the lug marking before you pull wire.
sections.sharma_note: S-10: branch circuits are copper by default — 14 AWG on 15A, 12 AWG on 20A. When CCA is used, go one AWG larger (12 on 15A, 10 on 20A) because Table 310.16 rates CCA in the aluminum column. Terminations must be marked for the conductor (110.14); wire connectors and lugs need AL-CU / CU-AL marking, CU-only connectors are not rated for CCA, and push-in terminals are 14 AWG solid copper only. Never backstab. The microwave circuit wire is PENDING under S-06 (12 AWG copper versus 10 AWG CCA).
sections.figure_idea: A printed Table 310.16 excerpt with the 12 AWG and 10 AWG rows highlighted, an arrow from 'CCA' into the aluminum columns, and the 240.4(D) caps written under the rows.
sections.edition_note:
NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 240.4(D)(3) / Table 240.6(A): 14 AWG copper-clad aluminum is protected at not more than 10 A, with continuous load not over 8 A, by a breaker or fuse listed and marked for 14 AWG CCA. 10 A is now a standard rating in Table 240.6(A). The 240.4(D) items renumber as (D)(1)–(D)(8).
• Table 310.16: the 2023 change sources reviewed show no change to the values in this page's tables. Confirm in a printed 2023 book.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: Every conductor heats as current flows, and insulation that runs too hot for years cracks and fails. The table keeps current within what the insulation can take. The termination rule exists because breaker and device lugs are often tested only at 60 or 75 °C. The 240.4(D) caps build margin into the small wire that runs bundled and insulated through every wall.
inspection_fails: 12 AWG on a 25 A or 30 A breaker because 'THHN is good for 30 A' (240.4(D)).
NM cable sized from the 90 °C column. 334.80 holds the result to the 60 °C value.
More than two NM cables bundled through a fire-caulked or foamed hole without derating (334.80).
CCA sized like copper. CCA reads the aluminum columns.
Aluminum or CCA landed on lugs marked CU only (110.14).
sections.exam_trap: THHN is 90 °C, so 12 AWG THHN carries 30 A? On the exam, the usable ampacity is the 75 °C or 60 °C value the terminations allow, and the breaker is still capped at 20 A by 240.4(D). The 90 °C column is only the starting point for derating. And 12 AWG aluminum is 15 A at 60 °C, not 20 A.

sections.title: CCA in every calculation — ampacity, voltage drop, fill, terminations, sizing
sections.plain_explanation:
Copper-clad aluminum is a material choice inside the same calculations, not a separate code. Run each calculation the same way; pick the CCA line where the table has one:
• (1) Ampacity — CCA reads the aluminum column of Table 310.16, with the 240.4(D) caps for aluminum. Cable-article minimums apply: the smallest CCA branch conductor in 2020 work is 12 AWG; there is no 14 AWG CCA NM.
• (2) Voltage drop — Chapter 9 Table 8 lists copper and aluminum only; there is no CCA row, so this page gives no CCA resistance for design use. A CCA figure must come from the cable maker's data for the actual product, at operating temperature — never from a resistivity-class calculation.
• (3) Terminations — follow the actual cable's identification and the marking and listing of the device, connector or lug in hand. Sources do not all state the same marking rule, so check the marking before the splice. Push-in backstab terminals are 14 AWG solid copper only: CCA is never backstabbed.
• (4) Fill — box fill (314.16) and conduit fill (Chapter 9 Tables 4 and 5) go by size and insulation, never by metal: 10 AWG CCA takes the same 2.50 cu in box allowance and the same Table 5 area as 10 AWG copper. The difference shows up one step earlier, in the bigger AWG the ampacity rule chose.
• (5) Loads and sizing — Article 220 load math does not change with metal; pick the conductor in the chosen material from Table 310.16. Whether Table 310.12's aluminum sizes may size a CCA dwelling service or whole-load feeder is unconfirmed in print — confirm before using it.
sections.on_the_job: Crew version: aluminum column, one size up. On a Marion Oaks house wired in CCA under S-10: 15 A circuits pull 12 AWG CCA, 20 A circuits pull 10 AWG CCA — check the roll before it is pulled, not at the panel. Do not use a CCA resistance from this page in a voltage-drop calculation: the calculator will not compute one until a cited 75°C source exists. Check the connector marking before the splice: if it does not say AL/CU or CC, it does not touch CCA.
sections.sharma_note: S-10 in calculation form: copper default; CCA one AWG up (12 on 15A, 10 on 20A); the microwave wire is PENDING under S-06 (12 AWG copper versus 10 AWG CCA). Sharma's CCA is Copperweld NM-B; torque CCA terminations to the printed value once — do not re-torque.
sections.figure_idea: One flow chart used five times: Load → material (Cu / Al / CCA) → column or resistance source → size → check (240.4(D) cap, fill, voltage drop), with the CCA path highlighted and the Table 8 'no CCA row' gap marked on the voltage-drop branch.
sections.florida_note: No 14 AWG CCA branch-circuit wiring in Florida 2020 work: 310.3(A) sets the minimum at 14 AWG copper or 12 AWG aluminum or copper-clad aluminum. Later editions debated 10-ampere branch circuits and 14 AWG CCA, and published sources disagree on what the 2023 edition actually adopted for 14 AWG CCA — do not rely on any later-edition 14 AWG CCA rule in 2020 work.
sections.unverified_reason: Still unverified after Mike Holt recheck (2026-11-25): Keep verified=false. Confirmed parts: CCA is read in the Al/CCA column of Table 310.16; Chapter 9 Table 8 has no CCA row; box fill (314.16(B), 2.50 in³ for 10 AWG) and Chapter 9 Tables 4/5 go by size and insulation, not metal; 310.3(A) minimum is 12 AWG Al/CCA; 334.104 NM conductors are 12 AWG and larger for Al/CCA. Still open: (1) no published 75°C resistance for the specific Copperweld NM-B product — get the manufacturer's datasheet; (2) the termination marking rule — see the CCA/UL ruling (connectors marked AL7CU/AL9CU, or CC/CU-CC per the UL guide, are the ones to look for; confirm on Product iQ for the exact product category); (3) whether Table 310.12's aluminum column says 'aluminum or copper-clad aluminum' needs a printed-2020 check; (4) the 2023 14 AWG CCA / 10A branch-circuit question needs a printed-2023 check. One edit now: delete the sentence quoting "2.46 and 1.55 ohm figures" — the page already says not to use them, so they should not appear at all.
sections.why_it_exists: CCA exists because copper is expensive: an aluminum core carries current, a copper skin takes the termination. The hazard is treating it as copper — it sizes and heats like aluminum — or inventing numbers no table gave it, above all a voltage-drop resistance.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer treats CCA as copper: '12 AWG is 12 AWG — 20 A.' CCA reads the aluminum column and takes the aluminum caps, so 12 AWG CCA is a 15 A conductor. The second trap invents a CCA resistance by splitting copper and aluminum — Table 8 has no CCA row to split.
inspection_fails: 12 AWG CCA landed on a 20 A breaker — sized as if it were copper (240.4(D)).
CCA terminated on connectors or lugs marked CU only — the marking was never checked before the splice (110.14).
CCA conductor backstabbed into a push-in terminal — those terminals are 14 AWG solid copper only.
Voltage-drop figure for a CCA run taken from an unsourced resistance instead of the cable maker's data.

sections.title: Medium-voltage conductors and cable
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 311 covers medium-voltage conductors and cable, Type MV: a single or multiconductor solid-dielectric cable rated 2,001 volts up to and including 35,000 volts, nominal. The article carries the use, installation, construction specifications and ampacities for that cable. It was new in the 2020 NEC, built from material formerly in Articles 310 and 328, and Article 328 was deleted. Sharma does not pull medium-voltage cable on ordinary work. This page exists so the book's map is complete, and so nobody cites the wrong edition's article number.
• Type MV: solid-dielectric cable, 2,001 V to 35,000 V nominal.
• The 2020 home of the MV rules: Article 311, built from Articles 310 and 328.
• Article 328 no longer exists in the 2020 book.
sections.on_the_job: If a job genuinely involves Type MV cable — systems rated over 2,000 volts, up to 35,000 volts — that is engineered, utility-coordinated work. Stop at this page and escalate to the office; do not extend house habits (NM, ordinary splices, ordinary terminations) into this article. On a Florida campus, hospital or industrial service, Sharma's part ends at the low-voltage side of the transformer unless an engineered MV scope is signed.
sections.figure_idea: Single-line of a campus feeder at medium voltage with a clear 'specialized work — engineered' tag.
sections.edition_note:
NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 311: Article 311 was renumbered and expanded as Article 315, 'Medium Voltage Conductors, Cable, Cable Joints, and Cable Terminations' (new 315.6 listing, 315.17 marking of MV joints and terminations).
• 305: Article 305, the general article for systems over 1,000 volts, is also new in the 2023 NEC. There is no Article 305 in the 2020 book.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: Medium-voltage conductors carry fault energy that ordinary 120/240 V work never sees. A bad MV splice or termination can fail explosively, and the stress grading inside an MV termination is engineered, not field-improvised. The article keeps that work inside listed construction and engineered design. The edition warning matters for the same reason: a citation to a deleted article sends the crew and the inspector to two different books.
inspection_fails: MV cable specified or cited from Article 328 on a 2020 permit set — 328 was deleted; plan review sends it back.
Ordinary wire connectors or a tape splice on a medium-voltage conductor, instead of listed MV joints and terminations.
MV feeder work started with no engineered design and no utility coordination — the AHJ stops the job.
Type MV cable terminated with house-wiring habits: no stress control at the termination, cable bent and supported like NM.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is the article number. On a 2020 permit or a 2020-based exam, the medium-voltage rules are in Article 311 — not 315, and not 328. Article 315 is the 2023 renumbering, and 328 was deleted in 2020. The second trap is the voltage floor: Type MV starts at 2,001 V, not at 600 V or 1,000 V.

sections.title: Cabinets, cutout boxes and meter socket enclosures
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 312 covers the enclosures the conductors in Article 310 land in: panel cabinets, cutout boxes and meter sockets. Its job is room and protection inside the enclosure:
• Enough space to deflect and bend conductors entering the top or bottom — deflection and bending space are set by 312.6 and Tables 312.6(A) and (B).
• No sharp edges cutting insulation, and unused openings closed (312.5(A)).
• Doors and covers that close properly.
• Enclosures kept out of damp and wet locations unless they are rated for them. In a damp or wet location a surface enclosure is mounted with at least 1/4 in. of air space behind it, and an enclosure in a wet location must be weatherproof (312.2). A nonmetallic enclosure on concrete, masonry or tile may go without the air space.
• Working space in front of the enclosure is a Chapter 1 rule (110.26), not this article.
sections.on_the_job: On a Sharma house this is the meter enclosure and the panel cabinet. Check conductor bending room before you land a 4/0 service conductor, not after, and keep the enclosure plumb so the deadfront and door seat correctly. In the S-09 back-to-back layout the meter can sits on an exterior wall in a wet location — it goes up weatherproof, on its 1/4 in. air space, not sealed flat to the stucco.
sections.sharma_note: S-09 puts the meter outside and the panel inside, back to back, where the house allows — both enclosures still have to meet this article and the 110.26 working space.
sections.figure_idea: Elevation of a meter socket beside a panel cabinet with the conductor bending space shaded at the top entry.
sections.florida_note: FPL and other Florida utilities have their own meter-socket approval lists on top of the NEC — the socket must be on the serving utility's list.

nec2023_change.change: For the first time, screws that poke into a cabinet, cutout box or meter can are limited: blunt tips only, and 1/4 in. of reach unless the tip is protected. A field-added screw for a label or other gear must be a blunt machine screw reaching 1/4 in. or less, unless its tip is protected.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 312.10 Fasteners in panels and meter cans

nec2023_change.change: New in 2023: cabinets, cutout boxes and meter cans all need a door or a cover. No open cans. Doors or covers are now mandatory on all three Article 312 enclosures: cabinets, cutout boxes and meter cans (312.102).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 312.102 Covers on cabinets and meter cans

sections.why_it_exists: The cabinet is where the biggest conductors in the building bend, land and get worked on for decades. Crowded bending space presses insulation against steel edges, an open knockout invites pests and fingers, and a can rusting against a damp wall fails from the back where nobody looks. The room, the closures and the air space keep the enclosure from becoming the fault.
inspection_fails: Surface-mounted cabinet on a damp or wet location wall with no 1/4 in. air space behind it (312.2).
Unused knockout openings left open in the panel cabinet (312.5(A)).
4/0 service conductors forced in against a sharp enclosure edge with no bending room (312.6).
Cabinet racked out of plumb so the deadfront and door will not seat and close.
sections.exam_trap: The exam swaps the articles: it credits Article 312 with the working-space rule. Working space in front of the panel is 110.26, in Chapter 1. Article 312 governs the enclosure itself — the bending space inside it (312.6), damp and wet mounting (312.2), and closed unused openings (312.5(A)).

page_quiz.question: A surface-type cabinet in a damp location must be mounted with at least how much air space between it and the wall?
page_quiz.explain_plain: 312.2 requires at least 1/4 in. of air space in damp or wet locations, so moisture cannot sit trapped behind the can.

page_quiz.explain_plain: Deflection and bending space are 312.6, sized by Tables 312.6(A) and (B). 110.26 is the working space in front of the enclosure, a different rule.

page_quiz.explain_plain: Outlet, device, pull and junction boxes are Article 314. Article 312 covers cabinets, cutout boxes and meter socket enclosures.

sections.title: Cables entering a cabinet — and the conduit-stub exception
sections.plain_explanation:
Ordinarily each cable entering an enclosure gets its own cable connector or clamp. The exception lets a group of cables enter the top of a surface-mounted enclosure through one short raceway instead — but only when every condition below holds:
• The raceway is nonflexible, at least 18 in. and not more than 10 ft long, and enters only the top of the surface-mounted enclosure.
• Each cable is fastened within 12 in. of the outer end of the raceway, measured along the sheath.
• The raceway is installed directly above the enclosure and does not penetrate a structural ceiling.
• A fitting provided at each end protects the cables against abrasion, and the fittings remain accessible after installation.
• The outer end of the raceway is sealed or plugged.
• The cable sheath extends through the raceway and continues at least 1/4 in. into the enclosure.
• The raceway is secured and supported at its outer end and as required by its article.
• Cable fill does not exceed Chapter 9, Table 1 — the 60% nipple rule does not apply to this raceway.
Miss one condition and the exception is gone: every cable goes back to its own connector.
sections.on_the_job: Sharma panel swap, Orlando garage: the new surface-mounted 200 A Siemens panel takes the home runs through one 6 ft EMT stub out the top. Each cable is strapped within 12 in. of the stub's outer end, the end is plugged against debris and critters, and every sheath runs through and 1/4 in. into the can. The checklist gets one look before the cover goes on — miss a condition and the cables get individual connectors instead.
sections.figure_idea: Surface panel with a short conduit stub out the top: NM cables entering through it, straps marked within 12 in of the stub end, and the 10 ft limit dimensioned.
sections.why_it_exists: An unsecured cable dumps every tug, snag and settling pull straight onto its terminations, and loose terminations overheat. The exception does not drop that protection — it moves it. The short, straight, sealed stub shields the cables as a group, and fastening each cable within 12 in. of the end does the strain-relief work the individual clamps would have done.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: 'the 60% nipple fill applies to the stub.' It does not — fill under this exception is Chapter 9, Table 1. Second trap: treating the exception as permission to skip connectors at any panel top. It covers only a nonflexible raceway, 18 in. to 10 ft, into the top of a surface-mounted enclosure, with every condition met.
inspection_fails: Conduit stub over 10 ft long used as the cable entry — outside the exception.
Cables not fastened within 12 in. of the raceway's outer end.
Outer end of the stub left open — not sealed or plugged.
Stub run through a structural ceiling.
Sheath cut off at the raceway end instead of running 1/4 in. into the enclosure.

sections.title: Conductor bending and deflection space in enclosures
sections.plain_explanation:
Large conductors cannot be bent around a thumb. This section sets the minimum space inside cabinets, cutout boxes and meter enclosures for conductors to deflect and bend where they enter and land — figured from the tables in the section by conductor size, the number of conductors per terminal, and whether the conductor turns or runs straight through. An enclosure can be big enough on the wall and still be too small for the 4/0 or 250 kcmil that has to land in it.
Two tables split the work:
• Table 312.6(B) — wire-bending space at terminals, where the conductor enters or leaves the enclosure through the wall opposite its terminal
• Table 312.6(A) — deflection space and gutter width, where the conductor does not enter or leave through the wall opposite its terminal and turns inside the enclosure instead
Two conductors landing on one terminal need more space than the one-conductor figure — the tables carry separate columns for that.
This page is not yet verified: the bending-space values an earlier draft listed here were removed until they are checked row by row against the printed 2020 Tables 312.6(A) and 312.6(B). Read the values from the printed tables (see Check in print).
sections.on_the_job: Size the enclosure from the conductor, not the wall space: check the bending-space table for the largest conductor and the entry direction (top, bottom, side) before the gear is ordered. Forcing a feeder into too-tight a bend is damaged insulation and a failed inspection in one move. On a Sharma service change, that check happens at the estimate stage, while a bigger can is still a line item and not a return trip.
sections.figure_idea: Panel interior with a large feeder conductor bending from a bottom entry to its lug, the required bending space shaded and dimensioned from the section's table (values left to the table, not restated).
sections.unverified_reason: Still unverified after Mike Holt recheck (2026-11-25): The Table 312.6(B) one-wire bending-space values on this page (4/0 = 5½ in., 250 = 6 in., 300 = 6½ in., 350 = 7 in., 400–500 = 8 in., ...) do not match my recollection of either Table 312.6(A) or 312.6(B), and I could not confirm them from a public source. Remove the number list until it has been checked row by row against the printed 2020 Table 312.6(B). Also make clear that Table 312.6(B) applies where the conductor enters or leaves through the wall opposite its terminal, and Table 312.6(A) covers gutter width and bending space where it does not.
sections.why_it_exists: A feeder forced around too tight a bend is damaged goods: the insulation stretches thin on the outside of the bend, the strands splay, and the lug takes a side load every time the conductor tries to spring back. Bending and deflection space is what lets a large conductor land flat on its lug and stay there for the life of the gear.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: picking whichever table gives the smaller number. The entry geometry picks the table — a conductor that enters or leaves through the wall opposite its terminal is a Table 312.6(B) bending-space case; one that turns inside the gutter is Table 312.6(A). The other trap is "the can fits the wall, so the wire fits": bending space is figured from the conductor, not from the enclosure's footprint.
inspection_fails: Large feeder forced into a bend the enclosure was too small for — insulation creased at the lug.
Gear ordered by wall footprint, with bending space never checked until the wire would not land.
Gutter width for a conductor turning inside the enclosure figured from Table 312.6(B) — the wrong table for that entry.

sections.title: What may live inside an enclosure for switches and overcurrent devices
sections.plain_explanation:
An enclosure that houses switches or overcurrent devices is not a general-purpose junction box, but it is not sealed against all other wiring either. Under 312.8(A), conductors may feed through, splice and tap inside the wiring space, within set limits:
• Feed-through conductors: the total of all conductors at any cross section of the wiring space does not exceed 40 percent of that space.
• Splices and taps: all conductors, splices and taps together do not exceed 75 percent at any cross section.
• A warning label on the enclosure identifies the location of the disconnecting means for the feed-through conductors.
Power-monitoring and energy-management equipment may also live in the wiring space under 312.8(B): it must be identified as a field-installable accessory of listed equipment, or a listed kit evaluated for field installation in these enclosures, and everything at any cross section — conductors, splices, taps and the equipment — stays at or under 75 percent.
sections.on_the_job: Do not treat a panel as free splice space on a remodel. If feed-through or splices are planned in an overcurrent enclosure, count the space and keep it in the wiring gutter area. Example: a gutter cross section of 20 sq in allows 8 sq in of feed-through conductors at the 40 percent limit, and 15 sq in total once splices and taps are added at the 75 percent limit. Be ready to show the inspector the section you relied on.
sections.figure_idea: Panel gutter detail with feed-through conductors occupying a measured share of the wiring space, splice bundle tagged separately.

nec2023_change.change: Switch and breaker enclosures carrying feed-through conductors, splices or taps now need enough bending space for 4 AWG and larger conductors, on top of the old 40 and 75 percent fill limits. New item (3): 4 AWG and larger conductors in the wiring space need bending room that meets 314.28(A)(2), the angle-pull rule for pull boxes.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 312.8 Splices and feed-through in panels

sections.why_it_exists: The wiring space in a breaker enclosure is sized for that enclosure's own conductors to bend, land and be serviced. Foreign splices packed into the gutter trap heat, block breaker work, and leave live feed-through conductors inside a panel the next electrician opened expecting one disconnect to make it safe. The limits and the label keep the enclosure's own job possible and its hidden hazards announced.
inspection_fails: A panelboard used as a junction box for unrelated circuits, with no fill count done at all.
Splices and taps packed into the gutter past 75 percent of the wiring space at a cross section.
Feed-through conductors passing through a panel with no warning label identifying where their disconnecting means is.
Monitoring equipment screwed into the gutter that is not a listed kit or an identified accessory for the enclosure.
sections.exam_trap: Splices and taps may fill 75 percent of the wiring space, so feed-through conductors may too. Wrong swap. Feed-through conductors alone are capped at 40 percent of the cross section. The 75 percent figure is the total — conductors, splices and taps together.

sections.title: Outlet, device, pull and junction boxes
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 314 is the box article: which box, how big, how it is set, how it is supported, and what may live in it.
• The sizing heart is 314.16: a box is big enough only if its marked volume holds every conductor, device, clamp and ground the counting rules charge against it.
• 314.17 covers conductors entering the box — cables secured to it, and the sheath carried at least 1/4 in inside, past the clamp.
• 314.23 covers support: the box must not move when devices are plugged in and pulled out for twenty years.
• 314.28 takes over at 4 AWG and larger, where sizing stops being cubic inches and becomes pull geometry.
• 314.29 requires every box to stay accessible without removing any part of the building.
The volume math is the part you can settle at the truck. The placement rules around it are what inspectors check after the math passes.
sections.on_the_job: Run the fill math before the rough-in, not at trim. A box that fails fill in the wall fails the same way on paper — cheaper to catch it on paper. Sharma kitchen case: two 12/2 NM cables and one receptacle in a 4 in square × 2-1/8 in box. The conductors charge four allowances, the grounds one, the clamps one and the yoke two — 8 × 2.25 = 18.0 cu in against the box's 30.3. It passes with room to work. Add a third cable and the count climbs past what the shallow 1-1/2 in box (21.0 cu in) should carry — that is the call to make before the drywall, not at trim.
sections.figure_idea: Cutaway of a 4-square box with a receptacle, two NM cables and clamps, each counted item tagged 1x, 2x or 'grounds = 1'.
sections.edition_note:
NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 314.24: New clearances where wiring enters a box: at a side entry, the device stays behind the knockout centerline or 1/2 in. off that wall. A center-back entry adds room behind 12 or 10 AWG equipment. With a side entry, the back of the device can't reach past the centerline of that knockout or entry (314.24(C)(1)).
• 314.25: Conduit bodies joined boxes in the closure rule: on a finished job, every LB and other conduit body needs a cover, faceplate, luminaire canopy or lampholder. On a finished job, every conduit body needs a cover, faceplate, luminaire canopy or lampholder, the same as a box.
• 314.5: New fastener limits for boxes and conduit bodies: blunt machine screws, set reach limits for cover and wall screws, and nothing poking past flush in small boxes or conduit bodies. Pointed screws are out: field-added screws in boxes and conduit bodies must be blunt-end machine screws, unless the manufacturer supplied or specified them.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: An overfilled box overheats its splices and crushes insulation when the device is forced in — and the damage hides behind the cover plate. A box nobody can reach turns one failed splice into a wall demolition. The fill count and the accessibility rule exist so the weakest point of every circuit stays cool, intact and findable for the life of the building.
inspection_fails: 4 in square × 1-1/2 in box (21.0 cu in) holding three cables and two devices — the count exceeds the marked volume (314.16).
Junction box covered by fixed kitchen cabinets — not accessible (314.29).
Box held up only by the NM cables entering it — a box must be supported (314.23).
Finished junction box left without a cover (314.25).
Straight pull through a 12 in box on a 2 in raceway — 314.28(A)(1) needs 16 in.
Sheath stripped off outside the box, conductors crossing the clamp unprotected (314.17).

sections.title: Box fill — volume, allowances and counting
sections.plain_explanation:
Box fill is a counting exercise with a hard ceiling: add up the volume allowances of everything in the box, and the total may not exceed the volume stamped or tabulated for that box. Table 314.16(A) gives the volume of standard metal boxes; Table 314.16(B) gives the allowance each conductor size costs. Both tables are reproduced below.
• What counts is decided by 314.16(B)(1) through (5): conductors, internal clamps, support fittings, device yokes, and equipment grounding conductors.
• The grounds rule is the 2020 version: up to four equipment grounding conductors or bonding jumpers together cost one allowance, and each one past four adds a quarter allowance.
• A plaster ring, extension ring or cover marked with its volume adds that volume to the box; an unmarked one adds nothing you may count on.
Count first, then pick the box — the worked example in On the Job shows how fast a standard box runs out of room.
sections.on_the_job:
Run the five counts in field order: (1) conductors — each conductor that enters from outside and is terminated or spliced counts once, a conductor passing through unbroken counts once, and a pigtail that starts and ends in the box counts zero; (2) clamps — all internal clamps together count once; (3) support fittings — one allowance for each type; (4) device yokes — each yoke counts twice; (5) grounds — up to four count once, each one past four adds a quarter.
Worked example: a 4 in square × 1-1/2 in box holds 21.0 cu in. Three 12/2 NM cables, one receptacle and internal clamps charge: 6 conductors × 2.25 = 13.50, grounds 2.25, device yoke 4.50, clamps 2.25 — total 22.50 cu in. It fails. The 4 in square × 2-1/8 in box at 30.3 cu in passes.
sections.sharma_note: Box height on the wall is not a 314 rule — Sharma S-04 (receptacles 18 in to the bottom of the box, plan silent) and S-05 (switches 48 in to center) govern placement; 314 governs whether the box you placed is big enough and set right.
sections.figure_idea: Worksheet-style figure: left side a box volume stamp '30.3 cu in', right side a tally list adding to 22.50, with a green check.
sections.why_it_exists: Conductors folded into a box are bent, pressed and heated in a tight space. The allowances guarantee free space around every splice and device, so insulation is not crushed against box edges and the device can sit flush without forcing the wires. An overfilled box fails slowly — chafed insulation and hot connections, long after the cover is on.
sections.exam_trap: Two traps meet here. First: 'pigtails count.' A pigtail that starts and ends in the box counts zero. Second, the 2017 habit: 'all the grounds together are one allowance, period.' In the 2020 book up to four grounds count once, but each ground past four adds a quarter allowance — in a crowded box, that quarter is the one that fails you.

Unmarked plaster ring counted toward the box volume.

sections.title: The five counting rules, one by one
sections.plain_explanation:
• (B)(1) Conductors: each conductor from outside the box that is spliced or terminated counts once; a conductor that runs through unbroken counts once; an unbroken loop or coil of at least twice the minimum free-conductor length required by 300.14 — so 12 in or more of loop — counts twice; pigtails that originate in the box count zero.
• (B)(2) Clamps: where one or more internal cable clamps are present, all of them together count once, at the largest conductor in the box; a cable connector with its clamping mechanism outside the box counts zero.
• (B)(3) Support fittings: count one allowance for each type of fitting present — all luminaire studs together count once, and all hickeys together count once, so a box with both a stud and a hickey counts two — at the largest conductor in the box.
• (B)(4) Devices: each device yoke or strap counts twice, at the largest conductor connected to that device; a device wider than a single 2 in device box counts twice for each gang required to mount it.
• (B)(5) Grounds — the count that changed in 2020: up to four equipment grounding conductors and equipment bonding jumpers entering the box together count once, at the largest ground in the box, and each additional one beyond four adds a quarter of that allowance. Isolated-ground conductors count in with the rest of the grounds; the old separate extra allowance for an isolated-ground set is a 2017 rule and does not apply in 2020.
sections.on_the_job: Say the counts out loud as you tally: wires, clamps, studs, yokes, grounds. Field example at 12 AWG (2.25 cu in): four grounds = 2.25 cu in; six grounds = 2.25 + (2 x 0.25 x 2.25) = 3.38 cu in. In a normal house box with two or three cables the ground count is four or fewer, so the old habit gives the same answer — the quarter rule only bites in crowded multi-cable boxes, which is exactly where fill was already tight.
sections.figure_idea: Five-row tally card with icons: conductor, clamp, stud, yoke, ground bar, each with its multiplier.
sections.florida_note: The 2020 quarter-allowance count is what this page, the calculator, the starter quiz, and lookup L-064 now teach. The printed 2020 text of 314.16(B)(5) was checked in the 2026-11-18 verification pass. The old 'all grounds count as one, however many' rule is the 2017 rule.

nec2023_change.change: New in 2023: a terminal block inside a box takes up box fill. Count one volume for the whole block, based on the biggest wire terminated on it. Add one volume allowance for each terminal block assembly, using the largest conductor terminated on it (314.16(B)(6)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 314.16 Terminal blocks in box fill

sections.why_it_exists: Boxes are where conductors get spliced, heated and crowded. The count is a heat-and-damage budget: every allowance is room for insulation and for the next electrician's hands. Undercount, and the box gets stuffed — insulation nicks on sharp edges, devices strain their terminations, and heat has nowhere to go.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is the 2017 habit: 'all the grounds count as one, however many enter.' In 2020 the first four grounds together count once, and every ground after that adds a quarter allowance. The second trap counts a pigtail that starts inside the box — pigtails count zero — or counts a device yoke once instead of twice.
inspection_fails: Six equipment grounds counted as a single volume allowance — the 2017 rule (314.16(B)(5)).
Device yoke counted once instead of twice in the fill tally (314.16(B)(4)).
Long unbroken loop of conductor left in the box counted once instead of twice (314.16(B)(1)).
Box filled past the cubic-inch capacity marked inside it (314.16).

figures.alt: Five-row tally card for box fill under 314.16(B): conductors count once each with a long loop counting twice and a pigtail zero, all clamps together count once, each support fitting type counts once, each device yoke counts twice, and grounds count once for the first four with a quarter allowance for each one past four.
figures.caption: The five counts — say them out loud as you tally.

page_quiz.question: Six 12 AWG equipment grounds enter a box. Their total volume allowance is:
page_quiz.explain_plain: The first four grounds count once (2.25 cu in at 12 AWG); grounds five and six add a quarter each: 2.25 + (2 × 0.25 × 2.25) = 3.38 cu in.

page_quiz.question: A receptacle yoke on 12 AWG conductors counts as how many conductor allowances?
page_quiz.explain_plain: Each device yoke or strap counts twice, at the largest conductor connected to that device.

page_quiz.question: A pigtail that originates inside the box counts:
page_quiz.explain_plain: Pigtails that originate in the box count zero — they never leave the box, so they take no allowance.

sections.title: Conduit bodies — fill and splices
sections.plain_explanation:
Conduit bodies follow fill rules too.
• Conductors passing through: the fill may not exceed what the Chapter 9 tables allow for the raceway size the body belongs to.
• Splices, taps and devices: allowed inside a conduit body only where the body is durably and legibly marked with its cubic-inch capacity by the manufacturer. Then the fill is counted the same way box fill is counted, against that marked volume, using the Table 314.16(B) allowances — 2.00 cu in for each 14 AWG, 2.25 for each 12 AWG, 2.50 for each 10 AWG.
• An unmarked LB is a pulling fitting, not a junction box: no splices live in it.
sections.on_the_job: Read the casting before you splice: no cubic-inch marking, no splice. The count, worked: a splice joining two 12 AWG conductors charges 2 × 2.25 = 4.50 cu in, the grounds count once at 2.25, total 6.75 cu in — so the casting has to read at least 6.75 cu in before that splice is legal in that body. If the job needs a splice at that point and the body is unmarked, the fix is a marked body or a real box — not a bigger wirenut. Plan the box at rough-in instead of discovering it at final.
sections.figure_idea: Two conduit bodies: one cast with its cubic-inch capacity marked, holding a splice (approved); one unmarked with a splice inside (crossed out).
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: A conduit body is a small sealed pocket. Cram splices into one that was never sized for them and the wirenuts sit crushed against the cover, insulation chafes on the casting, and the heat of a loaded splice has nowhere to go. The marking rule makes the manufacturer state the volume up front, so the splice count is a math problem with an answer — not a guess made with the cover in your hand.
inspection_fails: Splices wirenutted inside an unmarked LB — no cubic-inch marking, no splices (314.16(C)).
Marked body filled past its marked volume — the splice charge outran the casting number.
Capacity marking scraped off or illegible — the capacity must be durably and legibly marked.
Device mounted in a conduit body that was never marked for one.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is calling an LB a small junction box. An unmarked conduit body is a pulling fitting only; splices, taps and devices need a body durably and legibly marked with its cubic-inch capacity, and the fill then counts exactly like box fill. The mirror trap is using the Chapter 9 raceway fill for a body that holds splices — those tables govern conductors passing through, not splices.

tables.caption: What limits the fill
rows: Chapter 9 fill for the raceway size

figures.alt: Two conduit bodies side by side: one marked with its cubic-inch capacity holding a splice with a green check, one unmarked holding a splice crossed out in red, with the worked fill count below.
figures.caption: Marked body: the splice counts like a box. Unmarked body: pulling only.

page_quiz.question: Splices are permitted inside a conduit body when…
choices: Always — it is a small box
The body is durably and legibly marked with its cubic-inch capacity
page_quiz.explain_plain: 314.16(C) allows splices, taps and devices only in a body marked with its capacity, counted like box fill.

page_quiz.question: A splice joins two 12 AWG conductors in a marked body, with grounds entering too. The charge is…
page_quiz.explain_plain: 2 conductors × 2.25 = 4.50, plus grounds counted once at 2.25 — 6.75 cu in total, and the marked capacity must cover it.

page_quiz.question: Conductors passing straight through a conduit body are limited by…
choices: The Chapter 9 fill for the raceway size
page_quiz.explain_plain: Through conductors follow the raceway fill tables; the marked volume governs splices, taps and devices.

sections.title: Conductors and cables entering boxes
sections.plain_explanation:
Cables entering a box have to be secured to the box, or fastened close enough that the entry stays put, and the cable sheath has to continue into the box so the conductors are protected where they enter. Metal boxes with clamps secure the cable at the box itself; a box without a clamp leans on the fastening distance instead.
• Sheath: at least 1/4 in inside the box, past any clamp (the v1 field rule, L-065).
• Single-gang nonmetallic boxes: fasten the cable within 8 in of the box — the sheath still goes 1/4 in in.
• Unused openings get closed. An open knockout is a hole in the enclosure, not a spare.
sections.on_the_job: On a Florida rough-in with single-gang nonmetallic boxes, the staple is the securing: staple the NM within 8 in of every box, every time. Strip the sheath outside the box, not inside it: 1/4 in of sheath past the clamp is protection; 2 in of sheath inside the box is fill you did not count and a make-up fight at trim.
sections.figure_idea: Close-up of an NM cable entering a plastic box: sheath ending 1/4 in past the knockout, conductors separating after that point.

nec2023_change.change: The section now names cables in its title alongside conductors and was reworded for accuracy. The working rules for closing openings and securing NM and UF cable carry over. NM or UF through a clamp: jacket 1/4 in. or more into the box and past the clamp, and the cable secured to the box.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 314.17 Cables entering boxes

sections.edition_note:
NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 314.17: The section now names cables in its title alongside conductors and was reworded for accuracy. The working rules for closing openings and securing NM and UF cable carry over. NM or UF through a clamp: jacket 1/4 in. or more into the box and past the clamp, and the cable secured to the box.

sections.why_it_exists: The entry is where a cable gets yanked and chafed. If the cable is not secured, every tug lands on the terminations and works them loose — and loose terminations arc and overheat. The 1/4 in of sheath past the clamp means the clamp bites the jacket, not the bare conductors, so insulation is never the thing being squeezed. A closed unused opening keeps the enclosure an enclosure: fingers, dust and sparks stay on their own side of the box wall.
inspection_fails: Sheath stripped flush at the clamp — no jacket inside the box past the clamp (314.17).
NM drifting into a single-gang plastic box with the nearest staple 2 ft away — not fastened within 8 in.
Open knockout left in the back of a box — unused opening never closed.
Two inches of sheath left inside the box, eating fill that was never counted.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is stripping the sheath flush at the box face 'to keep the box neat.' The rule wants the opposite: the sheath continues at least 1/4 in into the box, past the clamp. The second trap is fastening 'close enough' on a single-gang nonmetallic box — the number is 8 in, not 'within a foot or so.'

figures.alt: NM cable stapled within 8 inches above a single-gang nonmetallic box, with an enlarged entry detail showing the sheath extending 1/4 inch past the clamp before the conductors separate.
figures.caption: Secured outside, sheath inside: the two numbers are 8 in and 1/4 in.

page_quiz.question: How far must the NM sheath extend into the box, past the clamp?
page_quiz.explain_plain: The jacket continues at least 1/4 in into the box, past any clamp, so the clamp bites jacket — not conductors (field rule L-065).

page_quiz.question: A single-gang nonmetallic box has no clamp. The cable must be fastened within what distance of the box?
page_quiz.explain_plain: With no clamp to secure it, the cable is fastened within 8 in of the box — and the sheath still extends 1/4 in inside.

page_quiz.question: An unused knockout in a box is…
choices: Fine if it faces the stud
An opening that must be closed
Only a problem in wet locations
page_quiz.explain_plain: Unused openings are closed so the enclosure stays complete.

sections.title: How a box sits in a wall or ceiling
sections.plain_explanation:
How far a box may sit behind the finished surface depends on what that surface is made of:
• Noncombustible — concrete, tile, gypsum board (drywall), plaster: the front of the box, plaster ring, extension ring, or listed extender may be set back no more than 1/4 in.
• Combustible — wood or other combustible material: the box or extender has to reach the finished surface or project past it. No setback.
• Gypsum board counts as noncombustible for this rule, even when it is screwed to wood studs.
A box buried farther than the rule allows is both a device problem — the yoke ears cannot reach — and a code problem.
sections.on_the_job: Set box depth off the stud face for the finish that is actually going on that wall: 1/2 in drywall is not tile on backer board. Use the adjustable-depth or extension option before the wall closes, not a stack of goof rings at trim. Tile makes the point: backer board and tile build a kitchen backsplash wall out about 7/8 in, so a box set for 1/2 in drywall alone can land 3/8 in behind the tile face — over the 1/4 in limit even though tile is noncombustible — and it needs its extension ring at rough-in, not at trim.
sections.sharma_note: S-04 and S-05 set the height (18 in to bottom for receptacles, 48 in to center for switches, plan silent); this section sets the depth. Both have to be right on the same box.
sections.figure_idea: Wall section: stud, drywall, and a box face drawn flush, with a second box drawn 1/4 in back marked 'noncombustible only'.
sections.why_it_exists: The gap is the hazard. A box sunk too deep leaves an open slot between the device and the box where an arc or a loose, hot connection can reach the wall cavity and the framing behind it. It also leaves the device floating on its yoke screws, so every plug insertion works the receptacle a little looser.
inspection_fails: Box set back 3/8 in behind a tile surface with no extension ring (314.20 allows 1/4 in max in noncombustible material).
Box recessed behind wood paneling instead of reaching or projecting past the finished surface (314.20).
Device floating on stacked goof rings with the box opening gaping into the wall cavity (314.20).
sections.exam_trap: The trap: "The studs are wood, so the wall is combustible and the box must sit flush." Wrong — the surface is what counts, and gypsum board is noncombustible for 314.20 even over wood studs, so the 1/4 in setback is allowed. Flip it onto a wood-paneled wall and that same setback fails.

figures.alt: Two wall sections: a box set back 1/4 inch behind a drywall surface marked as passing, and a box set back behind wood paneling marked as failing because combustible surfaces allow no setback.
figures.caption: The surface material sets the setback: 1/4 in in noncombustible, zero in wood.

page_quiz.question: A box in a tile wall is set back 3/16 in from the finished surface, with no extender. Verdict?
choices: Passes — 1/4 in is the maximum in noncombustible surfaces
Fails — boxes must always be flush
Passes only if the studs are metal
page_quiz.explain_plain: Tile is noncombustible, so a setback up to 1/4 in is allowed; 3/16 in is inside the limit.

page_quiz.question: On a wood-paneled (combustible) wall, the box front may be set back:
choices: Not at all — it must reach the surface or project past it
page_quiz.explain_plain: In combustible material the box, plaster ring or listed extender must reach the finished surface or project beyond it.

page_quiz.question: For 314.20, gypsum board screwed to wood studs is treated as:
choices: Neither — the rule does not cover drywall
page_quiz.explain_plain: The rule reads the finished surface, not the framing: gypsum board is noncombustible even on wood studs.

sections.title: Repairing the surface around a box
sections.plain_explanation:
Where a box is set in a noncombustible wall or ceiling, the broken or chipped surface around it has to be repaired so there is no gap or open space bigger than 1/8 in around the box. The plate cannot be the patch — the surface itself has to come back to the box.
• The limit is on the finished repair: no gap or open space over 1/8 in at any point at the edge of the box.
• The surfaces covered are the noncombustible ones — concrete, tile, gypsum board, plaster and the like, the same family 314.20 uses for box setback.
• Do not swap the two numbers: 314.20 lets the box face sit back up to 1/4 in in noncombustible material; 314.21 separately caps the gap around the box at 1/8 in.
• In combustible material this repair rule is not the governing one — 314.20 requires the box to reach the finished surface or project past it.
sections.on_the_job: On remodel work, check the gap before you set the device. A 1/4 in crater around a cut-in box is a fail here and a wobbly device later; use the right box or repair the opening. On a Florida bathroom remodel, that means patching the chipped tile or plaster back to the box edge before the device goes in — five minutes of patching beats a red tag at final and a callback for a receptacle that rocks every time a plug is pulled.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: The gap around a box is a chimney. Fire and hot gas in the wall cavity use it to reach the room, and smoke takes the same path. A cover plate hides the gap but does not close it — the plate is thin, often plastic, and is not part of the wall surface. Closing the surface itself keeps the wall the barrier it was built to be, and it gives the device yoke something solid to seat against.
inspection_fails: Gap of 1/4 in between the box edge and the broken drywall, hidden behind an oversized plate (314.21).
Tile chipped away around a cut-in box and left open behind the cover plate.
Cratered plaster around a box wider than 1/8 in at final inspection.
Device floating on its yoke screws because the surface around the box was never repaired.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is that an oversized — jumbo — cover plate fixes a broken opening. It does not: 314.21 requires the surface itself repaired so no gap over 1/8 in remains, whatever plate goes on top. The second trap is swapping the numbers: 1/4 in is the 314.20 box setback in noncombustible material; 1/8 in is the 314.21 gap around the box.

tables.caption: Two numbers, two sections
rows: Box face set back, noncombustible surface
Gap in the surface around the box

figures.alt: Two wall openings compared: a surface repaired to within 1/8 inch of the box passes, while a 1/4 inch crater hidden by a jumbo plate fails 314.21.
figures.caption: Repair the surface — the plate is not the patch.

page_quiz.question: A box in a plaster wall has a chipped opening leaving a 3/16 in gap on one side, covered by a jumbo plate. Verdict?
choices: Passes — the plate covers the gap
Fails — the surface must be repaired to no gap over 1/8 in
Passes if the device sits tight
page_quiz.explain_plain: 314.21 requires the surface itself repaired. The plate is never the patch.

page_quiz.question: Which limit belongs to 314.21?
choices: Gap around the box of 1/8 in
page_quiz.explain_plain: 1/8 in is the 314.21 gap limit. The 1/4 in setback belongs to 314.20.

sections.title: Supporting boxes
sections.plain_explanation:
A box has to be supported — screwed, nailed, braced or hung by a method the article allows for that box type — rigidly enough that it does not move when devices are plugged in and pulled out for twenty years. Surface boxes, pendant boxes and boxes in walls and ceilings each have their own allowed supports in this section, and a box supported by a raceway alone is allowed only in the narrow cases the section describes.
• Surface and structure (314.23(A) and (B)): fasten the box to a surface that can hold it, or to a structural member, directly or on a brace — metal braces at least 0.020 in thick, wood braces at least a nominal 1 by 2.
• Finished surfaces (314.23(C)): a cut-in box is held by clamps, anchors or fittings identified for the purpose.
• Suspended ceilings (314.23(D)): boxes of 100 cu in or less may fasten to the ceiling framing members, or hang from added independent support wires — never from the ceiling's own wires.
• Raceway support, no devices (314.23(E)): an enclosure with no device or luminaire, 100 cu in or less, threaded entries or identified hubs, held by two or more conduits threaded wrenchtight, each conduit secured within 3 ft — 18 in where every entry is on the same side.
• Raceway support, with devices (314.23(F)): the same 100 cu in cap and threaded entries, two or more conduits — and each conduit secured within 18 in of the box.
sections.on_the_job: Wiggle test at rough-in: grab the box and push. If it moves, the device will move at trim and the plate will never sit flat. Add the brace or bracket now. On a Sharma rough-in the test catches most of it: device boxes nailed to the stud with the bracket flange flat, ceiling boxes on listed bar hangers between the joists. The fan location gets a listed fan box — marked for the weight, good to 70 lb before the fan needs independent support (314.27(C)) — not a standard octagon box on a strap.

nec2023_change.change: Pendant boxes hung from cord: a box with a hub now has to hang from a listed cord grip that carries a threaded-hub marking. Cord-hung box with a hub? It has to be held by a listed cord grip marked for threaded-hub use (314.23(H)(1)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 314.23 Cord-hung pendant boxes

sections.why_it_exists: Devices get pushed, pulled and leaned on for decades. A box that gives a little at every plug-in works its splices loose, cracks the plate, and finally arcs inside a wall. Rigid support keeps the mechanical stress on the bracket and the stud, where it belongs, instead of on the terminations.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: 'the conduit holds it, so it is supported.' One EMT stub under a device box fails 314.23(F) three ways — it takes two or more conduits, threaded wrenchtight or on identified hubs, each secured within 18 in, and the box can be no bigger than 100 cu in.
inspection_fails: Device box supported by a single EMT stub; 314.23(F) wants two or more threaded conduits, each secured within 18 in.
Octagon box and luminaire hung from the ceiling grid wires; boxes need the framing members or their own independent wires (314.23(D)).
Pendant box on a cord with the cord's weight hanging on the terminals; the fitting has to keep tension off the joints (314.23(H)(1)).
Cut-in box loose in the drywall, rocking when the receptacle is plugged in (314.23(C)).

page_quiz.question: A device box hangs from two threaded rigid conduits. How close to the box must each conduit be secured?
page_quiz.explain_plain: With devices inside, 314.23(F) wants each conduit secured within 18 in of the enclosure.

page_quiz.question: The largest enclosure that may be raceway-supported with no devices inside is:
page_quiz.explain_plain: 314.23(E) caps a raceway-supported enclosure at 100 cu in, with threaded entries or identified hubs.

page_quiz.question: A ceiling box in a suspended ceiling may hang from:
choices: Added independent support wires, taut and secured
A cable tie to a duct
page_quiz.explain_plain: 314.23(D) allows the ceiling framing members or added independent support wires — never the wires holding the ceiling up.

figures.alt: Three comparison panels for box support: a device box screwed to a stud, a ceiling box on a listed bar hanger between joists, and a device box hung from a single conduit stub with the strap far away, marked as failing 314.23(F).
figures.caption: Two supports that pass — and the one-raceway shortcut that fails.

sections.title: Boxes at lighting outlets — the 50-pound rule
sections.plain_explanation:
A box used at a lighting outlet has to be listed for the purpose, and it may support a luminaire (or lampholder) weighing up to 50 lb. A heavier luminaire may be supported by the box only where the box is listed and marked for the weight it will actually carry; otherwise the fixture is supported independently of the box.
• Up to 50 lb: a listed lighting-outlet box carries the luminaire.
• Over 50 lb: the box must be listed and marked for the actual weight, or the fixture gets independent support from the structure.
• Ceiling fans are not luminaires under this rule — a fan needs a fan-rated box under 314.27(C), even if the fan weighs less than 50 lb. Fan boxes are listed for fan support and marked with the weight they may carry, up to 70 lb; a heavier fan is supported independently.
sections.on_the_job: Big foyer and lanai fixtures are the trap: weigh the fixture or look up its weight before trim-out. A 62 lb chandelier in a two-story Kissimmee foyer is over the line for a plain box — if the box is not listed and marked for 62 lb, the fixture gets an independent support from the structure. Plan that support at rough-in, not with the fixture hanging from your lift.
sections.figure_idea: Ceiling box with a 45 lb fixture (approved), a 65 lb fixture on an unmarked box (crossed out), and the same fixture on an independent support (approved).
sections.why_it_exists: A luminaire hangs over the people who live and work under it, held by screws and box ears that also carry its wiring connections. A box that lets go drops a live fixture into the room and tears conductors loose on the way down. The weight limit, the marking rule and the separate fan rule exist because weight plus vibration is what works a support loose over time.
inspection_fails: A 65 lb chandelier hung from a standard ceiling box with no weight marking on the box.
A ceiling fan mounted on a plain lighting box because 'it only weighs 30 lb' — no fan-support listing or marking.
A fixture over 50 lb supported by a box marked for less than the fixture's actual weight.
An 'independent support' that is screwed to the box itself instead of to the building structure.
sections.exam_trap: The fan weighs 42 lb — under the 50 lb limit, so a standard lighting box is fine. Wrong. The 50 lb limit is for luminaires. A ceiling fan is a moving, vibrating load, and 314.27(C) requires a box listed and marked for fan support no matter what the fan weighs.

tables.caption: Who carries the weight?
rows: Box listed and marked for the actual weight, or independent support
Fan-rated box listed and marked for fan support — 314.27(C)

figures.alt: Three ceiling boxes: a 45 lb fixture on a listed box marked OK, a 65 lb fixture on an unmarked box crossed out, and a 65 lb fixture carried by an independent support rod to the structure marked OK.
figures.caption: The 50 lb line: what the box may carry, and when the structure has to.

page_quiz.question: A listed lighting-outlet box may support a luminaire weighing up to:
choices: Any weight, if the screws are long
page_quiz.explain_plain: 314.27(A) allows a listed box to support a luminaire or lampholder up to 50 lb. Heavier needs a box listed and marked for the weight, or independent support.

page_quiz.question: A chandelier weighs 62 lb. The ceiling box has no weight marking. What is required?
choices: Hang it — the box is listed
Support the fixture independently of the box
Add a second box beside it
page_quiz.explain_plain: Over 50 lb, the box must be listed and marked for the actual weight it carries. An unmarked box cannot take it, so the fixture is supported independently.

page_quiz.question: A ceiling fan weighs 38 lb. May it hang from a standard listed lighting-outlet box?
choices: Yes, if the box is metal
No — a fan needs a box listed and marked for fan support
No — fans may not hang from boxes at all
page_quiz.explain_plain: Fans are not luminaires under 314.27(A). 314.27(C) requires a fan-rated box at any fan weight; fans over 70 lb are supported independently.

sections.title: Boxes at ceiling-fan outlets
sections.plain_explanation:
Where an outlet in the ceiling of a habitable room is in a spot that could support a ceiling fan — wired and placed the way a fan location is — the box has to be listed for fan support, and the maximum weight it may carry is marked on it.
• The box must be listed for the purpose and marked by the manufacturer as suitable for fan support.
• A fan over 35 lb up to 70 lb needs a box marked for that weight.
• A fan heavier than 70 lb is supported independently of the box.
• A lighting-outlet box does not qualify, even for a light fan: under 314.27(A) a fan is not a luminaire, so a fan outlet always needs the fan-rated box.
sections.on_the_job: If there is a ceiling outlet in a bedroom or living room with a switch leg, rough it in with a fan-rated box whether or not the plan shows a fan today — the next owner will hang one there. That is checklist BL-09. At trim, read the marking inside the box before the fan goes up: if the fan going in weighs 48 lb, the box marking has to cover 48 lb. A box marked for a lighter fan, or with no fan marking at all, does not pass.
sections.figure_idea: Ceiling box seen from below with its fan-support marking enlarged, and a fan outline above it.

nec2023_change.change: The rules for plug-in ceiling receptacles that hold up a fixture or fan now use the defined names WSCR and WSAF, and spell out when the pair can carry a paddle fan. A listed weight-supporting ceiling receptacle (WSCR) paired with a compatible attachment fitting (WSAF) can solely support a paddle fan, if 314.27(C) is met.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 314.27 Weight-supporting ceiling receptacles

sections.why_it_exists: A ceiling fan is a moving load: it vibrates, wobbles and pulls on its support every hour it runs, over the heads of the people below. A box chosen for a static light fixture works loose under that movement. The listed box, the weight marking and the 70 lb cutoff keep a spinning load on hardware that was tested to hold it.
inspection_fails: Ceiling fan hung on a standard lighting-outlet box — no fan-support listing or marking (314.27(C)).
Fan over 35 lb on a box whose marking does not cover the fan's weight.
Fan over 70 lb carried by the box instead of supported independently of it.
Fan-capable ceiling outlet in a bedroom roughed in with a plain lighting box because the plan showed a fixture.
sections.exam_trap: The exam answer is that a 40 lb fan can hang on a box listed for a 50 lb luminaire, because 40 is less than 50. Wrong twice: the 50 lb figure in 314.27(A) covers luminaires only, and a fan over 35 lb needs a box listed for fan support and marked for the fan's weight under 314.27(C).

figures.caption: Listed, marked, and capped at 70 lb: the fan box rule.

page_quiz.question: A 55 lb paddle fan is going on a bedroom ceiling outlet. The box must be:
choices: A box listed for a 50 lb luminaire
A box listed and marked for fan support, rated for at least 55 lb
No box — lag the fan bracket to the joist
page_quiz.explain_plain: Over 35 lb, the box must be listed for fan support and marked for the weight it carries. The 50 lb luminaire rule in 314.27(A) does not cover fans.

page_quiz.question: A ceiling fan weighs 78 lb. How is it supported?
choices: On a box marked 70 lb, with extra screws

page_quiz.explain_plain: Over 70 lb, the fan is supported independently of the box. The box is never the structure for a fan that heavy.

choices: A fan-rated box listed for fan support
No box until a fan is chosen
page_quiz.explain_plain: Where the outlet is in a spot that could support a fan, wired and placed as a fan location, 314.27(C) requires the fan-support box now, not when the fan arrives.

sections.title: Pull and junction boxes for conductors 4 AWG and larger
sections.plain_explanation:
Once conductors reach 4 AWG and larger, box sizing stops being a cubic-inch question and becomes a geometry question: the box must be big enough to pull and bend stiff conductors without damaging them.
• Straight pull — in one wall, out the opposite wall: the distance from the entry to the opposite wall must be at least eight times the trade size of the largest raceway.
• Angle pull, U pull or splices: that distance must be at least six times the largest raceway in the row, plus the sum of the trade sizes of the other raceways in the same row on the same wall.
• Raceways that enclose the same conductor: the distance between them must be at least six times the larger raceway.
• These rules are in 314.28(A)(1) and (A)(2).
sections.on_the_job: Worked example: a straight pull with a largest raceway of 2 in needs at least 16 in from entry to opposite wall. An angle pull in a row with a 2 in and a 1 in raceway needs at least (6 x 2) + 1 = 13 in to the opposite wall. Cubic inches do not rescue a box that fails this geometry. That is the check to run at layout, tape in hand, before the box is ordered — on a Sharma commercial job the box size comes out of this math, not out of the cubic-inch table.
sections.figure_idea: Two plan-view box diagrams side by side: straight pull dimensioned 8x, angle pull dimensioned 6x + sum of the row.
sections.why_it_exists: Conductors 4 AWG and larger are stiff, heavy and expensive. Force one around too tight a bend and the insulation scrapes, kinks or splits — damage that may not show until the feeder runs loaded and hot. The 8-times and 6-times geometry gives the wire a bend it can survive, and gives the electrician room to actually make the pull.
inspection_fails: Straight pull in an undersized box: 2 in raceway needs 16 in entry-to-opposite-wall; a 12 in box fails (314.28(A)(1)).
Angle pull box sized by cubic inches instead of six times the largest raceway plus the row sum (314.28(A)(2)).
Raceways enclosing the same conductor entering less than six times the larger raceway apart.
Smaller box substituted at trim with splices added — the angle/U geometry now applies and fails.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer sizes the box by cubic inches, the way 314.16 sizes device boxes. For conductors 4 AWG and larger, 314.28 is geometry, not volume: eight times for a straight pull, six times plus the row for an angle pull. A deep, high-volume box with a short wall-to-wall distance still fails.

tables.caption: 314.28 geometry at a glance
rows: 6 × largest in row + sum of others in row

figures.alt: Two plan-view pull boxes: a straight pull with a 2 inch raceway dimensioned 16 inches minimum from entry to opposite wall, eight times the raceway, and an angle pull with 2 inch and 1 inch raceways dimensioned 13 inches minimum, six times two plus one.
figures.caption: Straight pull: 8× the largest raceway. Angle pull: 6× plus the rest of the row.

page_quiz.question: A straight pull has a largest raceway of 2 in. Minimum distance from entry to the opposite wall?
page_quiz.explain_plain: Straight pull: eight times the largest raceway — 8 × 2 in = 16 in.

page_quiz.question: An angle pull row holds a 2 in and a 1 in raceway. Minimum distance to the opposite wall?
page_quiz.explain_plain: Six times the largest raceway in the row, plus the others: (6 × 2) + 1 = 13 in.

page_quiz.question: Two raceways enclose the same conductor. They must be at least how far apart?
page_quiz.explain_plain: Raceways enclosing the same conductor must be at least six times the larger raceway apart.

sections.title: Boxes must stay accessible
sections.plain_explanation:
A junction or pull box has to remain accessible without removing any part of the building — no drywall, no tile, no fixed cabinetry over the cover. If reaching the splice means cutting the building open, the box was in the wrong place when the walls were open.
• The rule covers boxes, conduit bodies and handhole enclosures alike: the wiring inside has to be renderable accessible without removing or damaging the building or structure (314.29).
• Accessible does not mean visible from the middle of the room. A cover above a lift-out ceiling tile, behind a removable access panel, or in a closet wall is fine — the test is reaching it with the building finished and intact.
• It pairs with 300.15: a box or conduit body is required at every splice, outlet, switch, junction, termination and pull point in the first place. A legal splice in a box nobody can reach still fails.
• Buried junction boxes fail twice — the splice is entombed and the cover can never come off. Underground work uses handhole enclosures that stay reachable from grade.
sections.on_the_job: Before close-in, walk the job and photograph every junction box location. If a cover will be behind a fixed finish, move the box or move the splice now. On Sharma houses the classic trap is the kitchen: a junction box drawn on the wall where the builder's fixed pantry cabinets land. Moving the splice 2 ft at rough-in costs minutes; after the cabinets are set, the same fix is a cabinet removal, a drywall patch, and a callback nobody bills.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: Splices are where installations fail first — a loose joint heats, arcs, and needs hands on it years later. Accessibility is what turns a hidden failure into a service call instead of a fire investigation. The rule protects the next electrician and the building owner, not the installer: the cheapest day to move a box is rough-in day.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is 'accessible means you can get to it by cutting a small hole — drywall is easy to patch.' The rule is accessibility without removing any part of the building. The moment the saw comes out, the installation has already failed: the box had to be reachable with the building finished and intact.
inspection_fails: Junction box buried behind drywall with no cover showing — 'the splice is in there somewhere' is the write-up (314.29).
Box cover blocked by fixed kitchen cabinetry or a tiled shower wall (314.29).
Splice made loose in a wall cavity with no box at all (300.15) — found years later with a toner on a service call.
Conduit body used as a junction point and then entombed in a slab pour.
Handhole enclosure paved over or left below finished grade.

figures.caption: The test: open the cover with the building finished — no saw, no demo.

page_quiz.question: A junction box cover ends up behind a screwed-down, fixed kitchen cabinet. What is the verdict?
choices: Fine, if the splice is listed
A violation only if the box has splices
page_quiz.explain_plain: 314.29 requires boxes to remain accessible without removing any part of the building. Fixed cabinetry over the cover fails that test.

page_quiz.question: Which of these keeps a junction box accessible?
page_quiz.explain_plain: A lift-out tile is not part of the building structure in the way tile, flooring and fixed paneling are — the cover can be reached without demolition.

page_quiz.question: A splice point in a conduit run is made with no box at all. Which section is violated first?
choices: 300.15 — a box or conduit body is required at each splice point
No violation if the splice is taped well
page_quiz.explain_plain: 300.15 requires the box at the splice point; 314.29 then requires that box to stay accessible. No box at all fails 300.15 before accessibility is even reached.

sections.title: Armored cable — Type AC
sections.plain_explanation:
Type AC is a factory cable with its conductors inside a flexible metal armor, with an internal bonding strip in contact with the armor so the armor can serve as the equipment ground path. Sharma meets this article most often through one cross-reference: 334.23 sends NM cable in accessible attics to the attic protection rules written here in 320.23.
• Across the top of floor joists, or within 7 ft of the floor or floor joists across the face of rafters or studding, cable in an accessible attic must be protected by substantial guard strips at least as high as the cable (320.23(A)).
• Where the attic is not accessible by permanent stairs or a ladder, that protection is required only within 6 ft of the nearest edge of the scuttle hole or attic entrance.
• Cable run parallel to the sides of rafters, studs, or ceiling or floor joists needs neither guard strips nor running boards (320.23(B)) — and the run must still comply with 300.4(D).
• The cable itself shows up on Sharma jobs mainly in older work and the occasional commercial job.
sections.on_the_job: Do not confuse AC with MC: AC carries its bonding strip and uses fittings listed for AC; MC (Article 330) usually carries a separate green ground conductor. The fittings are not interchangeable by habit — use the fitting listed for the cable in your hand. In a Florida attic this article is daily work even when no AC cable is on the truck: 334.23 applies the 320.23 guard-strip rule to the NM cable Sharma crews run every day.
sections.figure_idea: Detail of AC cable end: armor, bonding strip folded back, anti-short bushing at the connector.

nec2023_change.change: The attic rule now speaks of framing members instead of floor joists, and measures the 7-ft zone from the floor or an equivalent horizontal surface. The distances didn't change. Cable laid over the tops of framing members in an accessible attic needs guard strips as tall as the cable or taller.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 320.23 Cable protection in attics

sections.why_it_exists: Attic cable gets stepped on, knelt on and buried under stored boxes. A cable crushed flat across a joist is a fault waiting for the next footstep, so the guard strips take the traffic instead. In the cable itself, the bonding strip keeps the armor a continuous ground path, so a fault to the armor trips the breaker instead of energizing the run.
inspection_fails: MC fitting used on Type AC cable, or an AC fitting on MC — the fitting must be listed for the cable type in hand.
Cable across the tops of attic floor joists, within 7 ft of the floor, with no guard strips (320.23(A), applied to NM by 334.23).
Guard strips shorter than the cable they are supposed to protect.
Bonding strip cut off flush at the connector instead of folded back, breaking the armor's ground path.
sections.exam_trap: Two traps. First: AC and MC are the same cable with two names — they are not. AC's ground path is its armor with the internal bonding strip; MC usually carries a separate green conductor, and each takes its own listed fittings. Second: guard strips are an NM rule — they are written here in 320.23 for AC, and 334.23 is what applies them to NM.

figures.alt: Enlarged end of a Type AC cable at a box connector: flexible metal armor, the internal bonding strip folded back over the armor, an anti-short bushing at the cut end, and a connector listed for Type AC.
figures.caption: Armor plus bonding strip is the ground path — no green conductor inside.

page_quiz.question: In an accessible attic, cable run across the top of floor joists must have guard-strip protection where it is within ___ of the floor or floor joists.
page_quiz.explain_plain: 320.23(A) sets the zone at 7 ft, across the face of rafters or studding as well as across joist tops.

page_quiz.question: The equipment grounding path in Type AC cable is:
choices: A separate green conductor inside the armor
The armor, with its internal bonding strip in contact with it
A ground rod at each outlet
page_quiz.explain_plain: AC is built with a bonding strip in contact with the armor, so the armor itself serves as the equipment ground path.

page_quiz.question: An attic is reached only through a scuttle hole. Guard-strip protection across the joists is required only within ___ of the nearest edge of the opening.
page_quiz.explain_plain: Where the space is not accessible by permanent stairs or a ladder, 320.23(A) requires the protection only within 6 ft of the scuttle hole or attic entrance edge.
