sections.title: Flat cable assemblies — Type FC
sections.plain_explanation:
Type FC is a factory flat-cable assembly: parallel conductors formed integrally with an insulating web. It is made to be field-installed in a surface metal raceway identified for the use. It is a specialized listed system — cable, raceway, tap devices and fittings together — installed by this article and the manufacturer's instructions. It is not a substitute for NM run loose in a wall.
• Branch circuits only, rated not over 30 A.
• Loads: suitable tap devices for lighting, small appliances, or small power loads.
• Exposed work only, in locations where it will not be subject to physical damage.
• Installed less than 8 ft above the floor or a fixed working platform, it needs a cover identified for the use.
sections.on_the_job: Sharma does not install Type FC on ordinary work. If a spec calls for it — usually a specialty surface-raceway system on a retrofit — the listed system components come as a set: cable, raceway, tap devices and fittings from the same system. Do not mix in ordinary boxes or fittings, and do not substitute NM where the drawings show FC.
sections.edition_note:
NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 322.56(8): Made changes to flat cable assembly requirements by removing the term "color-coded" and replacing it with "marked" in Section 322.56(B).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: The flat cable has no armor and no raceway of its own — the surface metal raceway and its cover are the protection. Run loose or pinched, the thin web insulation is the only thing between the conductors and a nail, a chair leg, or a cleaning cart. The 30 A cap and the listed tap devices keep the system inside what that thin construction can safely carry.
inspection_fails: Type FC run without the surface metal raceway identified for the use — stapled or loose in the wall.
FC used as a feeder, or on a branch circuit over 30 A.
FC installed below 8 ft with no identified cover over it.
Ordinary device boxes and fittings mixed into the listed FC system.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer treats Type FC like flat NM: staple it in a wall and feed it from any breaker. Wrong twice. FC goes only in a surface metal raceway identified for the use, and only as a branch circuit of 30 A or less. A 40 A feeder on FC, or FC buried in a wall without its raceway, is not this article at all.

sections.title: Flat conductor cable — Type FCC
sections.plain_explanation:
Type FCC is a flat conductor cable system designed to be installed under carpet squares: flat cable taped down on a hard, smooth floor over insulating bedding, protected above and below by metal shields, feeding floor pedestals and outlets exactly where the desks land. It is a different method from Type FC flat cable assemblies (Article 322) — the two are not interchangeable, and neither is ordinary branch wiring in a flat jacket.
• Branch circuits only: general-purpose circuits at not over 20 A, individual branch circuits at not over 30 A; not over 300 V between ungrounded conductors and 150 V to ground (324.10).
• The cable and its fittings are listed as a system (324.6). A 20 A power run is three flat 12 AWG copper conductors — hot, neutral and equipment grounding conductor — sandwiched between the shields.
• Not permitted in residential buildings, and not in schools or hospitals outside their administrative areas (324.12).
• Not more than two cable runs may cross at any one point (324.18).
• Carpet squares over the system may not be larger than 1 m (39.37 in.) square, and they go down with release-type adhesive so the system stays reachable (324.41).
• The metal shields are grounded, with connectors made for that connection (324.60).
sections.on_the_job: Encountered almost only in specialized commercial fit-outs. Identify the system by its listing before touching an existing FCC installation. In an Orlando office remodel, the find is usually a floor pedestal with no conduit in the slab and no poke-through fitting: lift one carpet square — they come up, release adhesive — and the shielded flat run is underneath. Sharma does not extend FCC with field improvisation; a change means the manufacturer's transition fittings, and a check that the circuit still sits inside the 20 A and 30 A limits.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: People walk, roll chairs and drag desks across this wiring every day. The shields spread the load and guard the flat conductors against heels, casters and dropped equipment, and the shield grounding rule exists because a damaged shield that is not bonded can sit at line voltage under someone's feet. The carpet-square size cap keeps any section of the system liftable for inspection and repair.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is calling FCC and Type FC the same thing because both are flat. Type FC (Article 322) is a factory flat-cable assembly installed in a surface metal raceway. Type FCC (Article 324) is the under-carpet floor system with shields and carpet-square rules. Reaching for the FC numbers fails the FCC question: FCC general-purpose circuits cap at 20 A, not 30 A.
inspection_fails: Carpet squares larger than 1 m (39.37 in.) square over the system, or squares glued down with permanent adhesive (324.41).
Metal shields left ungrounded, or bonded with a random screw and lug instead of the connector made for the shield (324.60).
Three or more cable runs crossed at one point, lumping under the carpet (324.18).
FCC installed in a residence, or run through a school outside its administrative areas (324.12).
Type FC parts or ordinary flat cable mixed into an FCC system — the two systems are not interchangeable.

sections.title: Integrated gas spacer cable — Type IGS
sections.plain_explanation:
Type IGS is a specialized underground cable: a factory assembly of one or more individually insulated conductors — solid aluminum rods laid parallel — enclosed in a loose-fit nonmetallic flexible conduit, insulated with dry kraft paper and pressurized sulfur hexafluoride (SF6) gas.
• Rating: 0 through 600 V.
• Use: below grade only — service conductors, feeders and branch circuits, including direct earth burial.
• Never: as interior wiring, exposed in contact with a building, or above ground.
It exists in the book so the map is complete — far outside house and light-commercial branch work.
sections.on_the_job: No Sharma field use. If IGS appears on a drawing, it is an engineered system — escalate, do not substitute a familiar cable. That means a call to the engineer of record before rough-in, not a swap to UF or SE cable from the truck: nothing Sharma stocks replaces a gas-insulated assembly, and the 600 V rating does not make it interchangeable with ordinary 600 V building wire.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: The gas is part of the insulation system: pressurized SF6 inside a sealed assembly keeps moisture out and gives the cable its dielectric strength underground, where a conventional jacket would sit in wet soil for decades. That is also why the prohibitions are absolute. The assembly is engineered as a buried system; brought indoors, run above ground or laid against a building, it is outside everything it was built and listed for.
inspection_fails: IGS run above grade on a site job — Article 326 is a below-grade method only.
IGS brought inside and used as interior wiring — a prohibited use.
IGS left exposed in contact with the building instead of staying below grade.
IGS swapped for a familiar cable in the field — an engineered assembly is not field-substitutable.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating IGS like another direct-burial cable you can bring up into the building. You cannot: below grade only — never interior wiring, never exposed against a building, never above ground. The second trap is the gas: it is sulfur hexafluoride (SF6), and it is part of the insulation, not a tracer gas or a shipping fill.

page_quiz.explain_plain: IGS is a 0 through 600 V factory assembly for below-grade services, feeders and branch circuits.

page_quiz.question: IGS may be used…
page_quiz.explain_plain: Below grade only, including direct earth burial; interior, above-ground and building-contact uses are prohibited.

page_quiz.explain_plain: Dry kraft paper and pressurized SF6 gas form the insulation system.

sections.title: Metal-clad cable — Type MC
sections.plain_explanation:
Type MC is a factory assembly of insulated conductors inside a metal sheath — smooth, corrugated or interlocked armor — with its own equipment grounding arrangement. It is the commercial counterpart to NM: it can be used exposed or concealed, in dry locations and the other locations its listing allows, fished in existing walls, and run where NM cannot go, such as many commercial ceilings and walls. It may not be used where it will be subject to physical damage, in wet locations unless the specific cable is listed for it, or in the other prohibited uses its article lists.

The support numbers (330.30): MC is secured at intervals not exceeding 6 ft; cables with four or fewer conductors no larger than 10 AWG are also secured within 12 in. of every box, cabinet, fitting or other termination (330.30(B)). Listed cables with 250 kcmil or larger ungrounded conductors in vertical runs may be secured at up to 10 ft. Short lengths to luminaires and fished runs in existing walls have their own exceptions in that section — the 12 in and 6 ft figures are the default rhythm.
sections.on_the_job: Cut MC with the right tool and use listed MC connectors — a Romex connector is not an MC connector. Support and securing follow 330.30 (see the companion lookup), with the familiar pattern of securing close to boxes and supporting at regular intervals, plus exceptions for fished runs and short lengths to luminaires.
sections.sharma_note: S-01 applies on commercial work, where MC is most used: 20A minimum branch circuits, 12 AWG copper minimum.

sections.why_it_exists: The metal armor is the point of MC: it protects the conductors where NM would be exposed to damage, and it gives commercial work a factory assembly that can run exposed. The support rhythm keeps long runs from sagging, chafing at studs and pulling on terminations — most MC failures start as a loose run vibrating against a sharp armor edge.
inspection_fails: NM (Romex) connector used on MC cable — MC requires listed MC connectors.
MC supported at 8 ft intervals — 330.30 caps support intervals at 6 ft.
12 AWG MC landed in a box with nothing securing it within 12 in of the termination — 330.30(B).
MC run where subject to physical damage without protection.
MC installed in a wet location where the cable is not listed for wet locations.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer treats MC like NM: a Romex connector at the box and supports 'every so often.' Both fail. MC takes listed MC connectors, and 330.30 sets the rhythm — supports at intervals not exceeding 6 ft, and small cables (four or fewer conductors, 10 AWG or smaller) secured within 12 in of every termination.

sections.title: Where MC may — and may not — be used
sections.plain_explanation:
Type MC is the commercial workhorse because its list of permitted uses is long:
• Exposed or concealed, in dry locations.
• In cable tray.
• Fished into existing walls and ceilings.
• In wet locations — only where the specific cable assembly is listed for it. An impervious jacket or corrosion-resistant construction is what makes an MC cable wet-location legal; plain interlocked armor is not.
The not-permitted list is shorter but firm:
• Where subject to physical damage.
• As a direct-burial cable, unless the specific cable is identified for burial.
• Embedded in concrete or aggregate, unless identified for it.
Read the jacket print: the ratings live on the cable, not in the article's title.
sections.on_the_job: Before MC leaves the shop, match the jacket print to the location: wet location, tray, plenum — each is a marking on the actual cable. On a Sharma commercial job in Winter Park — six 20 A Siemens branch circuits for a retail tenant — standard interlocked MC above a dry ceiling is fine. The same reel is not fine for the two circuits that cross the damp mechanical yard wall: those get the jacketed, wet-listed assembly. 'MC is MC' is how a dry-location cable ends up in a damp mechanical room and fails inspection.
sections.figure_idea: Three MC reels with jacket legends highlighted: standard interlocked (dry), jacketed and wet-location listed, and tray rated, each with its location tag.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: The armor on ordinary MC is a spiral of interlocked metal tape. It is not sealed, it is not a shield against water, and it is not armor plate against a forklift. Water walks down the spiral into boxes, and one hard hit crushes conductors against the armor edge. The listing on the jacket — wet, burial, concrete — is the difference between the cable that survives the location and the one that fails in it.
inspection_fails: Plain interlocked-armor MC run in a wet location — no wet listing on the jacket print.
MC run exposed and low on a warehouse or shop wall where carts and lifts hit it — subject to physical damage.
MC direct-buried in a trench without a burial identification on the cable.
MC poured into a concrete slab when the cable is not identified for embedment.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is 'MC is MC.' The exam — and the supply-house counter — want you to treat every MC reel as wet-rated, burial-rated and concrete-rated. Plain interlocked armor is none of those. The rating is on the jacket print of the specific cable, and 330.12's short list (physical damage, burial, concrete) fails the generic reel every time.

sections.title: Securing and supporting MC cable
sections.plain_explanation:
MC cable is secured within 12 in of each box, cabinet, or fitting, and supported at intervals of not more than 6 ft. The exceptions carry the field cases:
• Fished through existing walls or ceilings — no securing required where the cable cannot be reached
• A length of not more than 6 ft from the last point of support to a luminaire or other equipment within an accessible ceiling — the ceiling whip
• Short lengths at terminals where flexibility is needed for equipment that moves or vibrates
• Flexibility after installation — not more than 3 ft from the last point of support or securing where flexibility is needed (330.30(D)(2))
Outside those cases, a long unsupported drape of MC across a ceiling is a violation even if it happens to be resting on the grid. The 12 in securing distance applies to cables with four or fewer conductors no larger than 10 AWG; the 6 ft support interval applies to all MC.
sections.on_the_job: On a Sharma tenant build-out in Orlando — 20 A Siemens circuits in MC over a lay-in ceiling — the run leaves the panel, straps within 12 in of the connector, then supports at 6 ft or less down the corridor. The drop to each lay-in fixture is a whip of not more than 6 ft, and that 6 ft is measured from the last real support — not from wherever the cable happened to leave the bundle. Strap MC like you mean it, with straps that fit the cable: a loose strap is not a support.
sections.figure_idea: MC run above a ceiling: strap at 12 in from the box, supports dimensioned at 6 ft, and a 6 ft whip dropping to a lay-in fixture.
sections.why_it_exists: Unsupported MC sags under its own weight. The armor edges work at the connectors, the terminations take mechanical stress they were never meant to carry, and a run dropped loose across a ceiling gets stepped on, buried under other trades' work, and damaged. Securing at the box and supporting the run keeps the stress off the terminations and keeps the cable where the next trade expects to find it.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: MC lying on the ceiling grid is "supported by the grid," and a whip can run 6 ft from wherever the cable leaves the bundle. Both are wrong. The grid is not a support, and the whip's 6 ft is measured from the last point of support. The other classic miss is giving MC the NM numbers — the 12 in securing distance is shared, but the support interval is 6 ft for MC, not 4-1/2 ft.
inspection_fails: MC draped across the ceiling grid with no supports — the grid is not a support.
Ceiling whip measured from the cable bundle instead of the last support, landing at 8 ft.
MC secured 18 in from the box connector instead of within 12 in.
Oversized straps that let the cable slide and sag between supports.

sections.title: Mineral-insulated, metal-sheathed cable — Type MI
sections.plain_explanation:
Type MI is a factory assembly: solid conductors packed in highly compressed magnesium oxide — a refractory mineral insulation — inside a continuous liquidtight, gastight sheath of copper or alloy steel. There is no plastic anywhere in it. That is why it is chosen where extreme heat, fire survival or mechanical abuse rules out ordinary methods: fire-pump and critical circuits, and harsh industrial spots.
Article 332 permits it almost anywhere (332.10):
• Services, feeders and branch circuits — power, lighting, control and signal circuits
• Dry, wet or continuously moist locations; indoors or outdoors; exposed or concealed
• Embedded in plaster, concrete or masonry, above or below grade
• Hazardous (classified) locations, and where exposed to oil or gasoline
• Underground runs, where protected against physical damage and corrosive conditions
The hard stop is 332.12: not where conditions are destructive or corrosive to the metal sheath, unless the sheath gets added protection. Bends stay gentle for a metal tube — inside radius at least 5 times the cable's outside diameter up to 3/4 in diameter, 10 times over 3/4 in up to 1 in (332.24). Supports run at intervals of not more than 6 ft (332.30). Terminations are sealing fittings, and the end seal goes on immediately after the sheath is stripped (332.40) — the mineral insulation drinks moisture from the air, so moisture control at the ends is part of the installation.
sections.on_the_job: Sharma meets MI mainly as existing work in older or specialized installations — a fire-pump feeder in a mid-rise, a heat-soaked run near commercial kitchen equipment. Do not cut or terminate it with NM/MC habits — the sealing fitting and its instructions govern. If an MI run has to be extended or replaced, treat it as engineered work and flag it for the office: there is no ordinary field splice for MI, and a stripped end left open over a weekend can ruin the run.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: Magnesium oxide does not burn, melt or smoke, and the metal sheath holds together through a fire that destroys ordinary insulation. That is the point: the fire-pump and egress circuits stay alive when everything around them is not. The sealing rule exists because the same powder that survives fire absorbs moisture from the air — a damp end quietly drops the insulation resistance until the circuit faults.
inspection_fails: Stripped MI end left unsealed over the weekend — moisture in the magnesium oxide, insulation resistance gone (332.40).
Bend kinked tight at a corner — inside radius under 5 times the cable diameter (332.24).
MI run through cinder fill or corrosive soil with the copper sheath unprotected (332.12).
Supports spaced over 6 ft, cable sagging between straps (332.30).
Termination made with a generic connector instead of the listed sealing fitting for Type MI.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating MI like armored cable with a fancy jacket: strip it Friday, seal it Monday. The mineral insulation absorbs moisture the whole time the end sits open, and the circuit fails its insulation test — or faults in service. The seal goes on immediately (332.40). Second trap: bending it like NM. The inside bend radius is 5 times the outside diameter, 10 times on the larger sizes (332.24).

The mineral insulation absorbs moisture from the air
The conductors oxidize and turn green
The sealant only cures when warm
page_quiz.explain_plain: Magnesium oxide is hygroscopic — it drinks moisture, and the insulation resistance falls until the circuit faults.

sections.title: Nonmetallic-sheathed cable — Types NM, NMC, NMS (Romex)
sections.plain_explanation:
This is Sharma's house cable. NM is two or more insulated conductors with an equipment ground, factory-wrapped in a nonmetallic sheath. Article 334 says where it may be used (334.10), where it may never be used (334.12), how it is protected and run (334.15, 334.17, 334.23), how it is bent (334.24), how often it is secured and supported (334.30), and how its ampacity is limited (334.80). Almost every Sharma rough-in decision — staple spacing, attic runs, the 60°C ampacity limit — traces back to this one article.
• Secured and supported (334.30): within 12 in of every box, cabinet and fitting, and at intervals of 4-1/2 ft or less; a run through bored holes counts as supported by the framing. Flat cable is never stapled on edge.
• Bends (334.24): the inner edge of a bend keeps a radius of at least five times the cable diameter — wide, lazy turns, no kinks.
• Ampacity (334.80): NM is sized from the 60 °C column. 12 AWG NM lands on a 20 A breaker, and no 90 °C math changes that.
• Protection (334.15, with 300.4): where the cable passes through framing it keeps the 1-1/4 in setback, or gets the 1/16 in steel plate.
sections.on_the_job: If you learn one article in this chapter cold, learn this one. The other methods are variations; NM is the daily work. A Sharma home run in 12/2: stapled within 12 in of the panel and of the device box, supported every 4-1/2 ft or less between, bored holes centered in the studs. The run feeds a 20 A circuit — Sharma commercial work also starts at 20 A — and 334.80 holds that 12 AWG to its 60 °C value, 20 A, whatever the conductors inside could carry in conduit.
sections.figure_idea: A coil of 12/2 NM beside a stapled stud bay run, with callouts to 334.30 (staples), 334.15 (protection) and 334.80 (ampacity).

nec2023_change.change: A new NM cable-entry section: wherever NM enters a box, cabinet or other enclosure, at least 1/4 in. of its jacket has to extend past the clamp or entry point. Where NM enters an enclosure, its outer jacket has to run at least 1/4 in. beyond the clamp or entry (334.19).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 334.19 NM jacket past the clamp

nec2023_change.change: Splicing NM cable with no box inside walls and ceilings is now allowed on new work too, not just repairs, as long as the splice uses a listed NM cable interconnector. Listed NM cable interconnectors can join nonmetallic-sheathed (NM) cable without a box, exposed or hidden in walls and ceilings, new or existing (334.40(B)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 334.40 Boxless NM cable splices

sections.why_it_exists: NM is a soft cable in a hard world: a plastic sheath over conductors that drywall screws, picture nails and careless staples all want to cut. Article 334's spacing, bend and ampacity limits keep the sheath whole and the conductors cool for the life of the house.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is the 90 °C escape: 'the conductors inside NM are rated 90 °C, so 12 AWG can carry 30 A.' 334.80 closes that door — NM ampacity is the 60 °C result, 20 A for 12 AWG, before any derating.
inspection_fails: Staples 6 ft apart on a vertical run; 334.30 caps the interval at 4-1/2 ft.
First staple 2 ft from the box; 334.30 wants it within 12 in.
Flat NM stapled on edge, the sheath crushed by the staple (334.30).
12 AWG NM protected at 30 A off the 90 °C column (334.80).

page_quiz.explain_plain: 334.30: secured within 12 in, and supported at intervals not over 4-1/2 ft.

page_quiz.question: Support intervals for NM may not exceed:
page_quiz.explain_plain: 334.30 caps NM support intervals at 4-1/2 ft; framing the cable passes through counts as support.

page_quiz.question: The largest breaker for 12 AWG NM is:
page_quiz.explain_plain: 334.80 sizes NM from the 60 °C column: 20 A for 12 AWG, and 240.4(D) agrees.

sections.title: Where NM may be used
sections.plain_explanation:
NM may be used exposed or concealed, but only in normally dry locations, and only in the buildings this section names:
• One- and two-family dwellings, and their detached garages and storage buildings.
• Multifamily dwellings permitted to be of Type III, IV or V construction.
• Other buildings and structures permitted to be of Type III, IV or V construction — and there the cable must be concealed inside walls, floors or ceilings that provide a thermal barrier with at least a 15-minute finish rating.
• In cable trays inside those permitted structures, where the cable is identified for tray use.
• In Type I and II construction, only inside a raceway.
• Fished into the hollow voids of masonry block or tile walls, in dry locations.
Two gates decide every NM call: the location is normally dry, and the building is one the section permits. The construction type is what the building code permits the building to be for its occupancy — not just what the framing in front of you happens to be.
sections.on_the_job: House, garage and accessory work in dry interiors: NM is the default. Anything wet, damp, underground or in a bigger occupancy: stop and check 334.12 and pick another method. On a Sharma single-family rough-in that means 12/2 NM on the 20 A kitchen and bath circuits and 14/2 on the 15 A lighting, all inside the dry envelope — and the detached garage is on the same permission. The lanai receptacles and the pool equipment are a different story: that is UF or THWN in PVC, because the location is not normally dry. On a Type V wood-frame retail shell, NM is allowed only concealed behind the 15-minute finish — the same cable run exposed across the ceiling is a violation.
sections.edition_note:
NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 334.10: NM can now wire the detached garages that serve Type III, IV and V multifamily buildings, the same as the buildings themselves. NM is allowed in Type III, IV or V multifamily dwellings, and now in their detached garages too (334.10(2)).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: The NM sheath is a light plastic jacket with no armor and no wet-location rating. Kept dry and protected, it lasts the life of the building. The building-type limits are fire rules: in combustible Type III, IV and V construction the cable hides behind rated finishes, and in noncombustible Type I and II buildings the wiring belongs in raceway, so a cable fault does not become a fire path through a rated building.
inspection_fails: NM run exposed across the ceiling of a Type V retail shell — 334.10(3) requires it concealed behind a 15-minute finish barrier.
NM feeding pool equipment and lanai receptacles — not a normally dry location.
NM run exposed above the drop ceiling of a Type II tenant space — Type I and II means raceway.
NM fished into a damp below-grade block wall — the masonry-void permission is for dry locations.
sections.exam_trap: The exam's favorite wrong answer: “NM is permitted exposed in any Type III, IV or V building.” In dwellings, exposed NM is fine. In other Type III, IV and V structures the cable must be concealed behind the 15-minute thermal barrier — exposed NM across a small commercial ceiling fails even though the building type is on the list.

sections.title: Where NM may not be used
sections.plain_explanation:
NM may not be used:
• In wet or damp locations — including inside a raceway that is itself underground or outdoors, because the interior of that raceway is a wet location (300.5(B), 300.9)
• As service-entrance cable
• In any dwelling or structure 334.10 does not permit — Type I and II buildings, outside a raceway
• Exposed within a dropped or suspended ceiling in anything other than one- and two-family and multifamily dwellings
• In commercial garages that have hazardous (classified) locations (511.3)
• In theaters, or in motion picture studios
• In storage battery rooms
• In hoistways, or on elevators or escalators
• Embedded in poured concrete or aggregate
• In hazardous (classified) locations, except where another article specifically permits it
• Where exposed to physical damage, unless it is protected
It is a dry, protected, interior method — every item on this list is one of those three words failing.
sections.on_the_job: The classic fail: NM sleeved in PVC down an outside wall and underground to a yard light. The PVC does not make the location dry. Use UF or conductors in raceway for that run (Articles 340 and 352). The same thinking kills two more Florida habits: NM as the cable between the meter and the panel on a service upgrade — that is Type SE cable or conductors in raceway, never NM — and NM stapled across a lanai ceiling for a pool light, where wind-driven rain makes the location damp.
sections.figure_idea: Red-X diagram: NM entering an underground PVC run; green-check diagram beside it with UF cable on the same route.
sections.florida_note: Florida's humidity does not reclassify an interior dry location, but any exterior or underground raceway interior is wet — plan the method for the location, not the weather.

sections.why_it_exists: Water inside the sheath wicks along the cable, corrodes the bare equipment ground and rots the filler, so a “protected” outdoor run fails from the inside years later. The occupancy bans are ignition rules: theaters, battery rooms and classified locations cannot carry a light plastic-sheathed method where fault arcs, hydrogen or solvent vapors are part of the design case. Embedded cable cannot be inspected or replaced, so concrete is out too.
inspection_fails: NM in PVC conduit underground to the yard light — the interior of the raceway is a wet location (334.12).
NM used as service-entrance cable between the meter and the panel.
NM embedded in the concrete slab for a floor outlet.
NM run exposed above the suspended ceiling in a retail tenant space.
NM feeding the pool pump across the lanai ceiling — damp and wet exposure.
sections.exam_trap: The wrong answer everyone reaches for: “The NM is inside PVC conduit, so the location is dry.” The Code counts the inside of an underground or outdoor raceway as a wet location, full stop. The conduit protects against physical damage, not against the location classification — the cable inside still has to be a wet-location method.

Permitted if the conduit is sealed at both ends
Not permitted — the raceway interior is a wet location

page_quiz.explain_plain: The dropped-ceiling ban in 334.12 exempts one- and two-family and multifamily dwellings. Commercial ceilings are off limits for exposed NM.

sections.title: NM in exposed work and through framing
sections.plain_explanation: Exposed NM has to follow the surface it is run on and be protected where it can be hit. Where it passes through a floor, a wall or framing, the Article 300 protection rules ride along: bored-hole setbacks and nail plates from 300.4, and protection where the cable passes through slots or notches. In unfinished basements and crawl spaces, this section sets how larger cables may run through joists and how smaller cables are run on running boards or through bored holes. The basement and crawl-space case has its own subsection, 334.15(C): where cable runs at angles with the joists, a cable at least as large as two 6 AWG or three 8 AWG conductors may be secured directly to the lower edges of the joists; smaller cables must run through bored holes in the joists or on running boards. NM on the wall of an unfinished basement must be protected — in listed conduit or tubing, or protected the way 300.4 requires — with a bushing or adapter where the cable enters the raceway.
sections.on_the_job: Florida has few basements, so here this is a crawl-space and garage rule. In a raised Kissimmee house, the 12/2 and 14/2 NM crossing the crawl space goes through bored holes in the joists or on running boards — never stapled along the joist bottoms. Treat the space like a wall someone will finish later: keep the cable tight to the framing, bore or board every small run, and plate anything in the strike zone. The one cable that may ride the lower joist edges is a feeder-sized run, at least two 6 AWG or three 8 AWG conductors.
sections.figure_idea: Basement joist bay with NM bored through joist centers and a smaller cable on a running board, both labeled.

nec2023_change.change: Conduit or tubing that protects exposed NM from damage now needs a bushing or adapter at both ends, where the cable goes in and where it comes out (334.15(B)). A conduit or tubing sleeve protecting exposed NM needs a bushing or adapter where the cable enters and where it exits (334.15(B)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 334.15 Bushings on NM sleeves

sections.why_it_exists: Exposed NM has a soft jacket and no armor. In a basement or crawl space it lives where stored boxes, tools and foot traffic can hit it, and where a later finish job can bury a mistake under drywall. Following the surface and protecting the cable at floors, walls and joist edges keeps the jacket — and the insulation under it — intact until the space is finished.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: "334.15(C) lets NM run on the bottom edges of the joists in a crawl space." Only the big cables — at least two 6 AWG or three 8 AWG conductors. The 12/2 and 14/2 branch-circuit cables everyone pictures must go through bored holes in the joists or on running boards. Picking "any NM, secured to the joist bottom" is the wrong answer.
inspection_fails: 12/2 NM stapled along the bottom edges of crawl-space joists — smaller cables go through bored holes or on running boards (334.15(C)).
NM passing through a floor with no 300.4 protection at the framing.
NM sleeved in conduit with the jacket skinned where it enters — no bushing or adapter at the raceway entry.
Exposed NM run loose across a garage wall instead of following the surface and protected where it can be hit.

None — bored holes are always required

sections.title: NM in accessible attics — the scuttle rule
sections.plain_explanation: For accessible attics, this section points NM cable at the attic rules written for AC cable in 320.23: 334.23 says the installation of cable in accessible attics or roof spaces shall also comply with 320.23. Under 320.23(A), cable run across the top of floor joists, or within 7 ft of the floor or floor joists across the face of rafters or studding, has to be protected by substantial guard strips that are at least as high as the cable; where the space is not accessible by permanent stairs or ladders, that protection is required only within 6 ft of the nearest edge of the scuttle hole or attic entrance. Under 320.23(B), cable installed parallel to the sides of rafters, studs, or ceiling or floor joists needs neither guard strips nor running boards, and the installation must also comply with 300.4(D). Sanjay's own ruling in the Sharma note is separate company practice — stricter and simpler than the code rule — and it is what Sharma crews follow on Sharma jobs.
sections.on_the_job: Route attic runs the Sharma way from the start and the inspection question mostly disappears: runs hug the framing, nothing crosses the scuttle opening, and nothing invites a foot. On a Sharma house, the run is planned that way from the panel — within 6 ft of a scuttle with no permanent stairs, NM runs along the sides of the joists or trusses only, parallel to the framing, bends stay at least 1.5 ft clear of the opening, and the attic light sits about 1.5 ft beside the opening with its switch at the entry. That is the company rule in the Sharma note below: stricter than 320.23, and the one the crews are graded on.
sections.sharma_note: SHARMA RULE (Sanjay, definitive 2026-11-09 — company practice, not a code quote): within 6 ft of an attic scuttle with no permanent stairs, run NM along the sides of the joists/trusses only, parallel to the framing, never diagonally across it and never across the opening; no guard strips; bends stay at least 1.5 ft clear of the opening; the attic light sits about 1.5 ft beside the opening with its switch at the entry. This is how BuzzDraws and the crews run it, regardless of how the 320.23 wording settles.
sections.figure_idea: Plan view of a scuttle opening with a 6 ft band shaded around it, NM runs drawn parallel along joist sides inside the band, one diagonal run crossed out.
sections.why_it_exists: Attics get traffic: insulators, HVAC techs and homeowners hauling storage boxes all climb through the same scuttle and step on whatever crosses the joists. NM lying across joist tops in that zone gets crushed and nicked, and a damaged jacket in a hot attic is a fault waiting for a load. Guard strips and the scuttle-zone rules keep cable out from underfoot, right where everyone enters.
inspection_fails: NM across the top of floor joists, or within 7 ft across the face of rafters, with no guard strips (320.23(A) via 334.23).
Cable crossing the scuttle opening, or run unprotected within 6 ft of the scuttle edge where there are no permanent stairs (320.23(A)).
Guard strips lower than the cable they are supposed to protect.
Diagonal run across joists inside the scuttle zone — fails the Sharma rule on every Sharma job.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is answering with a distance out of 334.23 itself. 334.23 sets no distances — it sends NM to the AC cable attic rules in 320.23: guard strips within 7 ft across joist tops and rafter faces, and protection within 6 ft of the scuttle edge where there are no permanent stairs or ladders. "NM is banned in attics" is also wrong; it is permitted, protected.

Runs hug the framing, along the sides
No guard strips or running boards needed
Protection within 6 ft of the opening
Within 6 ft: sides of joists only — never diagonal, never across the opening
Bends stay at least 1.5 ft clear of the opening

figures.alt: Plan view of an attic scuttle opening with a gold 6 foot zone shaded around it, NM cable runs drawn parallel along the sides of the joists inside the zone, one diagonal run crossed out in red, and the attic light marked about 1.5 feet beside the opening.
figures.caption: The scuttle zone: runs parallel along joist sides inside 6 ft — never diagonal, never across the opening.

page_quiz.question: NM run across the top of floor joists, or across the face of rafters, must be protected by guard strips within what distance?
page_quiz.explain_plain: 320.23(A) requires guard strips for cable across joist tops, or within 7 ft of the floor or joists across the face of rafters or studding.

page_quiz.question: The attic is reached only through a scuttle hole — no permanent stairs or ladder. Protection is required within how far of the nearest edge of the opening?
page_quiz.explain_plain: Where the space is not accessible by permanent stairs or ladders, 320.23(A) protection is required only within 6 ft of the scuttle edge.

page_quiz.question: NM installed parallel to the side of a floor joist needs:
choices: Neither guard strips nor running boards
page_quiz.explain_plain: 320.23(B): cable parallel to the sides of rafters, studs or joists needs neither guard strips nor running boards; 300.4(D) still applies.

sections.title: Bending radius of NM cable
sections.plain_explanation:
NM may not be bent so sharply that the bend damages the sheath or the conductors inside it; the rule of this section is expressed as a minimum radius measured to the inner edge of the bend — five times the cable diameter.
• Measure to the inner edge of the curve — not the centerline, not the outside.
• The multiplier is 5: a cable 1/2 in across needs an inside radius of at least 2-1/2 in.
• A kinked flat cable at a tight stud turn is exactly the damage this section is aimed at: a creased sheath and conductors pinched at the crease.
• Flat cable has no true diameter to measure. The 2020 wording still holds it to the same gentle-bend standard; the 2023 wording for flat cable is in the edition box.
sections.on_the_job: Make wide, lazy turns. If you have to force it around a corner with your thumb creasing the sheath, the bend is too tight — re-route or move the hole. Worked check on a Sharma rough-in: a flat cable whose widest dimension is 1/2 in needs an inside radius of 2-1/2 in or more — about the curve you get sweeping cable around a coffee mug, not folding it around your thumb. Staple back from the bend so the sweep survives drywall.

nec2023_change.change: Flat NM no longer gets measured by a diameter it doesn't have. The minimum bend radius is now 5 times the cable's widest dimension. Every NM bend needs an inside radius of 5 times the cable's widest dimension or more.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 334.24 NM bending radius

sections.edition_note:
NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 334.24: Flat NM no longer gets measured by a diameter it doesn't have. The minimum bend radius is now 5 times the cable's widest dimension. Every NM bend needs an inside radius of 5 times the cable's widest dimension or more.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: A tight bend does its damage quietly. The sheath creases and thins on the outside of the curve while the conductors inside are pinched and work-hardened at one point — and the fault shows up years later, inside a finished wall, at exactly that bend. A wide radius spreads the strain over length so no single point takes it all.
inspection_fails: NM kinked around a stud corner, the sheath creased white at the bend (334.24).
Cable folded flat back on itself to take up slack inside a wall.
Bend pulled tight against the edge of a bored hole, inside radius nearly zero.
Flat NM bent around its thin edge with a radius sized off the thickness, not the width.
sections.exam_trap: Two traps. First, measuring the radius to the centerline or the outside of the bend — the rule measures to the inner edge, the tightest point, so both of those measurements flatter a bad bend. Second, sizing a flat cable's bend off its thin edge: under the 2023 wording flat NM is measured by its widest dimension, and even under 2020 the damage standard bans the kink. The multiplier is 5 either way.

figures.alt: Flat NM cable sweeping around a framing corner with the inside bend radius marked at five times the cable diameter, next to a red kinked bend at the corner.
figures.caption: Five times, measured to the inner edge.

page_quiz.question: The bend radius of NM cable is measured to which part of the bend?
page_quiz.explain_plain: 334.24 measures the radius to the inner edge of the bend — the tightest point of the curve.

page_quiz.question: A flat NM cable's widest dimension is 1/2 in. Under the 2023 wording, the minimum inside radius is?
page_quiz.explain_plain: 5 × the widest dimension: 5 × 1/2 in = 2-1/2 in. (2023 wording; the 2020 rule measures 5 × diameter.)

sections.title: Securing and supporting NM
sections.plain_explanation:
NM must be secured and supported at intervals not exceeding 4-1/2 ft, and within 12 in of every box, cabinet and fitting. The hardware — staples, cable ties listed and identified for securement and support, straps, hangers or similar fittings — must be installed so it does not damage the cable.
• Cable run horizontally through bored holes or notches in framing counts as secured and supported by that framing, where the support spacing stays within the same limits (334.30(A)).
• Flat cable may not be stapled on edge, and the staple has to hold the cable snug without crushing the sheath.
• Two runs may go unsupported (334.30(B)): cable fished between access points in a finished building where support is impracticable, and a tail of not more than 4-1/2 ft from the last point of support to a luminaire or other equipment connection, inside an accessible ceiling in a dwelling.
• At a single-gang nonmetallic box with no cable clamp, the 12 in becomes 8 in — the cable must be secured within 8 in of that box (314.17(C) exception).
sections.on_the_job: Staple pattern on a stud run: within 12 in of the box, then at least every 4-1/2 ft, snug not crushed. A staple that deforms the sheath is a damage point, not a support point. On a Sharma rough-in with studs 16 in on center, the bored holes carry the horizontal runs — but the drop to each box still gets its own staple within 12 in, and within 8 in at a clampless single-gang plastic box. Save unsupported runs for fished old work and short luminaire tails in accessible ceilings.
sections.figure_idea: Stud bay with staple positions dimensioned: 12 in max from the box, 4 ft 6 in max between staples.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: An unsupported cable sags, rubs on framing edges, and levers against the terminations at the box every time something tugs the run. The 12 in rule keeps the last stretch from working the connector loose. The snug-not-crushed half matters just as much: a staple driven like a nail deforms the sheath and pinches the conductors — a support that damages the cable is a defect, not a support.
inspection_fails: NM stapled at 6 ft intervals — the MC spacing used on NM (334.30).
No staple within 12 in of the box; the cable hangs off the connector.
Flat 14/2 stapled on edge to fit a crowded stud.
Staples driven until the sheath is visibly crushed and deformed.
Long unsupported tail across an attic to a luminaire, well past the 4-1/2 ft allowance of 334.30(B).
sections.exam_trap: The trap is quoting MC cable numbers — MC gets 6 ft intervals; NM gets 4-1/2 ft. The second trap is the box number: 12 in is the rule, 8 in applies only at a single-gang nonmetallic box without a clamp, and neither one is the 4-1/2 ft run interval. An answer that mixes the three numbers is wrong.

figures.alt: Vertical NM run in a stud bay with staples dimensioned within 12 inches of the box and at intervals not over 4 feet 6 inches, stapled flat and snug.
figures.caption: 12 in at the box, 4 ft 6 in along the run.

page_quiz.question: Maximum interval between supports on an NM run?
page_quiz.explain_plain: 334.30 caps NM support intervals at 4-1/2 ft. The 6 ft figure belongs to MC cable.

page_quiz.question: NM enters a single-gang nonmetallic box that has no cable clamp. Secure the cable within?
page_quiz.explain_plain: The 314.17(C) exception tightens the usual 12 in to 8 in at a single-gang nonmetallic box without clamps.

Cable fished through a finished wall where support is impracticable

sections.title: Ampacity of NM cable — the 60°C limit
sections.plain_explanation:
The conductors inside NM are 90 °C rated, but the cable's ampacity is taken from the 60 °C column of Table 310.16.
• Start at 90 °C. Correction and adjustment under 310.15 may begin from the 90 °C value — that is what makes a bundled or hot-attic NM run survivable on paper.
• Finish at 60 °C. The final ampacity after 310.15 may not exceed the 60 °C value.
• The 240.4(D) small-conductor caps still apply on top: 15 A for 14 AWG copper, 20 A for 12 AWG copper.
sections.on_the_job: Field translation: 14 AWG NM on a 15 A breaker and 12 AWG NM on a 20 A breaker, full stop. Florida attic check: two 20 A NM home runs share a foamed hole in a 104 °F attic — four current-carrying conductors. Start at 90 °C: 30 A × 0.91 × 0.80 = 21.8 A on paper. But 334.80 caps the answer at the 60 °C value, 20 A, so the 20 A breaker stands and the extra 1.8 A buys nothing. Do the math from 90 °C, then cap the answer at the 60 °C column — the same place the 240.4(D) breaker cap lands.
sections.sharma_note: S-10 still governs the wire choice: copper by default; CCA one size up. NM ampacity limits apply the same either way, read in the correct 310.16 column for the metal.
sections.figure_idea: Two-column mini-table: 12 AWG NM — 90°C start 30A (Cu) for derating, 60°C final cap 20A, breaker cap 20A.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: The 60 °C cap is the limit of the finished cable, not of the conductor insulation. The conductors can take 90 °C; the cable assembly — jacket and all — is held to the 60 °C column by 334.80. Run NM at 90 °C ampacities year after year and the jacket ages early and turns brittle, and the margin the listing was built on is gone. The two-step math keeps the derating benefit of the 90 °C column without cooking the cable.
inspection_fails: 12 AWG NM on a 25 A breaker because 'the conductors are 90 °C' — the final ampacity is held to the 60 °C column (334.80).
Bundled NM home runs through a foamed hole with no adjustment taken at all.
10 AWG NM protected at 40 A from the 90 °C column — the 60 °C value and the 240.4(D) cap are both 30 A.
Derating started from the 60 °C column, then a circuit failed on paper that the code would have passed.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: 'The conductors in NM are 90 °C, so size it from the 90 °C column.' Wrong finish — the 90 °C column is only the starting point for correction and adjustment, and the result may never land above the 60 °C value. The mirror trap is derating from the 60 °C column, which throws away ampacity the code lets you keep on paper.

tables.note: CCA reads the aluminum columns of Table 310.16; S-10 puts CCA one size up.

page_quiz.explain_plain: 334.80 holds NM to the 60 °C column (20 A for 12 AWG), and 240.4(D) caps it at 20 A as well.

page_quiz.question: Derating NM in a hot attic: you start from ___ and the result is capped at ___.
page_quiz.explain_plain: Correction and adjustment may start from the 90 °C value; the final ampacity may not exceed the 60 °C value.

page_quiz.explain_plain: 21.8 A is the paper result; 334.80 caps the finished cable at the 60 °C value, 20 A.

sections.title: Power and control tray cable — Type TC
sections.plain_explanation:
Type TC is a factory assembly of two or more insulated conductors, with or without an associated grounding conductor, under one overall jacket. It is listed for power, lighting, control and signal circuits. Where it may run (336.10):
• In cable trays — including trays with mechanically discontinuous segments up to 1 ft
• In raceways
• In outdoor locations, supported by a messenger wire
• As Class 1 circuits (Article 725) and as non-power-limited fire alarm circuits (760.49)
• In wet locations, where the cable is also resistant to moisture and corrosive agents
• Direct buried, only where the cable is identified for direct burial
• In one- and two-family dwellings, a TC-ER cable that carries both power and control conductors and is identified for pulling through structural members (marked JP), installed under Part II of Article 334
Tray-rated is the load-bearing word: a cable in a tray must be a cable type Article 392 allows, and TC is the common one. Ratings beyond plain TC — exposed run, sunlight, burial — exist only when the jacket is marked for them.
sections.on_the_job: On a light-commercial tray job, read the jacket print before the cable leaves the shop: TC alone is not every rating — check for the marking that matches the actual installation. On an Orlando warehouse job, the tray runs themselves took plain TC. The drops down to the dock motors were the fight: 8 ft of exposed drop on plain TC is a 336.12 violation, so the drops were re-pulled in TC-ER on strut, secured at intervals not over 6 ft, with only the last short transition unsupported where nothing could hit it.
sections.edition_note:
NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 336.10: Type TC tray cable can now carry service-entrance conductors, but only when the jacket shows TC-ER and the cable is also identified for service use. Type TC power and control tray cable can now be used for service-entrance conductors (336.10(12)).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: TC's jacket is a covering, not armor. Inside a tray or raceway, the system around the cable provides the protection; outside, the cable has to bring its own. The TC-ER crush-and-impact tests are what separate a cable that may step out of the tray from one that may not — which is why the whole article turns on reading the jacket print instead of the cable's shape.
inspection_fails: Plain TC run exposed from the tray down to a motor — no TC-ER marking (336.12(2)).
TC-ER drop left unsupported for 12 ft between tray and equipment — transitions cap at 6 ft (336.10(7)).
TC in direct sun on a rooftop tray, jacket not marked sunlight resistant (336.12(3)).
TC direct buried to a sign, cable not identified for direct burial (336.12(4)).
TC strapped across a forklift route at bumper height — exposed to physical damage (336.12(1)).

sections.title: Type P cable
sections.plain_explanation:
Type P is a rugged, flexible cable construction that comes out of marine and drilling work. In the 2020 NEC it is listed in Article 337 for the applications the article describes, including certain hazardous-location uses noted in the 2020 changes.
• Origin: ships and drilling rigs — service with vibration, movement and rough handling.
• Status: its own listed cable type, with its own article.
• It is not a house cable, and it is not an ordinary commercial branch-circuit cable.
When Type P appears, it appears because an engineer specified it for a specialized job. It is never the cable that just happens to be on the truck.
sections.on_the_job: No Sharma field use on ordinary work. Its presence on a drawing signals a specialized, engineered specification. If a plan set for an industrial or marine job calls out Type P, the callout stays as drawn: the crew does not substitute a familiar cable type on its own, and any change goes back through the engineer who specified it.
sections.edition_note:
NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• Article 337: Changed all references to the former Type P cable to Type IM in Article 337.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: Marine and drilling service punishes cable. Constant vibration, flexing, moisture and rough handling destroy ordinary constructions, and a failed cable in that service can shut down equipment or start a fire where help is far away. Type P exists because that work needs a cable built to take the abuse. The same logic runs the other way: a specialty cable dragged into ordinary work it was not listed for is a mismatch the inspector and the engineer will both catch.
inspection_fails: Type P specification changed to a general-use cable type without the engineer's approval.
Type P installed outside the applications its article describes.
Type P pulled as ordinary branch-circuit wiring on a house or standard commercial job.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating Type P like a familiar general-use cable — a name you can substitute freely or pull for ordinary branch circuits. In the 2020 book it is its own listed type in Article 337, born in marine and drilling work, and it belongs only in the applications its article describes. A house or an ordinary commercial job is not one of them.

sections.title: Service-entrance cable — Types SE and USE
sections.plain_explanation:
Type SE cable is a single-conductor or multi-conductor assembly, primarily used for services.
• Type SE: a flame-retardant, moisture-resistant covering — the above-ground form.
• Type USE: identified for underground use, with a moisture-resistant covering, but not required to have a flame-retardant covering.
On a house, SE is the cable that can carry the service where individual conductors in a mast or raceway are not used. Where SE is used for interior branch-circuit or feeder wiring, 338.10(B)(4) makes the Article 334 installation rules apply to that run — see the 338.10(B)(4) page. Type SE and Type USE are not interchangeable:
• SE shall not be used underground, with or without a raceway.
• USE shall not be used for interior wiring.
A cable that is also marked and listed as another wiring type is used indoors under that other rating, not as USE.
sections.on_the_job: A 200 A service on a Florida block house: the utility drop lands on the mast, and 4/0 aluminum Type SE runs from the meter into a Siemens meter-main (S-02), sized from Table 310.12 (200 A — 2/0 copper / 4/0 aluminum). Where the layout allows, the panel sits back to back with the meter (S-09) and the SE run stays short. The same reel never goes in the trench to the detached garage: underground is USE territory, or conductors in raceway. Keep service work in its own lane — conductor sizing is 310.12 / 310.16 work, the disconnect and grounding live in Chapter 2 and 250 territory, and this article governs the cable itself.
sections.sharma_note: S-02: new meter-mains and disconnects are Siemens. S-09: meter and panel back to back where the house allows.
sections.figure_idea: House elevation: service drop to a mast, SE cable down through the meter to an inside panel.
sections.florida_note: The serving utility (FPL and the Florida co-ops/munis) controls the drop, meter and its own connection rules on top of the NEC.
sections.why_it_exists: SE and USE look alike on the reel, but their coverings are tested against different enemies. SE's covering resists flame spread above ground and inside a building; USE's covering resists ground moisture but was never required to resist flame. Bury SE and the soil works on a covering not identified for it; bring USE indoors and fire can travel along a covering that never passed a flame test. The wrong swap usually passes a glance on rough-in day and fails years later.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer: "USE is just the underground version of SE, so either cable works anywhere the other does." Wrong in both directions — 338.12 bars SE underground even inside a raceway, and bars USE for interior wiring. A dual-marked cable used indoors follows its other listing, not its USE marking.
inspection_fails: SE cable buried to a detached garage or pool panel — SE is barred underground, with or without a raceway (338.12).
USE cable run inside the house as a feeder — USE is not permitted for interior wiring.
Interior SE feeder with no nail plates where it passes within 1-1/4 in of a stud edge — indoors, SE follows Article 334 Part II protection.
Service SE sized off the breaker handle instead of Table 310.12 / 310.16.

sections.title: SE cable used as interior wiring
sections.plain_explanation:
Type SE cable is a service-entrance cable first, but 338.10(B)(4) also lets it be used as interior wiring for branch circuits and feeders inside a building. Used that way, the run is installed like NM cable — with one named exception:
• Routing, protection and support: Part II of Article 334 applies to the indoor SE run.
• Ampacity: 334.80 does NOT apply. The NM ampacity cap stays behind.
• SE has its own narrow ampacity rule instead: for ungrounded conductor sizes 10 AWG and smaller, where installed in contact with thermal insulation, the ampacity is in accordance with the 60 °C conductor temperature rating.
• Everything else about sizing comes from Article 310.
sections.on_the_job: An SE cable feeding a subpanel inside the house is roughed and protected like Romex once it is indoors: bored-hole and notch protection, and the Article 334 support intervals, travel with it. Staple it within 12 in of the subpanel and support it at intervals not over 4-1/2 ft (334.30). On a Kissimmee house the feeder crosses a stud wall: holes are drilled so the cable edge sits at least 1-1/4 in from the stud edge, or a 1/16 in steel plate goes on (300.4(A)(1)). The 334.80 ampacity cap does not travel — 338.10(B)(4) excludes 334.80. Size the conductors from Article 310, and apply the 60 °C column only where 338.10(B)(4) itself requires it: ungrounded conductors 10 AWG and smaller in contact with thermal insulation.
sections.why_it_exists: Once SE cable leaves the service and runs through studs, it faces the same nails, drywall screws and bored holes as Romex, so it gets the same physical protection and support rules. Its ampacity is a different story: SE conductors are not built like NM, so instead of borrowing NM's blanket cap, the Code keeps only the one heat case that matters for this cable — small conductors in contact with insulation.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: "SE indoors follows Article 334, so cap its ampacity at 60 °C like NM." 334.80 is the one section 338.10(B)(4) names as excluded. The 60 °C rating appears only in SE's own narrow rule — ungrounded conductors 10 AWG and smaller installed in contact with thermal insulation.
inspection_fails: SE feeder through studs with no nail plate where the cable passes closer than 1-1/4 in to the edge — indoors, SE takes Article 334 protection (300.4(A)(1)).
SE run supported at conduit intervals or left loose across the attic — 334.30 spacing (12 in at boxes, 4-1/2 ft max) applies to the indoor run.
Load calc sized off the 334.80 NM cap that 338.10(B)(4) excludes — or full Table 310.16 value claimed for 10 AWG SE buried in insulation, where the 60 °C rating governs.

page_quiz.explain_plain: That is SE's own narrow ampacity rule in 338.10(B)(4): 10 AWG and smaller, in contact with thermal insulation, uses the 60 °C rating.

sections.title: Where SE and USE cable may not be used
sections.plain_explanation: The prohibitions keep service cable in its lane. Type SE may not be used: (1) where subject to physical damage unless protected per 230.50(B); (2) underground, with or without a raceway; (3) for exterior branch circuits and feeders unless the installation meets Part I of Article 225 and is supported per 334.30, or is messenger-supported per Part II of Article 396. Type USE may not be used: (1) for interior wiring; (2) aboveground, except where it emerges from the ground and terminates in an enclosure at an outdoor location, with the cable protected per 300.5(D); (3) as aboveground cable except as permitted in 338.12(B)(2) (the single-conductor and multiconductor exceptions). A conductor dual-listed USE-2/RHH/RHW-2 may be used indoors under its RHW-2 listing. SE used as interior branch-circuit or feeder wiring is limited to the conditions on the 338.10(B)(4) page — outside those conditions, interior circuits get an interior wiring method. Service cable leaving the meter is service territory; it does not become a general-purpose house cable because it was on the truck.
sections.on_the_job: The classic misuse is USE pulled inside a building 'because it was already in the trench.' Once the run comes inside, the method has to change to one that is legal indoors — plan the transition at the entry, in a box or the panel, not mid-run. On a Sharma service change, the lateral comes up at the meter and the inside run is planned as an interior method from the panel — the transition is drawn on the layout before the trench is dug, not improvised at the wall.
sections.figure_idea: House wall section: USE stopping at the entry point and transitioning to an interior method (approved), versus USE continuing across the attic (crossed out).
sections.why_it_exists: SE and USE are service cables: their construction and listings are built for the service run, not for general interior or underground branch work. USE has no interior flame-retardant listing, so a fire inside a wall or attic is the hazard the interior ban prevents. SE buried underground fails early and is hard to fault-locate: the cable is not listed for burial, and a buried service fault is dangerous to dig up.
inspection_fails: USE cable continued inside the building to the panel — 338.12(B)(1) prohibits USE for interior wiring.
Type SE run underground to a detached structure — prohibited with or without a raceway, 338.12(A)(2).
SE used for an exterior feeder without meeting Article 225 Part I and without support per 334.30.
USE emerging from grade at the outdoor enclosure with no protection per 300.5(D).
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer: 'USE is rated for direct burial, so it can run anywhere the trench goes — including inside to the panel.' Wrong. 338.12(B)(1) prohibits USE for interior wiring, full stop. The reverse trap also appears: SE in a raceway underground is still prohibited — the rule says with or without a raceway.

sections.title: Underground feeder cable — Type UF
sections.plain_explanation:
UF is NM's underground sibling: the conductors are embedded in a solid moisture-resistant covering, so the cable itself is rated for direct burial and wet locations, and for sunlight exposure where it is marked sunlight resistant.
• Uses: yard lights, outbuildings, pool and landscape feeds, and other underground branch circuits and feeders.
• Cover: buried at the Table 300.5 depth for the location — 24 in for direct burial in the general case. The 12 in column is only for a 120 V, 20 A or less, GFCI-protected residential branch circuit (L-061).
• Not permitted: as service-entrance cable; in commercial garages, theaters, motion picture studios, storage battery rooms or hoistways; embedded in poured concrete; exposed to physical damage without protection; in hazardous (classified) locations except where specifically permitted.
• Ampacity: read at the 60 °C limit, the same as NM (340.80).
sections.on_the_job: A Winter Garden backyard: the shed feed is a 120 V, 20 A GFCI-protected branch circuit, so its UF run takes the 12 in column; the pool equipment feed is a 240 V feeder, so the same yard digs to the full 24 in for that run. Two depths, one trench day — read the row for the circuit, not the habit. UF is stiff and unforgiving to strip: score the covering carefully and do not nick the conductors. Above ground, protect it where it can be damaged, the same as any exposed cable, and sleeve risers where 300.5 requires protection.
sections.figure_idea: Trench detail: UF at 24 in with a sleeved riser at the house wall, warning about the 12 in GFCI residential exception noted as a separate case.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: Underground is the harshest seat on the job: the cable sits in wet soil for decades, gets found by shovels, and nobody can watch it age. UF's solid covering keeps moisture off the conductors along the whole run — there is no hollow jacket for water to travel in. The Table 300.5 cover is the other half of the protection: deep enough that garden tools, aerators and fence posts stay above the cable.
inspection_fails: UF buried at 12 in on a 240 V pool feeder — the 12 in column is only the GFCI-protected 120 V residential branch circuit.
UF run as the service to a detached garage — UF is not service-entrance cable (340.12).
UF riser up the wall unprotected where the mower and string trimmer reach it.
UF embedded in the poured pool deck — not permitted in poured concrete.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is 'UF only needs 12 in of cover.' Twelve inches is one narrow column of Table 300.5 — 120 V, 20 A or less, GFCI-protected, residential branch circuit. The general direct-burial depth is 24 in. Second trap: 'UF is rated underground, so it can serve as the service cable.' It cannot — 340.12 keeps UF out of service-entrance use.

page_quiz.explain_plain: UF's home turf is underground branch circuits and feeders; 340.12 bars service use, poured concrete and hoistways.

sections.title: Where UF may — and may not — be used
sections.plain_explanation:
UF's permitted list is the underground counterpart to NM's.
• Permitted: direct burial; wet locations; corrosive locations; and sunlight exposure where the cable is marked sunlight resistant.
• Where UF is used in place of NM for a branch circuit, it is installed under the NM framework it points to (Article 334's protection and support rules). UF used in place of NM follows Parts II and III of Article 334 and must be the multiconductor type (340.10(4)).
• Not permitted: as service-entrance cable; in commercial garages, theaters and similar locations, motion picture studios, storage battery rooms, or hoistways; embedded in poured concrete; or left exposed to physical damage without protection.
• UF is also not permitted in any hazardous (classified) location except where specifically permitted elsewhere, or as overhead cable except as messenger-supported wiring under Part II of Article 396.
sections.on_the_job: Yard lights and outbuilding feeds are UF's home turf — but the moment the feed becomes the building's service, UF is the wrong cable. And like NM, its ampacity is read at the 60°C limit (340.80), so size it the way the 334.80 page teaches. In the Florida sun, check the jacket before the run leaves the truck: exposed UF has to be the type marked sunlight resistant.
sections.figure_idea: Yard cross-section: UF buried to a pedestal light (approved); UF rising into a meter base as a service cable (crossed out).
sections.why_it_exists: UF's solid, moisture-proof jacket is built for burial and wet ground that would destroy NM. But UF is still a light branch-circuit cable. The bans keep it off services, where fault energy and inspection demands run higher, and out of theaters, commercial garages and battery rooms, where damage and ignition risks are different. Set in poured concrete, it can be damaged by the pour and can never be inspected or replaced.
inspection_fails: UF used as the service-entrance cable to a house or detached garage (340.12).
UF embedded in a poured concrete patio slab.
UF run in a commercial garage or theater — locations on the not-permitted list (340.12).
UF exposed where subject to physical damage, with no protection.
UF run overhead with no messenger support under Article 396, Part II.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: "UF is underground NM, so it can do anything NM does — including serve as the service cable to the detached garage." Wrong. 340.12 bars UF as service-entrance cable, in commercial garages, theaters and similar locations, motion picture studios, storage battery rooms and hoistways, and embedded in poured concrete. And its ampacity still reads at the 60 °C limit (340.80).

sections.title: Intermediate metal conduit — IMC
sections.plain_explanation:
IMC is the middle-weight steel raceway: thinner wall than rigid metal conduit, heavier and stronger than EMT, threaded like RMC and usable in most of the same places, including many wet and exposed locations with the right fittings. Sharma meets it mainly on commercial and service work where EMT is not tough enough and full rigid is not needed.
The support numbers (342.30): IMC must be fastened within 3 ft of each box, cabinet, conduit body, or other termination. For straight runs, Table 344.30(B)(2) (applied through 342.30(B)(2)) spaces supports by size:
• 1/2 in and 3/4 in — every 10 ft
• 1 in — every 12 ft
• 1-1/4 in and 1-1/2 in — every 14 ft
• 2 in — every 16 ft
• 3 in and larger — every 20 ft
The 3 ft fastening distance may be increased to 5 ft where structural members do not readily permit fastening within 3 ft.
sections.on_the_job: On a Sharma warehouse job in Lakeland, a 2 in IMC run crosses the ceiling: fastened within 3 ft of the panel and of each box, then supported every 16 ft — the 2 in row of the table. One trade size note that matters in the field: IMC and RMC have nearly the same outside diameter and use the same threads and fittings, but IMC's thinner wall gives it a larger inside area, so its Chapter 9, Table 4 fill values are its own — do not use the RMC row for an IMC run. Link to Chapter 9 for the actual numbers; do not re-derive them here.

nec2023_change.change: IMC can now go up to trade size 6, two sizes bigger than the old limit of 4 and the same top size rigid metal conduit already had. Intermediate metal conduit (IMC) now comes in two more allowed sizes: trade size 5 and trade size 6 (342.20(B)).

nec2023_change.change: IMC no longer needs a strap when one unbroken length is fished into a wall that's already finished or prefinished. Rigid metal conduit got the same break. New exception: a single unbroken length of IMC, no couplings, fished inside an existing wall or a prefinished wall doesn't have to be secured (342.30(A)).

sections.why_it_exists: A threaded steel run is heavy, and its couplings and threads are not hangers. Fastened at every termination and supported by size, the run stays straight, the threads stay made up, and the raceway keeps its continuity as a ground path. A sagging run works its couplings loose under its own weight and the building's vibration.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: "IMC is thin-wall rigid, so use the RMC rows for everything." Threads and fittings match, but the Chapter 9, Table 4 fill values do not — IMC's larger inside area gives it its own row. The second trap runs the other way: trade size 5 and trade size 6 IMC are a 2023 allowance; on a 2020 permit the top size is still 4.
inspection_fails: 2 in IMC supported every 20 ft, on the 3 in row — the 2 in interval is 16 ft.
IMC run with no fastening within 3 ft of a conduit body.
IMC filled from the RMC row of Chapter 9, Table 4.
Trade size 6 IMC ordered for a job permitted under NEC 2020 — sizes 5 and 6 are 2023.

sections.title: Rigid metal conduit — RMC
sections.plain_explanation:
RMC is the heavy-wall threaded steel raceway — the toughest common raceway in this chapter. It may be used in nearly every location, including underground — where its 6 in cover in the general open-ground row of Table 300.5 is the payoff for its strength — wet locations, and places subject to physical damage, with fittings and supports made for it. Under a one- or two-family dwelling driveway that same rigid metal conduit needs 18 in of cover, the same as PVC and direct-burial cable; streets, roads, and other driveways and parking lots demand 24 in for every method. Underground, corrosion protection and the soil conditions govern how long it lasts.

The support numbers (344.30): RMC must be fastened within 3 ft of each box, cabinet, conduit body, or other termination — with the section's allowances where threaded couplings make that impractical. For straight runs, Table 344.30(B)(2) spaces supports by size:
• 1/2 in and 3/4 in — every 10 ft
• 1 in — every 12 ft
• 1-1/4 in and 1-1/2 in — every 14 ft
• 2 in and 2-1/2 in — every 16 ft
• 3 in and larger — every 20 ft
sections.on_the_job: The 6 in burial depth is why RMC still earns its cost in open ground and in shallow-rock trenches that are not under a driveway. It is not a 6 in depth under a one- or two-family dwelling driveway — that row is 18 in for RMC and for PVC. Under streets, roads, alleys, and other driveways or parking lots, Table 300.5 requires 24 in of cover for every method, RMC included.
sections.figure_idea: Open-ground cross-section: RMC at 6 in beside a PVC run at 18 in. A one- or two-family dwelling driveway is a different Table 300.5 row — 18 in for both.

nec2023_change.change: Clarified adherence to the manufacturer's requirements for reaming and threading of PVC-coated rigid metal conduit (RMC) in Section 344.28.
nec2023_change.source: Carosella/NFPA-based 2023 NEC change workbook: 344.28 Reaming and Threading (Rigid Metal Conduit)

sections.why_it_exists: Cover is time. Six inches of soil over a conduit in open ground is only acceptable because RMC's heavy steel wall takes the shovel hit that would crack PVC — the table trades the raceway's strength for depth. Under driveways the load is vehicles, not shovels, so every method goes deeper and the strength discount disappears.
inspection_fails: RMC buried 6 in under a one-family driveway — that row of Table 300.5 requires 18 in.
RMC under a street at 18 in — streets, roads and other driveways require 24 in for every method.
3/4 in RMC supported every 20 ft — Table 344.30(B)(2) allows 10 ft for 1/2 in and 3/4 in.
RMC not fastened within 3 ft of a box or conduit body — 344.30.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer buries RMC 6 in under the house driveway because 'RMC is 6 in everywhere.' The 6 in figure is only the general open-ground row of Table 300.5. The one- and two-family dwelling driveway row is 18 in for RMC, PVC and direct-burial cable alike, and streets, roads and other driveways are 24 in for every method.
