sections.title: Flexible metal conduit — FMC ('Greenfield')
sections.plain_explanation:
FMC is the 'Greenfield' whip: an interlocked spiral of steel or aluminum strip that bends by hand and carries conductors the last few feet to motors, air handlers, ballasts and other equipment that vibrates, moves or needs a flexible final connection. It is a dry-location method — wet locations belong to LFMC, Article 350.
Support and fastening (348.30):
• Fasten within 12 in. of each termination, and support at intervals of 4-1/2 ft or less.
• Exceptions: FMC fished in finished work in existing construction; lengths of 3 ft or less at terminals where flexibility is needed; and whips up to 6 ft to a luminaire in an accessible ceiling.
• Where flexibility is needed after installation, the unsecured length is capped by trade size: 3 ft for 1/2 through 1-1/4 in., 4 ft for 1-1/2 through 2 in., and 5 ft for 2-1/2 in. and larger.
As a ground path (348.60, 250.118(5)) — all three together:
• The fittings are listed for grounding.
• The total length of FMC in the ground return path is 6 ft or less.
• The circuit conductors are protected at 20 A or less — whatever the FMC trade size.
Do not borrow LFMC's bigger steps: 20 A for 3/8 through 1/2 in. and 60 A for 3/4 through 1-1/4 in. belong to LFMC under 250.118(6), not to FMC.
sections.on_the_job: Final connection to an air handler in a Kissimmee mechanical room: a 4 ft FMC whip, fastened within 12 in. of both ends, with a green equipment ground pulled in — Sharma does not rely on the spiral. The moment that whip moves outdoors to the condenser, it becomes LFMC with fittings listed for the location, because FMC is a dry-location method.

nec2023_change.change: New in 2023: flexible metal conduit (FMC) can't be reconditioned. Liquidtight flexible metal conduit and ENT got the same ban in their own articles. Reconditioning flexible metal conduit (FMC) is off the table (348.2). Damaged FMC gets replaced, not rebuilt.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 348.2 No reconditioned flexible conduit

sections.why_it_exists: Flex exists to move — across vibration gaps and into equipment that comes out for service. But an interlocked spiral is a long, springy, easily damaged conductor, so the Code trusts it as a ground path only in short lengths on small circuits, and never where water can follow the spiral in.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is borrowing LFMC's numbers: 60 A for 3/4 through 1-1/4 in. trade sizes belongs to LFMC, 250.118(6). For FMC the overcurrent cap is 20 A whatever the trade size, the ground return path may not exceed 6 ft, and the fittings must be listed for grounding — all three, or the spiral is not the ground.
inspection_fails: FMC run outdoors or in a wet location instead of LFMC (Article 350).
Spiral used as the only ground path on a 30 A circuit — FMC grounding caps at 20 A.
FMC ground return path longer than 6 ft.
Whip not fastened within 12 in. of a termination, or a span over 4-1/2 ft unsupported.

page_quiz.explain_plain: Within 12 in. of each termination, and supported every 4-1/2 ft or less.

sections.title: Liquidtight flexible metal conduit — LFMC
sections.plain_explanation:
LFMC is FMC with a liquidtight plastic jacket over the metal core — the flexible method for wet locations, outdoors, and vibrating equipment. On Sharma work this is the condenser whip: LFMC from the disconnect to the outdoor unit, with listed liquidtight fittings, supported close to each end, and a separate equipment ground inside.

The working numbers (350.30 and 350.60): LFMC is fastened within 12 in of each termination and supported at intervals not over 4-1/2 ft; a length of up to 6 ft is permitted unsupported at a luminaire or equipment connection within an accessible ceiling, and short lengths at terminals may go unsupported where flexibility is needed. As a grounding path, the jacketed spiral counts only in trade sizes 3/8 in through 1-1/4 in, with listed fittings, a total ground-path length not over 6 ft, and the overcurrent limits this article sets — which is why the condenser whip still gets its own equipment grounding conductor inside, sized from Table 250.122.
sections.on_the_job: A Sharma condenser change-out in Winter Park: 4 ft of 3/4 in LFMC from the disconnect to the unit — inside the 6 ft ground-path limit — with its own 10 AWG copper equipment ground inside, sized from Table 250.122 for the 40 A circuit, and the whip strapped within 12 in of each end. The whip is not the support for the disconnect and the disconnect is not the support for the whip — strap both, keep the whip off the ground where it will be weed-eaten, and seal the outdoor end with the listed fitting, hand-tight plus the manufacturer's turn, not channel-locks.
sections.figure_idea: Condenser pad detail: disconnect on the wall, LFMC whip looping down to the unit with support straps marked.
sections.florida_note: 210.8(F) GFCI enforcement on outdoor HVAC outlets has varied by AHJ and amendment — see the Chapter 2 note; confirm locally before choosing the condenser breaker.
sections.why_it_exists: The condenser lives outdoors in the rain, the sun and the weed trimmer. LFMC's liquidtight jacket keeps water out of the raceway, and its flexibility absorbs the unit's vibration instead of working the fittings loose. The support and ground-path limits exist because a long, loose whip gets stepped on, cut and pulled — and a spiral ground path that is too long, or in too large a trade size, is a high-impedance path that may not clear a fault.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: "LFMC's metal spiral is the ground, so the whip needs no equipment grounding conductor." The spiral counts as a ground path only in trade sizes 3/8 in through 1-1/4 in, with listed fittings, a total ground-path length of 6 ft or less, and inside the overcurrent limits the article sets. Outside that box it is just a raceway — and Sharma pulls a wire equipment ground inside the whip either way.
inspection_fails: Condenser whip lying on the soil, unsupported and in the weed trimmer's path.
An 8 ft LFMC run used as the only ground path — past the 6 ft limit.
Outdoor whip on non-listed fittings, jacket open at the connector and taking water.
Disconnect hanging off the whip with no support of its own.

rows: Unsupported at a luminaire or equipment in an accessible ceiling
Trade sizes 3/8 in through 1-1/4 in, listed fittings, total path not over 6 ft

page_quiz.explain_plain: 350.30: fastened within 12 in of each termination and supported at intervals not over 4-1/2 ft.

page_quiz.question: LFMC may serve as the ground path only when the total ground-path length is not over:
page_quiz.explain_plain: 350.60: the jacketed spiral counts as a ground path only with listed fittings, in trade sizes 3/8 in through 1-1/4 in, and a total length not over 6 ft.

sections.title: Rigid polyvinyl chloride conduit — PVC
sections.plain_explanation:
PVC is the nonmetallic rigid raceway Sharma uses underground and in wet and corrosive spots: services and feeders in the yard, pool-area runs, and sleeves. Schedule 40 is the standard wall; Schedule 80 is the heavier wall used where the run is exposed to physical damage. PVC may not be used where ambient or conductor heat will exceed its temperature rating, in the hazardous and theater-type locations its article bars, or as a support for fixtures and equipment hanging off it. Underground cover for PVC is 18 in in the general Table 300.5 case. Two field behaviors define the method: it expands and contracts a lot with temperature, and its joints are solvent-welded, not threaded (except at listed threaded fittings and adapters). PVC is nonmetallic, so the raceway itself is never the ground path — an equipment grounding conductor goes in the run where one is required.
The support numbers (Table 352.30) — PVC is supported far more often than metal raceway:
• 1/2 in through 1 in — every 3 ft
• 1-1/4 in through 2 in — every 5 ft
• 2-1/2 in through 3 in — every 6 ft
• 3-1/2 in through 5 in — every 7 ft
• 6 in — every 8 ft
And the expansion numbers (Table 352.44): a 100 ft run of PVC changes length about 2 in with a 50°F temperature swing, and about 4.1 in with a 100°F swing. An expansion fitting is required where the expected change in length reaches 1/4 in — a threshold a short exposed Florida riser can cross on a summer afternoon.
sections.on_the_job: Expansion is the inspection item apprentices forget: a long straight run in Florida sun moves. A 60 ft PVC feeder down a south-facing Orlando block wall grows about 2-1/2 in across a 100°F swing (the Table 352.44 rate of about 4.1 in per 100 ft) — ten times the 1/4 in trigger — so the expansion fitting goes in at layout, not as a callback. Supports follow this article's table: a 2 in run straps every 5 ft, not at metal-raceway spacing.
sections.figure_idea: Long PVC run down a block wall with an expansion fitting mid-run, sun arrows on the wall, and a support strap spacing callout.
sections.florida_note: Florida sun on an exposed PVC riser is the textbook expansion case — check every long south- and west-wall run.

nec2023_change.change: Schedule 80 PVC conduit and Schedule 80 elbows are now named in the rule for spots exposed to physical damage, and concrete encasement got its own item. In spots where PVC can get hit or crushed, use Schedule 80 conduit and elbows plus listed fittings (352.10(K)). Schedule 40 doesn't belong there.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 352.10 PVC in concrete and damage areas

sections.why_it_exists: PVC is cheap, corrosion-proof and easy to glue, but it is plastic: it sags, softens with heat, and grows and shrinks with the weather. Tight support spacing keeps runs from belly-sagging and ponding water; the expansion fitting gives a run somewhere to move before it pushes boxes apart or pulls fittings loose.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is spacing PVC like EMT: 'straps every 10 ft.' Table 352.30 is much tighter — 3 ft for 1/2 through 1 in, 5 ft for 1-1/4 through 2 in. The mirror trap: 'the PVC raceway is the ground path on a short run.' It never is — the raceway is nonmetallic, so the equipment grounding conductor goes in the run.
inspection_fails: Long exposed PVC run with no expansion fitting where the expected length change reaches 1/4 in (352.44) — bowed runs and fittings pulled apart.
PVC supported at metal-raceway spacing: 2 in PVC strapped every 10 ft instead of every 5 ft (Table 352.30).
Schedule 40 PVC run where it is exposed to physical damage (352.10) — that is Schedule 80 territory.
PVC run with no equipment grounding conductor in it, treating the raceway itself as the ground path.

page_quiz.explain_plain: Table 352.30: PVC from 1-1/4 through 2 in is supported every 5 ft. PVC sags, so its spacing is much tighter than metal raceway.

page_quiz.explain_plain: 352.44 sets the trigger at 1/4 in of expected movement — a short exposed Florida riser can cross it between a winter morning and a summer afternoon.

sections.title: Supporting PVC — the Table 352.30 intervals
sections.plain_explanation:
PVC is secured within 3 ft of each box, cabinet, or termination, and supported at the intervals of Table 352.30, which grow with the conduit size:
• 1/2 in through 1 in — every 3 ft
• 1-1/4 in through 2 in — every 5 ft
• 2-1/2 in through 3 in — every 6 ft
• 3-1/2 in through 5 in — every 7 ft
• 6 in — every 8 ft
The table assumes the conduit is supported so it cannot sag between straps; a run that bellies between supports will belly worse once the Florida sun and the conductors are in it.
sections.on_the_job: On a 1 in yard run, a strap every 3 ft feels like a lot — until you see the same run in August with two straps missing. Strap to the table at rough-in; adding straps after the trench is closed means hand-digging your own work. A 30 ft run of 1 in takes about ten straps at the table spacing, plus one within 3 ft of each end — count them on the takeoff, not at the trench. And when the run steps up to 2 in, let the spacing open up to the table's 5 ft instead of strapping it like 1 in.
sections.figure_idea: PVC run along a wall with support intervals dimensioned for 1 in (3 ft) and 2 in (5 ft), and straps marked within 3 ft of the panel.
sections.florida_note: Florida sun is the stress test: exposed PVC grows with heat, so long straight runs on roofs and exterior walls need the 352.44 expansion provision, not just closer straps.
sections.why_it_exists: PVC is stiff in the morning and soft by afternoon. Heat and the weight of the conductors make an under-supported run creep downward between straps until it bellies, pulls at its boxes and stresses its joints. The bigger sizes get wider spacing only because the bigger pipe is stiffer — the table is a sag limit, not a suggestion.
inspection_fails: 1 in PVC supported every 10 ft on the EMT pattern — Table 352.30 allows 3 ft.
No strap within 3 ft of the panel, box or termination.
PVC run bellied between supports — spacing too wide for the size, and worse in summer heat.
Long straight sun-exposed run strapped rigid at both ends with no expansion provision (352.44).
sections.exam_trap: The trap is strapping PVC on the EMT pattern — within 3 ft of the box, then every 10 ft. EMT's 10 ft interval is not in Table 352.30: small PVC straps every 3 ft, and the spacing only opens up as the pipe gets bigger and stiffer. The other wrong answer reverses the table — bigger pipe, closer straps.

tables.caption: Table 352.30: PVC support intervals
tables.note: Secure within 3 ft of each box, cabinet or termination (352.30).

page_quiz.explain_plain: Table 352.30 puts 1/2 in through 1 in PVC at 3 ft — the tightest row in the table.

page_quiz.question: Maximum support interval for 2 in PVC?
page_quiz.explain_plain: 1-1/4 in through 2 in PVC is supported every 5 ft.

page_quiz.question: PVC must be secured within what distance of each box or termination?
page_quiz.explain_plain: 352.30: secured within 3 ft of each box, cabinet or termination, then supported to the table.

sections.title: Expansion fittings — PVC moves
sections.plain_explanation:
PVC grows and shrinks with temperature far more than the building it is attached to — roughly 4 in of length change per 100 ft of run for a 100°F temperature swing (Table 352.44 gives the exact characteristic). Where the expected length change is 1/4 in or more, a listed expansion fitting is required, so the movement happens at the fitting instead of pulling couplings apart, pushing into boxes, or bowing the run off the wall. Underground runs meet the same rule where they rise out of the ground into the sun.
• The check is arithmetic, not judgment: the run length, the Table 352.44 characteristic, and the temperature swing the run will actually see.
• Set the fitting at mid-travel for the installation temperature, so the run can move both ways from the day it is installed.
sections.on_the_job: Worked example: a 40 ft PVC run on a sunny Florida wall, installed at 70°F, with surface temperatures reaching 150°F — an 80°F swing. Movement is about 40 ft × (4 in per 100 ft) × 0.8, roughly 1.3 in. That is five times the 1/4 in threshold: the run gets an expansion fitting, set at mid-travel for the installation temperature.
sections.figure_idea: Long PVC wall run with an expansion fitting at mid-run, arrows showing the piston travel, and a thermometer scale from installation temperature to summer peak.
sections.florida_note: Florida is expansion-fitting country: attic, roof, and sunlit-wall temperatures swing far past the indoor range, and a long PVC run glued rigid at both ends will find the weakest coupling by the second summer.

nec2023_change.change: PVC expansion fittings now cover earth movement, not just temperature. A buried PVC run rising through grade on soil that can settle or frost-heave gets an expansion fitting on the riser, above grade. New 352.44(B): direct-buried PVC rising out of soil that can settle, shift or frost-heave gets an expansion fitting, installed above grade.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 352.44 PVC expansion fittings and earth movement

sections.why_it_exists: The movement is not optional — a heated run gets longer whether the fitting is there or not. Without a fitting, the growth spends itself on the weakest point: a coupling pulls apart, a box connector breaks, or the run bows and works a strap loose. The fitting gives the movement one planned place to happen.
inspection_fails: Long sunlit PVC run glued rigid at both ends with no expansion fitting; a coupling has pulled apart (352.44).
Expansion fitting installed with the piston set fully closed on a cold morning — no travel left for the summer swing (352.44).
PVC riser rising out of the ground into the sun with no expansion fitting where the run's movement exceeds 1/4 in (352.44).
sections.exam_trap: The trap is a length test: "Expansion fittings are for runs over 100 ft." There is no length in the rule — the trigger is movement: 1/4 in or more of expected length change. A 40 ft Florida wall run moves about 1.3 in, five times the trigger, and needs the fitting.

page_quiz.explain_plain: The characteristic is roughly 4 in of movement per 100 ft of run for a 100°F temperature swing.

choices: Needs no fitting — it is under 100 ft
Needs an expansion fitting — movement is over 1/4 in
Needs a fitting only if it is underground

page_quiz.explain_plain: The trigger is movement, not length: 1.3 in is five times the 1/4 in threshold.

sections.title: High-density polyethylene conduit — Type HDPE
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 353 covers high-density polyethylene conduit, Type HDPE: the coiled, flexible nonmetallic raceway used mainly for long underground runs — directional-bored and trenched duct for utilities, site feeders and communications. Its strength is the continuous long run with no joints in the bore.
• Where it runs: underground — directional-bored or trenched duct, utility and site work, service laterals and communications runs.
• How it joins: by fusion or listed couplings, never solvent cement. The joint has to be a method identified for the conduit.
• What it is not: a general-purpose building raceway. Its home is the underground run between two points.
• Whose it is: much of the HDPE in the ground belongs to the utility or the site contractor, not to the electrical contractor who pulls through it later.
sections.on_the_job: Sharma meets HDPE most often as the duct the utility or site contractor provides. Confirm what is actually in the duct and who owns it before planning a pull through it. On a Central Florida site job that means three checks before the pull is priced: prove the bore is open with a mandrel or a blown mouse, confirm a pull line is in place or plan to jet one in, and confirm in writing whose duct it is — utility duct is not yours to occupy without their say-so. If the run is empty and open, a 4/0 feeder pull through 200 ft of bored HDPE is routine work; if the bore is crushed, it is a re-bore at someone's cost, and that argument happens before the wire is on the truck, not after.

nec2023_change.change: Section 353.48 was revised by CMP 8 to specify that the joining methods of High Density Polyethylene Conduit (HDPE) are to be made by a method identified by the manufacturer. Heat fusion or butt fusion joints are not to be permitted.
nec2023_change.source: Carosella/NFPA-based 2023 NEC change workbook: 353.48 Joints

sections.edition_note:
NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 353.48: Section 353.48 was revised by CMP 8 to specify that the joining methods of High Density Polyethylene Conduit (HDPE) are to be made by a method identified by the manufacturer. Heat fusion or butt fusion joints are not to be permitted.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: A buried duct fails quietly. A joint that separates underground, or a coupling that lets the bore collapse, turns a finished run into an excavation job, and a separated duct can leave conductors unprotected in soil and water. The joining rules exist so every joint in the run is a listed, identified method that stays together for the life of the installation, not just until the trench is backfilled.
inspection_fails: HDPE joints solvent-welded or made with unlisted couplings — joints must be fusion or listed fittings (353.48).
Conductors pulled into a duct that was never proved open — crushed bore found with the feeder half pulled.
HDPE brought into the building as the interior raceway instead of transitioning to a listed wiring method at the entrance.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating HDPE like PVC: reaching for solvent cement, or assuming any coupling in the truck is fine. HDPE is joined by fusion or listed couplings, and the joint method must be one identified for the conduit — a glued PVC coupling is not a listed HDPE joint, and the 'solvent-weld the joints' answer is wrong.

page_quiz.explain_plain: HDPE is joined by fusion or listed couplings, never solvent cement — it is not glued together like PVC.

sections.title: Nonmetallic underground conduit with conductors — Type NUCC
sections.plain_explanation:
NUCC is a factory assembly: conductors already installed inside a nonmetallic underground conduit, supplied and installed as one listed system — conduit and conductors together (354.2). Because it arrives as a system, its fittings, joints and repairs follow its own article and listing — it is not field-pulled PVC with a head start.
• Permitted: direct burial underground; encased or embedded in concrete; in cinder fill; underground where subject to severe corrosive influences and approved for the chemicals present; aboveground only where encased in at least 2 in. of concrete (354.10).
• Not permitted: in exposed locations, or inside buildings — only the conductor or cable portion of the assembly may extend into a building, and only to terminate (354.12).
• Sizes run from trade size 1/2 minimum to trade size 4 maximum (354.20).
• Burial cover follows the minimum cover required for rigid nonmetallic conduit in Table 300.5.
• Bends follow the article's own Table 354.24(A) for minimum radius, with not more than 360 degrees of bends between pull points (354.24, 354.26). An assembly bent tighter than its radius is damaged — it does not get buried anyway.
sections.on_the_job: Rare on Sharma work. Treat any NUCC found underground as a system to be identified before it is cut or extended. On a Florida site job — a Marion County gate and well feed found during a service upgrade — the giveaway is a smooth nonmetallic duct that already has conductors in it. Before anyone cuts: identify the listing, find both ends, and plan any transition with fittings made for the system. Sharma's default for new underground work stays field-pulled conductors in PVC or HDPE, where a damaged run can be re-pulled.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: The factory assembly trades flexibility for certainty: the conductors are protected and correctly installed before the trench is ever opened, and nothing can be pulled in crooked or skinned on a burr in the field. The flip side is why the article fences it in — a damaged assembly cannot be re-pulled or easily repaired underground, and the raceway material is not made to live exposed or inside a building.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer treats NUCC as 'PVC conduit that happens to have wire in it' — pull the factory conductors out, add your own, or extend it with ordinary PVC fittings. It is a listed factory system under its own article: trade sizes 1/2 to 4, its own bend-radius table, no exposed runs, and no runs inside buildings.
inspection_fails: NUCC stubbed up exposed at a pad or pole — not permitted in exposed locations (354.12).
Assembly run inside the building and across the ceiling — only the conductor portion may extend in, and only to terminate (354.12).
Buried with less cover than Table 300.5 requires for rigid nonmetallic conduit.
Field-cut and coupled with ordinary PVC fittings not listed for the NUCC system.
Bent tighter than the Table 354.24(A) radius and buried anyway — a kinked assembly is damaged goods.

sections.title: Reinforced thermosetting resin conduit — Type RTRC
sections.plain_explanation:
RTRC is a fiberglass-reinforced resin raceway chosen where corrosion resistance and strength matter and metal raceways would rot or are barred — chemical, wastewater and harsh outdoor industrial environments. It is joined with its own fittings and adhesives and supported under its own article.
• Its baseline support table, Table 355.30, carries the same spacings as PVC's Table 352.30 — 3 ft for trade sizes 1/2 through 1, rising to 8 ft for trade size 6.
• Conduit listed for support at a different spacing is permitted to be installed in accordance with that listing.
sections.on_the_job: Specialized work only. If a corrosive-environment job specifies RTRC, its support table and joining instructions come with the material — get them before the run is laid out. Lay the straps out by the table, not by habit: a 3/4 in. run straps every 3 ft, a 2 in. run every 5 ft, and the big 6 in. run every 8 ft. Price the manufacturer's fittings and adhesive with the conduit, not as an afterthought. If the material arrives listed for a different support spacing, that listing is the number the inspector will hold you to — keep it with the job paperwork.
sections.why_it_exists: The resin conduit shrugs off chemicals that eat steel, but the run is only as good as its supports and joints. An over-spanned run sags and works its glued joints, and a joint made with the wrong cement fails in the same corrosive air the conduit was chosen to survive. The support table and the manufacturer's joining system are part of the corrosion protection. That is why this article carries its own support table instead of borrowing one from another raceway.
inspection_fails: 2-1/2 in. RTRC strapped every 8 ft — Table 355.30 allows 6 ft for that size.
Joints made with PVC cement or fittings not part of the RTRC system, instead of the manufacturer's adhesive and fittings.
RTRC listed for a different support spacing installed at table spacing against its listing.
Metal conduit installed in place of specified RTRC in a corrosive environment.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is reaching for the EMT support table because RTRC is 'just another conduit.' RTRC has its own table — 355.30 — and its spacings match PVC's Table 352.30, not EMT's. The second trap is ignoring the table for a listed product: where the conduit is listed for a different support spacing, the listing governs.

page_quiz.explain_plain: Table 355.30 matches Table 352.30: trade sizes 1-1/4 through 2 in. support every 5 ft.

sections.title: Liquidtight flexible nonmetallic conduit — LFNC
sections.plain_explanation:
LFNC is the all-plastic liquidtight flexible raceway — no metal core — used for short flexible connections in wet and outdoor locations where a nonmetallic method is wanted, including many pool and equipment connections. It comes in listed types with different fittings and limits, and may not be used where subject to physical damage or beyond its temperature and listing limits.
The working numbers (356.30): LFNC is fastened within 12 in of each termination and supported at intervals not over 3 ft, with the familiar flex exceptions:
• fished lengths, where support is not practicable
• short lengths at terminals where flexibility is needed
• up to 6 ft at a luminaire or equipment connection in an accessible ceiling
The tubing itself is plastic and carries nothing: where LFNC is the raceway for a circuit, the equipment grounding conductor runs inside it like any other nonmetallic method.
sections.on_the_job: On pool and outdoor equipment, confirm the specific LFNC type and its fittings are listed for the location before it goes on the truck — 'liquidtight' on the box is a listing claim, not a description. A Florida pool pump gets a short LFNC whip from the disconnect to the motor, fastened within 12 in of each end, with the equipment grounding conductor pulled inside it. At 3 ft the whole whip sits inside one support interval, and the pump can be swapped later without touching the raceway.

nec2023_change.change: Liquidtight flexible nonmetallic conduit (LFNC) is now allowed in severely corrosive locations, as long as its material is approved for the chemicals in that space. New item 356.10(8): LFNC can go where severe corrosive conditions exist (see 300.6), as long as its material is approved for the specific chemicals there.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 356.10 LFNC in corrosive areas

sections.why_it_exists: The flex whip at the equipment end absorbs vibration and lets a motor or pump be serviced without re-pulling the run. The support numbers keep the whip from sagging into a water trap or chafing on the pad edge. And because the plastic tube carries no fault current, the green wire inside it is the only ground path the equipment has — leave it out and a faulted pump case can sit live in a wet location.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: "LFNC is the plastic version of LFMC, so the raceway itself is the ground path." LFNC has no metal core and never carries fault current — the EGC runs inside it. Second trap: supporting it like rigid pipe. 356.30 wants a fastening within 12 in of each termination and supports at intervals not over 3 ft.
inspection_fails: LFNC whip to a pool pump or condenser with no equipment grounding conductor inside — the plastic tube grounds nothing.
A 5 ft whip strapped only at its two ends — 356.30 requires supports at intervals not over 3 ft.
LFNC run across a traffic path where it is subject to physical damage — a uses-not-permitted write-up (356.12).
Fittings not listed for LFNC or for the wet location — 'liquidtight' is a listing, not a look.

sections.title: Electrical metallic tubing — EMT
sections.plain_explanation:
EMT is the thin-wall steel raceway that carries most of Sharma's light-commercial work: unthreaded, joined with set-screw or compression couplings and connectors, and bent on the job with a hand or mechanical bender.
• Where it may be used: exposed or concealed, in dry, damp and wet locations. In wet locations the fittings must comply with 314.15, and supports, straps, bolts and screws must be corrosion-resistant material or protected against corrosion.
• In concrete and earth: galvanized steel and stainless steel EMT may be installed in concrete, in direct contact with the earth, and in areas subject to severe corrosive influences where protected by corrosion protection and approved as suitable for the condition. Aluminum EMT encased in concrete or in direct contact with the earth must have approved supplementary corrosion protection.
• Cinder fill: in cinder concrete or cinder fill subject to permanent moisture, galvanized or stainless EMT is allowed only when protected on all sides by at least 2 in. of noncinder concrete, or installed at least 18 in. under the fill.
• Grounding: EMT serves as its own equipment grounding conductor when installed with listed fittings made up properly.
• Where it may not be used: where subject to severe physical damage; to support luminaires or other equipment, except a conduit body no larger than the largest trade size of the tubing; and it is never threaded in the field like rigid conduit — EMT is not threaded, except for factory-threaded integral couplings.
• Sizes in the 2020 book top out at trade size 4 — sizes 5 and 6 are a 2023 change (see the edition note).
sections.on_the_job: Sharma tenant build-out: a 3/4 in EMT home run is strapped within 3 ft of the panel and every 10 ft after that (358.30), carrying 20 A commercial circuits on 12 AWG copper minimum (S-01). On the rooftop leg the same tube gets compression fittings listed for wet locations and corrosion-resistant straps — a set-screw coupling that fills with rain is a failed ground waiting for a fault.
sections.sharma_note: S-01 on commercial EMT work: 20A minimum branch circuits, 12 AWG copper minimum.
sections.figure_idea: EMT run across a commercial ceiling with a bend, a compression coupling and a support strap, each tagged.

nec2023_change.change: EMT can now go up to trade size 6, two sizes past the old limit of 4, so trade size 5 and 6 EMT is a code option. Electrical metallic tubing (EMT) can now be installed in trade sizes 5 and 6 (358.20(B)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 358.20 EMT up to trade size 6

sections.why_it_exists: The thin wall is the trade: EMT is light, cheap and fast to bend, so the article protects the two things a thin wall cannot forgive — corrosion and loose joints. Rust eats the mechanical protection, and a loose coupling breaks the ground path, because on EMT the tube itself is the equipment ground.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer: 'EMT goes anywhere rigid goes, in any size.' In the 2020 book EMT stops at trade size 4 — sizes 5 and 6 are 2023 — and it is never threaded in the field and never a luminaire support. The second classic: 'EMT always needs a separate ground wire.' Made up tight with listed fittings, the tube is the ground path.
inspection_fails: Set-screw fittings installed in a wet location without a wet-location listing (314.15).
EMT threaded in the field to fit a rigid coupling.
Aluminum EMT in concrete or earth contact with no supplementary corrosion protection.
EMT used to support a pendant luminaire.
Loose set-screw coupling — the run lost its equipment ground at that joint.

sections.title: Where EMT may — and may not — be used
sections.plain_explanation:
EMT's permitted list covers most of a commercial building. The not-permitted list is short — but every item on it is a real write-up.
• Permitted: exposed or concealed; in wet locations where the fittings are listed for wet use (raintight); embedded in concrete; and in masonry in contact with the earth where protected against corrosion.
• EMT is itself steel, and it is permitted as the equipment grounding path (250.118(4)) — which is why its couplings must be made up tight.
• Not permitted: where it will be subject to severe physical damage during installation or afterward.
• Never threaded in the field — EMT is joined with threadless fittings only.
• 358.12 also bars EMT from supporting luminaires or other equipment, except conduit bodies no larger than the largest trade size of the tubing, and from use where protected from corrosion solely by enamel, or in cinder concrete or fill unless protected.
• Couplings and connectors in wet locations must be listed for wet locations (358.42).
sections.on_the_job: On a Sharma retail job in Orlando, run the two field checks. First: a wet location means raintight-listed fittings, not standard compression fittings and a prayer — the EMT on the exterior wall gets fittings listed for wet use (358.42). Second: every coupling wrench-tight, because on an EMT job the raceway is the ground path — a loose set-screw is a loose ground. And where the run crosses the loading dock at pallet height, EMT is the wrong raceway entirely: that is severe-physical-damage territory (358.12).
sections.figure_idea: EMT run at a wet exterior wall with raintight fittings tagged, and a hand-cut thread on a piece of EMT crossed out.

nec2023_change.change: EMT in the ground now has to use direct-burial fittings, and EMT joined the list of raceways allowed for manufactured wiring systems. EMT in direct contact with the earth has to use fittings that are identified for direct burial (358.10(A)(1)). Ordinary fittings don't qualify.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 358.10 Buried EMT and its fittings

sections.why_it_exists: EMT is thin-wall steel: light, cheap and easy to bend, but that thin wall is exactly what crushes under severe physical damage, so the bans keep it out of impact zones. The tight-coupling rule exists because the tubing itself carries fault current back to the source. A loose set-screw coupling is a break in the ground path — and fault current that cannot get back cannot trip the breaker.
inspection_fails: EMT run where subject to severe physical damage — loading dock, pallet traffic (358.12).
Standard compression fittings in a wet location; fittings not listed for wet locations (358.42).
Loose set-screw couplings — the raceway is the equipment grounding path and must stay continuous (250.118(4)).
EMT threaded in the field and joined with threaded couplings — threadless fittings only.
EMT used to support a luminaire (358.12).
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer: "EMT is steel conduit, so thread it like rigid." Wrong — EMT is never threaded in the field; threadless fittings only. The second trap: "a compression fitting is a compression fitting" outdoors. In a wet location the fitting must be listed for wet use (raintight), or the installation fails 358.42.

• 358.10: EMT in the ground now has to use direct-burial fittings, and EMT joined the list of raceways allowed for manufactured wiring systems. EMT in direct contact with the earth has to use fittings that are identified for direct burial (358.10(A)(1)). Ordinary fittings don't qualify.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

sections.title: How many conductors fit in EMT — the Chapter 9 handoff
sections.plain_explanation:
This section does not carry its own fill numbers: the number of conductors in EMT is whatever Chapter 9 allows.
• Table 1 percentages: 53% for one conductor, 31% for two, 40% for more than two, and 60% for a nipple 24 in or shorter.
• Table 4 gives the usable areas of the raceway; Table 5 gives the area each conductor occupies.
• Worked example from the Chapter 9 tables: 1/2 in EMT has a 40% area of 0.122 sq in; a 12 AWG THHN conductor occupies 0.0133 sq in; 0.122 / 0.0133 = 9.17, so nine 12 AWG THHN fit.
• Equipment grounds count toward fill.
The same Chapter 9 tables serve every raceway type in Chapter 3 — this section is simply the EMT door into them, and the count is made before the pull, not discovered during it.
sections.on_the_job: Do the area math, do not eyeball a stuffed pipe at trim time. When all conductors are the same size, Annex C gives the same answer as a shortcut — but the tables are the rule, Annex C is the shortcut.
sections.figure_idea: Calculation card: 0.122 ÷ 0.0133 = 9.17 → 9 conductors, with a 1/2 in EMT cross-section holding nine dots.
sections.why_it_exists: An overfilled raceway is damaged on the way in: the pull drags insulation across every coupling and bend, and the finished bundle runs hot with no room around it. The fill limits keep the pull survivable, keep heat from building in a packed pipe, and leave enough room that a conductor can be pulled back out and replaced years later.
inspection_fails: A conduit stuffed by eye, with more conductors than the Chapter 9 percentage allows.
Equipment grounding conductors left out of the fill count, putting the run over the limit.
A long run filled to 60 percent as if it were a nipple — the 60 percent figure is only for nipples 24 in or shorter.
Annex C used for a mixed-size pull, where only the Table 1, 4 and 5 math gives the answer.
sections.exam_trap: Annex C is in the code book, so use it for every fill question. Annex C only works when every conductor is the same size and the same insulation type. Mix sizes and you are back to Tables 1, 4 and 5 — and the equipment grounding conductor counts toward fill either way.

figures.alt: Cross-section of a 1/2 in EMT holding nine conductor dots, beside a calculation card: Table 4 gives 0.122 sq in at 40 percent, Table 5 gives 0.0133 sq in for 12 AWG THHN, 0.122 divided by 0.0133 equals 9.17, so nine conductors fit; a strip below shows the Table 1 percentages 53, 31, 40 and 60.
figures.caption: The worked example: area divided by area, rounded down.

page_quiz.question: Four current-carrying conductors plus a ground go into one EMT. The Table 1 fill limit is:
page_quiz.explain_plain: More than two conductors: 40 percent. The 60 percent figure is only for nipples 24 in or shorter, and the ground counts toward fill.

page_quiz.question: Using Tables 4 and 5, how many 12 AWG THHN conductors fit in 1/2 in EMT?
page_quiz.explain_plain: 0.122 sq in (40 percent of the EMT) divided by 0.0133 sq in per conductor = 9.17, which rounds down to nine conductors.

page_quiz.question: Do equipment grounding conductors count toward raceway fill?
page_quiz.explain_plain: Equipment grounds occupy area like any other conductor and count toward the Chapter 9 fill percentages.

sections.title: EMT bends — radius and the 360-degree rule
sections.plain_explanation: Bends in EMT have to be made so the tubing is not damaged and its inside diameter is not effectively reduced. The radius of the curve of any field bend, measured to the centerline of the tubing, must not be less than the radius shown in Chapter 9, Table 2 for that trade size. Offsets and saddles count toward the run's total bend. Between pull points, the total bend in one run may not exceed 360 degrees: the equivalent of four quarter bends, in any combination. A run that needs more than 360 degrees needs a pull point — a box or conduit body — not a stronger pull.
sections.on_the_job: Count every bend on your fingers as you lay out: stub-up 90, offset 30 + 30, three-point saddle 22.5 + 45 + 22.5 — you are at 240 before the run leaves the room, with 120 degrees to spare. Plan the pull points while the ceiling is open; a box added at layout costs minutes, and the same box added after the ceiling closes costs a day.
sections.figure_idea: Run diagram with bend angles added in a running total: 90 + 30 + 30 + 45 = 195°, marked 'under 360 — OK'.
sections.why_it_exists: Every bend adds friction, and friction is what shaves insulation and stalls pulls. A run bent past 360 degrees can be impossible to pull without damaging the conductors — and a bend crushed tight to save space reduces the tubing's inside diameter the same way. The radius rule protects the wire going in; the 360-degree rule protects the wire for the whole pull. The count runs between pull points, so the rule is won at layout, not at the pull.
inspection_fails: Five 90-degree bends between boxes — 450 degrees with no pull point (358.26).
Offsets and saddles left out of the bend count, putting the run over 360 degrees.
Field bend kinked flat, inside diameter effectively reduced (358.24).
Bend radius tighter than Chapter 9, Table 2 for the trade size.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is counting only the 90s. Offsets and saddles count too, and the limit is the total between pull points — 360 degrees in any combination, not four bends of any size. The second trap is the fix: more pulling lubricant and a stronger pull do not cure an over-bent run. The cure is a pull point.

tables.caption: Bend tally for the run in On the job

page_quiz.question: Maximum total bend between pull points in one EMT run?
page_quiz.explain_plain: 358.26 caps the total at 360 degrees — the equivalent of four quarter bends, in any combination.

page_quiz.question: A run has a 90 stub-up, a 30 + 30 offset, and a 22.5 + 45 + 22.5 saddle. Total bend?
page_quiz.explain_plain: 90 + 60 + 90 = 240 degrees. Every bend counts, including offsets and saddles.

page_quiz.question: A field bend's radius is measured to the tubing's centerline and must not be less than:
choices: Chapter 9, Table 2 for the trade size
page_quiz.explain_plain: 358.24 sends the minimum radius to Chapter 9, Table 2 for that trade size.

sections.title: Securing and supporting EMT
sections.plain_explanation:
EMT must be securely fastened in place and supported by this section:
• Securely fastened within 3 ft of each outlet box, junction box, device box, cabinet, conduit body or other tubing termination.
• Fastened and supported at intervals not exceeding 10 ft.
• Where structural members do not readily permit fastening within 3 ft of a termination, an unbroken length of EMT — a length without couplings — may be fastened up to 5 ft from that termination.
• For concealed work in finished buildings or prefinished wall panels where securing is impracticable, unbroken lengths without a coupling may be fished.
• Horizontal runs supported by openings through framing members count as supported by that framing — where the openings are at intervals not exceeding 10 ft and the run is securely fastened within 3 ft of a termination.
sections.on_the_job: Strap rhythm in the field: strap at 3 ft from the box, then every 10 ft, and a strap on each side of a coupling run that wants to sag. Worked example: a 44 ft ceiling run in a Lake Mary office, box at each end. Straps land within 3 ft of both boxes and at 10 ft intervals between — five straps cover the run with no span over 10 ft. If the tube moves when you pull wire, it was not supported.
sections.figure_idea: Ceiling run with straps dimensioned: 3 ft max from the box, 10 ft max between straps.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: EMT is thin-wall tubing. Left to span too far, it sags at the couplings, and a sagging run works its set-screws loose every time wire is pulled or the building moves. Loose couplings mean a broken fault path, because EMT itself serves as the equipment grounding conductor. The 3 ft and 10 ft numbers keep every termination and every coupling inside a supported span.
inspection_fails: EMT strapped at 12 ft intervals across a ceiling — over the 10 ft maximum.
First strap 6 ft from the panel on a coupled length — the 5 ft allowance needs an unbroken length and structure that blocks the 3 ft strap.
Fished EMT in a finished wall built from coupled short pieces — fished lengths must be unbroken, without couplings.
Run resting on ceiling grid wire with no straps of its own.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer gives EMT the NM numbers, or reads the 5 ft exception as the rule. The rule is 3 ft from every termination and 10 ft between supports. Five feet is allowed only for an unbroken length — no couplings — where the structure will not let you fasten within 3 ft. A coupled length strapped at 5 ft fails.

tables.caption: EMT support at a glance
rows: Unbroken length may fasten at 5 ft max
Counts as support — openings ≤ 10 ft apart, fastened within 3 ft of terminations

figures.alt: Ceiling run of EMT from a panel, with straps dimensioned: first strap within 3 feet of the box, then straps at intervals not exceeding 10 feet, plus the 5 foot exception for unbroken lengths.
figures.caption: 3 ft from the box, 10 ft between straps — the EMT rhythm.

page_quiz.question: EMT must be securely fastened within what distance of a junction box?
page_quiz.explain_plain: Within 3 ft of every box or termination. Five feet is a limited exception for unbroken lengths.

page_quiz.question: The maximum interval between EMT supports is…
page_quiz.explain_plain: EMT must be fastened and supported at intervals not exceeding 10 ft.

page_quiz.question: A strap lands 5 ft from a termination. When is that legal?
choices: Always, if the run is level
Only for an unbroken length, where structural members do not permit fastening within 3 ft
page_quiz.explain_plain: The 5 ft distance applies only to an unbroken length — no couplings — where the structure blocks the 3 ft fastening.

sections.title: EMT couplings and connectors — tight, and listed for the location
sections.plain_explanation: EMT couplings and connectors must be made up tight so the raceway is mechanically continuous and electrically continuous as a ground path. Where buried in masonry or concrete, they must be of the concrete-tight type. Where installed in wet locations, they must comply with 314.15 — listed for use in wet locations and installed so moisture does not enter or accumulate in the enclosure. The Code rule is the listing for the location, not the fitting style: use the type, compression or set-screw, that is listed concrete-tight or listed for wet use for the job in front of you.
sections.on_the_job: Match the fitting to the location on the purchase order, not at the truck: a fitting listed concrete-tight for masonry or concrete, a fitting listed for wet use for wet locations, and ordinary fittings only where the run stays dry and is not buried in masonry or concrete.
sections.figure_idea: Two fittings side by side: set-screw marked 'dry', compression marked 'wet / concrete-tight'.
sections.why_it_exists: EMT is not just a pipe — made up tight, it is also the ground path. A loose coupling is a break in that path, and a fitting that is not listed for its location lets concrete slurry or rainwater into the raceway, where it sits on the conductors for years. The listing is how the Code knows the fitting seals and holds where it is installed. Florida makes both cases weekly: fittings disappear into concrete pours, and exterior runs live wet half the year.
inspection_fails: Ordinary fittings buried in a concrete pour, not listed concrete-tight.
Fittings in a wet location with no wet-location listing — water standing in the raceway (314.15).
Couplings left finger-loose — the raceway is not mechanically or electrically continuous.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is the style rule of thumb: 'compression for wet, set-screw for dry.' The Code does not grade the style — it grades the listing. A set-screw fitting listed concrete-tight is legal in concrete; a compression fitting with no wet listing is not legal in a wet location. Match the listing to the location.

page_quiz.question: EMT fittings buried in concrete must be:
page_quiz.explain_plain: 358.42: where buried in masonry or concrete, couplings and connectors must be of the concrete-tight type.

page_quiz.question: EMT fittings in wet locations must comply with:
page_quiz.explain_plain: Wet-location fittings must comply with 314.15 — listed for wet locations and installed so moisture does not enter or accumulate.

page_quiz.question: What decides whether a fitting is legal in a wet location?
page_quiz.explain_plain: The Code rule is the listing for the location, not the fitting style.

sections.title: Flexible metallic tubing — Type FMT
sections.plain_explanation:
Flexible metallic tubing — Type FMT — is a small, flexible metallic tubing method for specific limited applications — not a general raceway and not the same thing as FMC (Article 348), despite the similar name and look. Its permitted uses are narrow and its size range is small.
FMT is a raceway: circular in cross section, flexible, metallic, and liquidtight without a nonmetallic jacket (360.2). The tubing and its fittings must be listed (360.6).
Uses permitted (360.10) — branch circuits only, and only where all of these hold:
• In dry locations
• Where concealed
• In accessible locations
• On systems of 1000 volts or less
Uses not permitted (360.12): in hoistways; in storage battery rooms; in hazardous (classified) locations unless another article permits it; underground, direct-buried, or embedded in poured concrete or aggregate; where subject to physical damage; and in lengths over 6 ft.
Sizes are just as tight (360.20): trade size ½ is the minimum and ¾ the maximum. Trade size ⅜ exists only for connections in air-handling spaces under 300.22(B) and (C), or in lengths of 6 ft or less as part of a listed assembly or a luminaire connection.
sections.on_the_job: Orlando office fit-out: a 4 ft FMT whip from a junction box to a lay-in luminaire above an accessible ceiling — the connection FMT exists for, on a 20 A commercial lighting circuit in trade size ½. The bend at the luminaire stays at or above the 12½ in minimum radius for ½ in tubing that will flex in service. Name-check before use: FMT on a print is a specific listed method. Do not substitute FMC, EMT or LFMC for it by appearance.
sections.why_it_exists: FMT is a light, specialized tubing built for short final connections, and every limit in the article defends that role. The 6 ft cap keeps runs short enough to inspect end to end. The dry-location and no-burial rules keep a thin liquidtight skin from being asked to do armored cable's job underground or in concrete, where damage would stay hidden until it faulted.
inspection_fails: FMT run longer than 6 ft — a long whip snaking across a ceiling (360.12(6)).
FMT installed outdoors, in a wet location, or embedded in concrete (360.10, 360.12(4)).
FMT bent tighter than the Table 360.24 radius — kinked flat at the luminaire.
FMT carrying a feeder, or a circuit over 1000 V — branch circuits only, 1000 V maximum (360.10).
Unlisted fittings, or FMC fittings forced onto FMT (360.6, 360.42).
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer swaps FMT and FMC because the names and the coil look alike. FMC is a general-purpose raceway with a full size range and no 6 ft cap. FMT stops at trade size ¾, at 6 ft, and at branch circuits — an answer that treats them as interchangeable fails on all three.

tables.caption: Minimum bend radii for FMT (Tables 360.24(A) and (B))
tables.note: Flexing radii apply where the tubing may be flexed in service after installation; fixed-bend radii where bends are made at installation and stay put.

page_quiz.explain_plain: 360.12(6) prohibits FMT in lengths over 6 ft — the cap is what keeps it a final-connection method.

page_quiz.question: What is the largest trade size of FMT?
page_quiz.explain_plain: FMT comes in trade sizes ½ and ¾ only; ⅜ is limited to air-handling connections and listed assemblies.

sections.title: Electrical nonmetallic tubing — ENT ('smurf tube')
sections.plain_explanation:
ENT is a pliable, corrugated nonmetallic raceway used concealed in walls, floors and ceilings, in slab on grade and in other locations its article allows — common on Sharma-adjacent work for low-voltage and island/concrete runs in houses, and as a sleeve where a future pull is wanted. It is not a general substitute for PVC conduit: its locations, support rules and temperature and damage limits are its own.
• Support (362.30): fasten it within 3 ft of each box and at intervals of not more than 3 ft.
• Bends (362.26): not more than the equivalent of four quarter bends — 360 degrees total — between pull points.
• Permitted (362.10): concealed in walls, floors and ceilings; encased in concrete and in slab on grade with listed fittings; exposed only in buildings not more than three floors above grade. In taller buildings, concealed ENT needs a thermal barrier with at least a 15-minute finish rating.
• Not permitted (362.12): where subject to physical damage, direct earth burial, ambient over 50 °C (122 °F), or circuits over 600 V.
sections.on_the_job: Island receptacle in a slab house is the classic ENT case: stub it accurately, cap it, photograph it with measurements before the pour — a lost stub in concrete is a saw-cut later. On a Kissimmee slab, Sharma's crew strapped the run every 3 ft in the slab prep, kept the run to two 90s — half the 360-degree bend budget — and shot the photo with the tape reading to two walls. After the pour, that photo is the as-built.
sections.figure_idea: Slab section with a corrugated ENT run to a kitchen island stub-up, tape measure to two walls in the photo callout.

sections.why_it_exists: ENT is thin-walled corrugated plastic. Sunlight, heat and a shovel all beat it, so the article keeps it concealed, encased or indoors, and under a temperature ceiling. The tight 3 ft support keeps a soft raceway from sagging and kinking between straps, and the 360-degree bend limit keeps the pull possible through corrugations that grip the conductors harder than smooth conduit does.
inspection_fails: ENT direct-buried in the yard as a sleeve to a gate light (362.12).
ENT run sagging between straps 6 ft apart — support is 3 ft max, and within 3 ft of boxes (362.30).
Five 90-degree bends in one run between pull points — over the 360-degree limit (362.26).
ENT exposed on a four-story building's corridor wall with no thermal barrier (362.10).
sections.exam_trap: The trap: 'ENT is just flexible PVC, so it goes anywhere PVC goes.' It does not. ENT has its own article: no direct burial, no physical-damage locations, no ambient over 50 °C, exposed work stops at three floors above grade, and it is supported every 3 ft — not on PVC's spacing.

sections.title: Where ENT may — and may not — be used
sections.plain_explanation: ENT ('smurf tube') is permitted concealed in walls, floors, and ceilings, encased in concrete and in slab-on-grade work with listed fittings, and in wet locations where the tubing and fittings are listed for them. Its exposed use is height-limited: exposed ENT is permitted only in buildings not more than three floors above grade (with this section's own allowances), which is why it disappears into slabs and walls on taller work. It may not be used where subject to physical damage, in sunlight unless marked sunlight resistant, in hazardous (classified) locations except as specifically allowed, for circuits over 600 volts, or as a support for fixtures or other equipment. In buildings over three floors above grade, ENT is permitted concealed in walls, floors and ceilings only where they provide a thermal barrier with at least a 15-minute finish rating (362.10(2)). ENT is also not permitted for direct earth burial, where ambient exceeds 50°C, for conductors operating above its listed temperature, or in theaters and similar locations except as Articles 518 and 520 allow (362.12).
sections.on_the_job: In a Florida slab, ENT is a sleeve and low-voltage raceway more than a branch-circuit method: coil and stub it where the island and floor outlets will land, cap the ends against concrete, and photograph every run before the pour — after the pour, the photo is the as-built.
sections.figure_idea: Slab plan with ENT coils stubbed at an island and a floor outlet, caps on the ends, and a camera icon marking the pre-pour photo.

nec2023_change.change: The ENT uses list got cleaned up: the sprinkler standard moved to a note, and concrete use now has two separate items, one for encasement and one for slabs. Above three floors, ENT has to be hidden behind walls, floors or ceilings that carry a 15-minute finish rating or better (362.10(2)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 362.10 ENT uses

sections.why_it_exists: ENT is a plastic raceway with real limits: it softens with heat, it burns, and it has no strength against physical damage. The floor limit and the thermal-barrier rule keep it out of the fire path in taller buildings, and the sunlight and temperature limits keep the tubing from going brittle or sagging before the conductors are ever pulled.
inspection_fails: ENT run exposed in a four-story building — exposed use stops at three floors above grade (362.10).
ENT direct-buried in the yard — prohibited by 362.12.
ENT used to support a luminaire — ENT may not support fixtures or other equipment.
Unmarked ENT run in direct sunlight — permitted only where marked sunlight resistant.
ENT concealed above three floors without the 15-minute finish thermal barrier — 362.10(2).
sections.exam_trap: The trap: 'ENT is just blue plastic conduit, so it can run exposed anywhere and be direct-buried like UF.' Wrong on both counts. Exposed ENT stops at three floors above grade, and 362.12 prohibits direct earth burial entirely. A second trap answer uses ENT to support a fixture — also prohibited.

sections.title: Auxiliary gutters
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 366 covers auxiliary gutters: a sheet-metal enclosure hung at switchboards, panelboards and service equipment to give conductors room to enter, turn and distribute where the equipment's own wiring space runs out.
• What it does: supplements the equipment — adds wire-bending and turning room at the gear, and a place for conductors to distribute to several enclosures.
• What it is not: a raceway run across a building. It lives at the equipment it serves.
• How it is sized: by its own article — conductor fill and splicing room follow 366, and the conductors still need their bending room, like 312.6.
• Where you see it: larger services and multi-meter lineups, where several sets of conductors have to land in a row of equipment.
sections.on_the_job: On larger services and multi-meter work, a gutter is what makes a clean, legal lineup possible. Size it for the conductors and their bending, like 312.6, before the gear is set. Take a six-meter retail service: six sets of conductors come up from the underground lateral into the gutter, turn, and drop into their meter sockets and disconnects in a row. If the gutter is picked by what fits the wall instead of by the conductor count and bend radius, the crew finds out at trim, with the gear already hung — and the fix is a bigger gutter bought twice.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: Big conductors forced into too little room get their insulation cut on enclosure edges and their strands stressed at the lugs, and a gutter crammed past its fill runs hot and cannot be worked on safely. The gutter exists to give service and feeder conductors a legal amount of room to bend, turn and spread out to the gear — the article's fill and space rules are what keep 'more room' from becoming 'stuffed box.'
inspection_fails: Auxiliary gutter used as a raceway run across the building instead of at the equipment it supplements (Article 366).
Gutter overfilled past its article's conductor fill — cover forced on over stuffed conductors.
Conductors bent into the gutter with no bending room — insulation cut on the enclosure edge (312.6).
sections.exam_trap: The trap is calling the gutter a wireway and running it like one — across the building, filled by wireway rules. An auxiliary gutter supplements the equipment it hangs on; its fill and splicing room follow Article 366, and a 30 ft run of 'gutter' used as a raceway is the wrong method and the wrong answer.

page_quiz.explain_plain: The gutter supplements switchboards, panelboards and service equipment — it adds room where the equipment's own wiring space runs out.

page_quiz.explain_plain: Fill and splicing room follow the gutter's own article, and conductors still need their bending room, like 312.6.

sections.title: Busways
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 368 covers busways: a factory-built distribution system — busbars in a metal housing, with plug-in units that tap power off along the run. It is the backbone distribution of larger commercial and industrial buildings.
• Built as a system: sections are joined, supported and tapped as a listed system, with fittings made for the busway — not field-fabricated.
• Tapped along the run: plug-in units land where the loads are, each with its own disconnect and overcurrent protection.
• Protected as distribution: overcurrent protection and grounding follow this article and the system design, not branch-circuit rules of thumb.
• Handled as equipment: a busway is energized distribution equipment, not a big wireway — nobody opens, moves or taps it casually.
sections.on_the_job: Outside Sharma's ordinary scope, but common in the larger commercial spaces Sharma works in. Never open, move or tap a busway as if it were a big wireway — it is energized distribution equipment. On a tenant job the usual task is narrower: the design calls for a new plug-in unit on the existing busway to feed a 200 A tenant panel. That is the busway manufacturer's listed unit, set during a coordinated shutdown — Sharma's scope is the feeder from the plug-in unit down to the tenant gear, new Siemens panel and breakers, and the coordination to get the busway de-energized for the tap. Price the shutdown and the listed unit, not just the conduit.

sections.why_it_exists: A busway carries feeder-level current in exposed bars inside a housing that runs the length of a building. A loose joint overheats under load, a tap made without the listed plug-in unit puts conductors on a high-energy source with no proper protection, and the available fault current at a busway tap can be far beyond what small equipment is rated to interrupt. The article's rules on joints, supports, taps and protection exist to keep that energy inside a tested system.
inspection_fails: Busway tap made with a field-fabricated connection instead of the manufacturer's listed plug-in unit (Article 368).
Busway joints or covers left open or unsecured after another trade's work above the ceiling.
Plug-in unit added or swapped with the busway energized — no shutdown, no lockout.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer calls a busway a wireway with bars in it and applies wireway thinking — field taps, splices where convenient, working it hot because 'it is just a raceway.' A busway is listed distribution equipment: taps are made with its plug-in units, and the work starts with a shutdown, not a screwdriver.

sections.title: Cablebus
sections.plain_explanation:
Cablebus is an engineered power-distribution assembly: insulated conductors supported in a ventilated metal enclosure. The run is built to a specific design for large feeders, typically between major pieces of equipment — switchgear at one end, a large load at the other.
• It is designed and supplied as a system for that one job.
• It is not assembled in the field from shelf parts.
• The enclosure is ventilated metal; the conductors inside are insulated and supported.
Think of cablebus as a feeder that arrives as an engineered product. It is closer in spirit to equipment than to conduit-and-wire pulled off a rack, and it is handled that way from delivery to final connection.
sections.on_the_job: Industrial and large-commercial work only. Field changes to a cablebus run are engineering changes, not electrician improvisation. If a run does not fit as drawn on a big commercial job, the fix goes back through the engineer and the supplier who designed the system. The crew does not move supports, change the enclosure layout, or re-route conductors to make it fit, and the change is not made on a Friday afternoon to keep the schedule.
sections.edition_note:
NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 371: New Article 371, Flexible Bus Systems.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: Large feeders carry enough energy that a failure is a major event, not a tripped breaker and a service call. The engineered assembly keeps the conductors supported and the enclosure ventilated so heat can leave, and it keeps every support and spacing where the design put it. Improvise on a run this size — move a support, change the layout, re-route a conductor — and you have changed the engineering without redoing it. Nobody checked your version.
inspection_fails: Cablebus run modified in the field without engineering — supports moved or conductors re-routed.
Cablebus assembled from shelf parts instead of the designed, supplied system.
Ventilated enclosure covered or blocked so the run cannot shed heat.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer treats cablebus as a wiring method you assemble on site — conduit-and-wire thinking with parts off the shelf. Cablebus is designed and supplied as a system for a specific job, built around large feeders between major equipment. If the description has the crew inventing the run in the field, it is not cablebus.

sections.title: Cellular concrete floor raceways
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 372 covers cellular concrete floor raceways. In this system the raceway is not conduit or duct added to the building — it is formed in the floor itself. The cellular concrete floor is built with hollow cells inside the slab, and those cells are the distribution paths. Header ducts run across the cells and feed them. An outlet is not roughed in with a box during the pour; it is activated later, out of a cell, with a fitting made for that floor system.
• The floor structure is the distribution system: cells in the slab, fed by header ducts.
• Outlets are activated from the cells, using the system's own fittings.
• You meet this system in larger commercial buildings, almost always as existing construction.
Nothing here is generic. The fittings, the way a cell is opened, and the way an outlet is set all belong to the floor system the building was built with.
sections.on_the_job: Encountered in existing commercial buildings, not new Sharma construction. Identifying the floor system correctly is the whole job before any outlet work. On a tenant renovation in an older Orlando office building, the first task is detective work, not demo: find the header duct runs, confirm which cells are in use and which were never activated, and match the outlet fittings to the floor system before ordering material. Until the system is identified, nobody cuts into the floor.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: The conductors live hidden inside the structure of the floor. That is safe only while the system stays a system: the cells protect the conductors, and the header ducts and fittings keep every access point controlled and covered. Open a cell the wrong way, or set an outlet with hardware that was not made for the floor, and you can damage conductors you cannot see and cannot pull out — they are cast into the building. A repair stops being a device swap and becomes concrete work.
inspection_fails: Outlet activated in a cellular concrete floor with a generic floor box not made for the floor system.
Floor cut into for an outlet before the floor system was identified.
Header duct left open or uncovered after outlet work in the system.
Conductor damaged where a cell was opened blindly.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating a cellular floor like a slab full of empty conduit you can use any way you like — fish any cell for any circuit and set a generic floor box. The cells and header ducts are one distribution system, and outlets are activated from the cells with that system's fittings. The second trap is the article number: a concrete floor is 372. The cellular steel deck is 374.

sections.title: Cellular metal floor raceways
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 374 is the metal counterpart to Article 372. The raceways are formed by the cells of a cellular steel floor deck in commercial construction. Header ducts feed the cells, and outlets are set with the system's own outlet fittings.
• Floor structure: a cellular steel deck — metal, not concrete.
• Header ducts feed the cells; outlets use system fittings.
• Because the system is metal, bonding and continuity of the metal parts are part of this article.
The deck and ducts are not just a pathway for wire. They are metal parts of one system, and they have to stay electrically continuous. As with 372, you meet this in existing commercial buildings, and the fittings belong to the floor system, not to a generic parts shelf.
sections.on_the_job: Existing-building work. As with 372, the system has to be identified before it is extended or abandoned in place. On a renovation, check the continuity of the deck and header ducts before tying new work into the system: a deck section replaced in an earlier remodel can break the bonding path without leaving any sign at the outlet. Identify the system first, prove it is continuous, then extend it.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: A metal raceway system sits in the fault picture whether you plan for it or not. If the steel deck and header ducts lose continuity, faulted metal can stay energized instead of giving fault current a solid path back to trip the breaker. Bonding keeps the metal parts at the same potential and the path intact. That is why continuity is written into this article instead of left to chance — a floor system gets cut, patched and remodeled over a building's life, and every cut is a chance to break the path.
inspection_fails: Cellular metal floor system extended with fittings not made for that floor system.
Bonding or continuity of the metal floor system broken where deck sections were cut or replaced.
System extended or abandoned in place without first being identified.
sections.exam_trap: Two traps. First, the number: a cellular concrete floor is 372, but the steel deck is 374 — answering 372 for metal loses the point. Second, treating the metal system as only a wire pathway and skipping bonding and continuity. The metal staying continuous and bonded is part of this article, not an extra you add if there is time.

page_quiz.explain_plain: 374 is the metal counterpart to 372's concrete floor.

choices: A paint specification for the deck
Bonding and continuity of the metal system

page_quiz.explain_plain: Bonding and continuity of the metal system are part of the article.

page_quiz.explain_plain: The system has to be identified before it is extended, and its continuity proven.

sections.title: Metal wireways
sections.plain_explanation:
A wireway is a sheet-metal trough with a hinged or removable cover, used in light commercial work to carry feeders and branch circuits where conductors need to be laid in and remain accessible along a run — above panels, along shop walls, in electrical rooms. Conductors are laid in, not pulled, and the cover is what makes the system legal: no cover, no wireway.
• Fill (376.22): the conductors at any cross section may not exceed 20 percent of the wireway's interior cross-sectional area.
• Derating (376.22): ampacity adjustment factors do not apply while a cross section holds 30 or fewer current-carrying conductors. Past 30, they apply in full.
• Splices and taps (376.56) are permitted inside a wireway that remains accessible, provided they fill no more than 75 percent of the wiring space at that cross section.
• Supports (376.30): horizontal runs are supported at each end and at intervals not exceeding 5 ft, and never more than 10 ft between supports. Vertical runs are supported at intervals not exceeding 15 ft, with not more than one joint between supports.
sections.on_the_job: On a Winter Park tenant fit-out, Sharma ran a 6 in × 6 in wireway above a row of new Siemens panels. Twenty-eight current-carrying conductors at the busiest cross section stayed under the 30-conductor line, so no adjustment factors applied. When the tenant added one more 3-phase circuit, the count passed 30 and derating entered the job — the fix was a second wireway, not bigger wire stuffed into the same trough. Do the 20 percent fill math at layout, not with the cover in your hand.
sections.figure_idea: Electrical room wall: panel with a wireway trough above it, conduits dropping out of the bottom of the trough.

nec2023_change.change: The wireway article now has its own grounding section, 376.60: a listed metal wireway is allowed to be the equipment grounding conductor (EGC). A listed metal wireway can act as the equipment grounding conductor (EGC) for the circuits run through it (376.60).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 376.60 Wireways as the EGC

FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: A wireway packed solid traps heat around every conductor, and bundled conductors heat each other — that is why the fill cap and the 30-conductor line exist. The cover and the access rules exist because a splice nobody can reach again fails silently. A wireway is a raceway you can open along its whole run; the rules keep it that way.
inspection_fails: Conductors packed past the 20 percent fill limit, cover forced on (376.22).
More than 30 current-carrying conductors at one cross section with no ampacity adjustment applied (376.22).
Splices and taps filling more than 75 percent of the wiring space at a cross section (376.56).
Horizontal wireway supported 12 ft apart — over the 10 ft maximum span (376.30(A)).
sections.exam_trap: The trap: treating the wireway like conduit, where derating starts at four current-carrying conductors — or like a trough you may fill to the brim. In a wireway the fill cap is 20 percent, adjustment factors wait until you pass 30 current-carrying conductors, and then they apply in full.
