sections.title: Wireway fill — 20 percent, and splices inside
sections.plain_explanation:
A metal wireway is a trough with a cover, not a pipe to stuff full. Three numbers run the page:
• Conductor fill: the conductors at any cross section may not exceed 20 percent of the wireway's interior cross-sectional area (376.22).
• Splices and taps: splices and taps are permitted inside a wireway that remains accessible, provided they do not fill more than 75 percent of the wiring space at that cross section (376.56).
• Derating relief: the ampacity adjustment factors of Table 310.15(C)(1) do not apply where the number of current-carrying conductors in the wireway is 30 or fewer. Past 30, derating enters the job (376.22).
sections.on_the_job: Do the 20 percent math at layout, not with the cover in your hand: list the conductors, take their areas from Chapter 9 Table 5, and check the total against one-fifth of the wireway's inside area. If the count of current-carrying conductors passes 30, derating enters the job — that is the moment to upsize the wireway or split the run. Worked check: a 4 in by 4 in wireway over a Siemens panel has 16 sq in of interior, so the 20 percent cap is 3.2 sq in. Twenty-four 12 AWG THHN conductors at 0.0133 sq in each (Chapter 9, Table 5) total about 0.32 sq in — the area passes easily. The count is the watch item: 24 current-carrying conductors is under 30, so no derating. Two more 20 A circuits put the count at 28, still clear — but the next tenant's circuits will not be.
sections.figure_idea: Wireway cross-section shaded to 20 percent conductor fill, with a splice bay shaded to its 75 percent limit.
sections.why_it_exists: A wireway packed past its fill cooks its conductors: the heat has nowhere to go, insulation ages fast, and the next man cannot pull a wire out or land a new one. The splice cap and the access rule exist because a splice you cannot reach is a splice you cannot inspect — and splices are where wireway jobs fail first.
inspection_fails: Conductors packed past 20 percent of the wireway's interior area at a cross section (376.22).
Splices filling more than 75 percent of the wiring space at the splice point (376.56).
More than 30 current-carrying conductors in the wireway with no Table 310.15(C)(1) derating applied (376.22).
Splice made in a wireway section that no longer remains accessible (376.56).
sections.exam_trap: The trap is the conduit number: "Raceways fill to 40 percent, so the wireway does too." Wrong — a wireway is 20 percent, half the conduit figure. The second trap is reading the 30-conductor relief as a 30-conductor limit: past 30 the wireway is still legal, but Table 310.15(C)(1) derating applies.

page_quiz.question: What is the maximum conductor fill at any cross section of a metal wireway?
page_quiz.explain_plain: Wireways are 20 percent. The 40 percent figure is conduit fill from Chapter 9, Table 1.

page_quiz.question: A wireway carries 34 current-carrying conductors. What changes?
page_quiz.explain_plain: The derating relief ends at 30 current-carrying conductors; past 30, the adjustment factors apply.

page_quiz.question: Splices inside an accessible wireway may fill no more than what share of the wiring space at that cross section?
page_quiz.explain_plain: 376.56 allows splices and taps in an accessible wireway up to 75 percent of the wiring space at that point.

sections.title: Nonmetallic wireways
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 378 is the nonmetallic counterpart to Article 376's metal wireways: a flame-retardant trough with a removable cover, listed as a system, with conductors laid in after the wireway is installed. Use it where a nonmetallic system is wanted — above all where corrosion makes a metal trough a poor choice.
• Exposed work only (378.10). It may pass transversely through a wall if the length in the wall is unbroken and the conductors stay accessible on both sides.
• Wet locations only where listed for the purpose; corrosive environments only where identified for the use.
• Not permitted where subject to physical damage, in hazardous (classified) locations, in sunlight unless listed and marked for it, or at temperatures outside its listing (378.12).
• Fill: conductors at any cross section may not exceed 20 percent of the interior area (378.22). Splices and taps are permitted inside, may fill up to 75 percent at that cross section, and must stay accessible (378.56).
• Derating is the trap in this article: the 310.15(C)(1) adjustment factors apply to the current-carrying conductors here. There is no 30-conductor free pass — that relief is written for metal wireways in 376.22(B).
• Support: horizontal runs at intervals not over 3 ft, and never more than 10 ft between supports; vertical runs at intervals not over 4 ft (378.30).
• The plastic trough cannot be the ground path. Run an equipment grounding conductor with the circuits.
sections.on_the_job: Use where corrosion makes metal wireway a poor choice and the location is permitted. The cover still makes the system — no cover, no wireway. On a coastal Florida job, a beachside condo electrical room in Brevard County, a 4 in. by 4 in. nonmetallic wireway has 16 sq in. inside, so the 20 percent limit allows 3.2 sq in. of conductors. Lay in six 20 A circuits of 12 AWG THHN and the current-carrying count already forces the 310.15(C)(1) adjustment — do that math before the wire is ordered, not with the cover in your hand.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: The cover and the fill limits are the heat and damage controls. Conductors laid in a trough still heat each other, and plastic gives up strength sooner than steel as temperature climbs — which is why this article makes you derate bundled conductors instead of borrowing the metal wireway's 30-conductor relief. The exposed-only and no-damage-location rules exist because a plastic trough has no impact strength to forgive a forklift or a ladder strike.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is borrowing the metal-wireway rule: 'wireways never derate under 30 conductors.' That is 376.22(B), metal only. In a nonmetallic wireway the 310.15(C)(1) adjustment factors apply to the current-carrying conductors from the start, so the same conductor count that passes in a steel trough fails in a plastic one.
inspection_fails: Wireway run where carts and lifts can hit it — nonmetallic wireway is not permitted where subject to physical damage (378.12).
Thirty current-carrying conductors with no ampacity adjustment — the 30-conductor relief belongs to metal wireways (376.22(B)), not this article.
Conductors stuffed past 20 percent fill, or a splice packed past 75 percent at its cross section (378.22, 378.56).
No equipment grounding conductor run with the circuits — a plastic trough is not a ground path.
Supports 6 ft apart on a horizontal run — 3 ft maximum for nonmetallic wireways (378.30).

figures.alt: Cross-section of a 4 by 4 inch nonmetallic wireway with the 20 percent fill zone shaded and conductors laid in, beside the support spacing, derating and permitted-location rules of Article 378.
figures.caption: Nonmetallic wireway: 20% fill, derating applies, supports at 3 ft.

page_quiz.question: What is the maximum conductor fill at any cross section of a nonmetallic wireway?
page_quiz.explain_plain: 378.22 caps the sum of conductor areas at 20 percent of the wireway's interior cross-sectional area. The 75 percent figure is only for splices and taps at their cross section.

page_quiz.question: Twelve current-carrying conductors run in a nonmetallic wireway. What applies?
choices: More than 10 conductors is not permitted

page_quiz.explain_plain: 378.30 limits horizontal supports to 3 ft intervals for nonmetallic wireways (and never more than 10 ft between any two supports). The 5 ft figure is the metal wireway value.

rich_sources.source: Solar365, NEC Article 378 — Nonmetallic Wireways (article text)

sections.title: Multioutlet assemblies
sections.plain_explanation:
A multioutlet assembly is a surface, flush or freestanding raceway designed to hold conductors and receptacles, assembled at the factory or in the field — the hard-wired strip over a workbench or lab counter, in metal or nonmetallic form.
• It is permitted in dry locations only.
• It may not be installed concealed — except that a metal assembly may be surrounded on its back and sides by the building finish and a nonmetallic one may be recessed in a baseboard.
• It is barred where subject to severe physical damage, in hoistways, and in the other locations its article lists (380.12).
• A metal assembly may pass through a dry partition if no outlet sits inside the partition and the cover can be removed on both sides.
• In a dwelling it is not a dodge around the receptacle rules, but it is not banned from counting either: for kitchen countertop spacing, each 12 in of assembly containing two or more receptacles counts as one receptacle outlet under 210.52(C).
sections.on_the_job: Use it where it belongs — benches, counters, retail and lab work — and count its load like any receptacle run; the strip does not create capacity, it only distributes outlets. On a Kissimmee kitchen remodel, a 4 ft assembly under the upper cabinets with receptacles every 12 in: for 210.52(C) spacing, each 12 in length with two or more receptacles counts as one receptacle outlet, so the strip counts as four — and it still lands on the same small-appliance branch-circuit rules as any other countertop receptacle.
sections.why_it_exists: The strip packs receptacles and splices into one long raceway that people lean on, plug into and clean around every day. Keeping it in dry locations, out of hoistways and out of impact zones protects a device-dense assembly that takes daily abuse. Keeping it unconcealed means the cover can come off — a failed splice inside a buried assembly would cook inside a wall nobody can open.
inspection_fails: Multioutlet assembly installed where it is not a dry location (380.10).
Assembly concealed behind the building finish with no way to remove the cover.
Metal assembly through a partition with an outlet inside the partition.
Assembly installed in a hoistway or where subject to severe physical damage (380.12).
sections.exam_trap: The trap: "It's just a raceway, so bury it in the wall like one." Wrong — 380 bars concealed installation, with only the two narrow exceptions (metal surrounded on back and sides by the finish; nonmetallic recessed in a baseboard). The second trap counts every receptacle in a kitchen strip separately for 210.52(C) spacing; the rule counts each 12 in length holding two or more receptacles as ONE receptacle outlet.

Metal only; no outlet in the partition; cover removable on both sides
Each 12 in with 2+ receptacles = 1 receptacle outlet (210.52(C))

page_quiz.explain_plain: Article 380 permits multioutlet assemblies in dry locations only.

page_quiz.explain_plain: Each 12 in of assembly containing two or more receptacles counts as one receptacle outlet under 210.52(C).

No outlet is in the partition and the cover can be removed on both sides

sections.title: Nonmetallic extensions
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 382 covers nonmetallic extensions: listed surface extension wiring systems that start from an existing outlet and serve additional outlets along a wall surface. It is a narrow, specific method with its own fittings and limits — not a license to surface-run ordinary cable.
• What it is: a listed assembly — base, cover, fittings and receptacles made as one system — that extends an existing outlet along the wall.
• How it starts: from an existing outlet only. It extends a circuit; it does not create one.
• Where it cannot go: the article bars it from many of the places people first think of. It is a short list of permitted uses, not a general wiring method.
• The Sharma answer: know it to recognize it. A proper surface raceway (386 or 388) or a new circuit is usually both legal and better.
sections.on_the_job: Rarely the right answer on Sharma work; a proper raceway (386/388) or a new circuit is usually both legal and better. Know the article mainly to recognize the method. The call usually comes from a tenant finish-out: a desk row needs two more receptacles and someone suggests a surface extension kit off the supply-house shelf. Price the real fix instead — a short run of surface metal raceway on a new 20 A circuit with a Siemens breaker, done once. The extension kit still leaves the tenant on the old circuit, and the callback lands on Sharma.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: An extension run lives exposed on the wall, where furniture, feet and vacuum cleaners hit it, and it taps an existing circuit that was never sized for the added load. The listing and the use limits exist because a surface run has none of the protection of cable inside a wall — the system has to provide that protection itself, and the circuit behind it has to stay within what it was built for.
inspection_fails: Ordinary NM cable surface-run under a cover strip and called a nonmetallic extension — only the listed system is permitted (Article 382).
Extension tapped from a junction box or a new source instead of from an existing outlet.
Cover, base and fittings mixed from different systems — the extension is listed as one assembly.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer treats a nonmetallic extension like surface raceway — a general way to add outlets anywhere. It is not: it is one listed system, fed from an existing outlet, with its own fittings and a short list of permitted uses. 'Run NM cable on the surface under a cover' is never the answer; ordinary cable has no place in it.

figures.alt: Side-by-side panels: a listed nonmetallic extension starting at an existing outlet and adding outlets of the same system, versus ordinary cable under a cover strip crossed out in red.
figures.caption: A listed extension system — and what it is not.

page_quiz.question: A nonmetallic extension must start from:
choices: Any point on a receptacle circuit
page_quiz.explain_plain: The system extends an existing outlet along the wall surface. It does not create a circuit or tap a new source.

page_quiz.question: A tenant wants two more desk receptacles. The Sharma answer is usually:
choices: A proper raceway (386/388) or a new circuit
page_quiz.explain_plain: A real raceway or a new circuit is usually both legal and better; the extension is a narrow method to recognize, not a default.

sections.title: Strut-type channel raceway
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 384 covers strut-type channel raceway: a listed wiring system built on metal strut channel with covers and fittings made for electrical use — the channel is the raceway.
• What makes it a raceway: the listed covers, fittings and conductor limits of this article. Ordinary structural strut by itself is a support, not a raceway.
• What goes inside: conductors installed as a wiring method, in the sizes and counts the listing allows — not cable assemblies dropped into open channel.
• What strut usually is on our jobs: a support system — trapeze racks and stands holding conduit and equipment. That strut follows the support rules of whatever it holds.
• The test: if conductors run inside the channel, it is this article and it must be the listed system. If conduit runs on top of it, it is support work.
sections.on_the_job: Common confusion on commercial jobs: strut holding conduits is support work; strut carrying conductors inside it is this article. Keep the two apart in the takeoff and the inspection conversation. On a retail tenant job the miss shows up as a takeoff line: 'strut channel' priced once, when the job actually needs the listed raceway system — covers, fittings and all — for the counter run, plus plain strut for the trapeze racks overhead. Price them as two different materials, because the inspector will treat them as two different things.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: Conductors inside bare structural channel sit against sharp steel edges with no listed cover, no tested fill limits and no protection from the next trade's screws and straps. The listing exists so the channel, covers and fittings are tested as one wiring system — insulation protected, fill controlled, covers secured — instead of a steel trough that only looks like a raceway.
inspection_fails: Conductors laid in ordinary structural strut with no listed covers — channel is not a raceway without the listed system (Article 384).
Strut raceway covers missing or unsecured at inspection.
Cable assemblies run inside the channel instead of the conductors the listing permits.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is 'strut is strut.' A length of ordinary structural channel with conductors laid in it is not a raceway, however neat it looks — without the listed covers, fittings and conductor limits of Article 384 it is a support with wire in it, and the exam answer that calls it a wiring method is wrong.

figures.alt: Two panels of the same strut channel: left with a listed cover and conductors inside as a 384 raceway, right carrying conduit on top as support work only.
figures.caption: Same steel, two jobs: raceway on the left, support on the right.

page_quiz.question: What turns strut channel into a raceway?
choices: Painting it to match the wall
Listed covers, fittings and conductor limits used as a system
Bolting it tight to the wall
Filling it less than half full
page_quiz.explain_plain: The listed covers, fittings and conductor limits of Article 384 make the channel a wiring system. Plain structural strut is a support.

page_quiz.question: Strut on a trapeze rack holding three conduits is:
page_quiz.explain_plain: Strut holding conduit is support work. Strut only becomes this article when conductors run inside the listed channel system.

sections.title: Surface metal raceways
sections.plain_explanation:
Surface metal raceway is the low-profile metal channel system mounted on walls and ceilings in finished spaces — the office and retail retrofit standard — carrying branch circuits to surface boxes and devices made for the system. Fill, fittings and grounding are the system's own; it is a raceway, not a decorative cover for loose cable.
• Dry locations (386.10). It may pass transversely through dry walls, partitions and floors if the length passing through is unbroken, with access to the conductors on both sides.
• Not permitted where subject to severe physical damage (unless approved), where subject to corrosive vapors, in hoistways, or concealed (386.12).
• A voltage condition: at 300 V or more between conductors, the metal must be at least 0.040 in. (1.02 mm) thick nominal (386.12).
• No conductor larger than the raceway is designed for, and never more conductors than it is designed for (386.21, 386.22).
• The derating break: the 310.15(C)(1) adjustment factors do not apply when all three hold — raceway cross section over 4 sq in., current-carrying conductors 30 or fewer, and conductor fill not over 20 percent of the interior (386.22).
• Splices and taps are permitted where the cover is removable and stays accessible, and conductors including the splice may not fill over 75 percent at that point. Without a removable cover, splices live in boxes (386.56).
• Support follows the manufacturer's instructions (386.30).
sections.on_the_job: The retrofit answer where walls cannot open. Plan device boxes and fittings from the same system — mixing ordinary boxes defeats the listing. On a Winter Park retail refresh, Sharma runs a listed two-piece raceway down an existing block wall to feed new counter receptacles: circuits at 20 A on Siemens breakers, one manufacturer's system end to end, and every splice under a cover the next tech can pop with a screwdriver.

sections.why_it_exists: Finished spaces still need power where the walls cannot open, and this system answers without demolition. The limits guard its weak points: thin metal dents and opens under impact, a concealed run disappears from inspection forever, and a packed channel cooks its conductors — hence the damage, concealment, voltage and fill conditions written into the article.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is the fill answer: 'surface raceway derates like conduit, always.' Under 386.22, when the raceway is over 4 sq in., holds 30 or fewer current-carrying conductors and stays at 20 percent fill, the 310.15(C)(1) adjustment factors do not apply. Miss any one of the three conditions and derating is back on.
inspection_fails: Raceway buried behind new drywall 'to hide it' — concealed is prohibited (386.12).
480 V run in light-gauge raceway under 0.040 in. thick — at 300 V and up, the metal must be 0.040 in. nominal (386.12).
Splice buried inside a raceway section with no removable cover (386.56).
Ordinary 4-square boxes and devices mixed into a listed raceway system, defeating its listing.
Raceway run into a damp back room — the article permits dry locations (386.10).

tables.caption: The 386.22 derating break — all three, or it does not apply
tables.note: Meet all three and the 310.15(C)(1) adjustment factors do not apply (386.22).

page_quiz.question: Conductors at 480 V between conductors are run in surface metal raceway. What does 386.12 require?
choices: Metal at least 0.040 in. thick nominal
page_quiz.explain_plain: At 300 V or more between conductors, surface metal raceway is permitted only where the metal is not less than 0.040 in. (1.02 mm) thick nominal.

page_quiz.question: A splice is needed inside a surface metal raceway that has no removable cover. Where does it go?
choices: Anywhere — tap it and close up
Only at the ends of the run
Splices are never allowed with this system
page_quiz.explain_plain: 386.56 permits splices inside raceway with a removable, accessible cover (75 percent fill at that point). Without a removable cover, splices and taps are made only in boxes.

page_quiz.question: When do the 310.15(C)(1) adjustment factors NOT apply in surface metal raceway?
choices: When the raceway is over 4 sq in., with 30 or fewer current-carrying conductors at 20% fill or less
On all branch circuits under 30 A
page_quiz.explain_plain: 386.22 waives the adjustment factors only when all three conditions hold together: cross section over 4 sq in., 30 or fewer current-carrying conductors, and fill not over 20 percent.

sections.title: Surface nonmetallic raceways
sections.plain_explanation:
The nonmetallic counterpart to Article 386: surface-mounted plastic raceway systems for finished spaces, common for both power and low-voltage in offices and homes. Power and communications sharing one system is allowed only where the system is listed and arranged for it.
The system — raceway and fittings — must be listed (388.6), and it is secured and supported following the manufacturer's instructions (388.30).
Uses permitted (388.10) are only two:
• In dry locations
• As an extension passing transversely through dry walls, partitions and floors, where the length passing through is unbroken and access to the conductors is maintained on both sides
Uses not permitted (388.12): where concealed, except for that through-wall case; where subject to severe physical damage; where the voltage between conductors is 300 volts or more, unless the raceway is listed for the higher voltage; in hoistways; in hazardous (classified) locations, except as other articles permit; where ambient temperatures exceed the raceway's listing; and with conductors whose insulation temperature rating exceeds the listing.
Combination raceways (388.70) carry power and signaling or communications in separate, identified compartments of the same listed system. Splices and taps (388.56) are permitted where the cover stays accessible, and conductors, splices and taps together may not fill more than 75 percent of the raceway at that point. No conductor larger than the raceway is designed for (388.21).
sections.on_the_job: Neat retrofit work, within its damage and location limits — it is surface wiring, so it lives where people and furniture can reach it. Protect or re-route accordingly. Orlando medical office: two new 20 A receptacle circuits in a listed combination raceway along a private-office wall — power in one compartment, data in the other — passing unbroken through one dry partition with access on both sides. At 120 volts the run sits well under the 300 volt between-conductors cap, and the run stays high on the wall, out of the chair and cart zone.
sections.why_it_exists: This is a light plastic channel living on a finished wall — no armor, no metal to shed heat, nothing hidden. The dry-location, damage, voltage and temperature limits keep it in the gentle indoor work it was listed for. Conceal it, cook it, or hang it where carts and lifts run, and the first anyone knows of the damage is the fault.
inspection_fails: Surface raceway concealed behind new drywall — only the unbroken through-wall length may pass through (388.10(2), 388.12(1)).
Raceway run at cart height in a warehouse or garage — severe physical damage exposure (388.12(2)).
277/480 V circuits in a raceway not listed for 300 V or more between conductors (388.12(3)).
Power and data mixed in one compartment of a raceway not listed and arranged as a combination system (388.70).
Raceway installed in a damp or wet location — dry locations only (388.10(1)).
sections.exam_trap: The trap is assuming 388 goes everywhere its metal twin 386 goes. It does not: the nonmetallic article drops the Class I, Division 2 and raised-floor permissions, adds ambient and conductor temperature limits, and caps the system at 300 volts between conductors unless it is listed for more.

sections.title: Underfloor raceways
sections.plain_explanation:
Underfloor raceways are distribution ducts set in or under a concrete floor — the older office-building system of floor ducts and junction boxes feeding floor outlets. New work is uncommon; existing systems are met on commercial remodels, where inserts and outlets must match the system.
The installation rules (390.3): permitted beneath the surface of concrete or other flooring, and in office occupancies laid flush with the concrete floor under linoleum or equivalent covering. Not permitted where subject to corrosive vapors or in hazardous (classified) locations, and unprotected metal raceways, boxes and fittings do not go in concrete or severe corrosive areas.
• Covering (390.4): raceways not over 4 in wide need at least ¾ in of concrete or wood above them; wider flat-top raceways need 1 in of concrete, or 1½ in where spaced less than 1 in apart
• Conductors (390.5, 390.6): no conductor larger than the raceway is designed for, and all conductors together may fill no more than 40 percent of the raceway's interior
• Splices and taps (390.7): only in junction boxes. Loop wiring — a continuous, unbroken conductor running through the outlets — is not a splice or a tap
• Discontinued outlets (390.8): when an outlet is abandoned or removed, its conductors come out of the raceway; no splices or re-insulated conductors stay behind
Junction boxes sit level with the floor grade, sealed against water and concrete, and runs are laid straight, box center to box center, with markers at the ends so the system can be found under the finished floor.
sections.on_the_job: On a remodel, find the junction boxes before promising floor outlets. An abandoned duct with no access is archaeology, not distribution. Orlando office remodel: the survey is markers first, then open every junction box on the run, check the existing fill against the 40 percent limit before adding two 20 A receptacle circuits, and pull the conductors of every outlet the new plan deletes — 390.8 does not let them stay in the duct, taped off and forgotten.
sections.why_it_exists: Once the floor is poured, this system is invisible for decades. Straight runs, end markers and boxes flush at grade are what let the next electrician find it, open it and pull new conductors. The splice and abandoned-conductor rules keep hidden joints and dead copper out of a duct nobody can see into.
inspection_fails: Splice or tap made inside the duct run instead of in a junction box (390.7).
Conductors of a removed outlet left in the raceway, taped or re-insulated (390.8).
Junction box set below floor grade or unsealed — concrete and water inside the system.
Raceway filled past 40 percent of its interior cross-section (390.6).
Floor outlet insert that does not match the raceway system, or a dead-end run left open.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer says loop wiring is a splice at every outlet it passes through, so it can't be used. 390.7 says the opposite: a continuous, unbroken conductor connecting the outlets is not considered a splice or tap. The real splice rule is the location — junction boxes only.

sections.title: Cable tray systems
sections.plain_explanation:
Cable tray is a support system, not a raceway: an open ladder, ventilated or solid-bottom structure that supports cables.
• What may lie in it: the wiring methods listed in Table 392.10(A) — including tray-rated Type TC, metal-clad cable, raceways, and, where identified for the use, nonmetallic-sheathed cable in the structures Article 334 permits.
• The restricted case: single insulated conductors. Outside the industrial-establishment rules of 392.10(B), they do not belong in tray.
• The tray itself must be bonded and grounded as the article requires.
• Fill is figured by the cable-area and sum-of-diameters rules of 392.22, not by the Chapter 9 conduit tables.
sections.on_the_job: If Sharma reaches for tray on a light-commercial job, the cable choice changes first (a wiring method Table 392.10(A) permits for that building), then the tray size. Do not lay loose single building conductors in tray and call it supported — apart from the narrow industrial exception in 392.10(B), they are not a tray wiring method. NM is not automatically barred either: it may sit in tray only where Article 334 permits it and the cable is identified for tray use.
sections.figure_idea: Warehouse bay with a ladder tray carrying bundled tray cable above a conduit drop to a disconnect.
sections.why_it_exists: A tray holds cables up; it does not enclose or protect them the way a raceway does, and it becomes a ground path only if it is bonded on purpose. Cables never identified for tray were not evaluated lying in an open structure where they can be abraded, stepped on or loaded past their limits. The 392.22 fill rules keep a tray from becoming a solid mat of cable that traps heat and crushes the bottom layer.
sections.exam_trap: Two trap answers share one page: "tray is just an open raceway, so figure fill from Chapter 9," and "single conductors are fine in tray anywhere." Fill comes from 392.22, and single insulated conductors in tray are the industrial-only case of 392.10(B).

sections.title: Low-voltage suspended ceiling power distribution systems
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 393 covers listed low-voltage power distribution systems that use the suspended ceiling structure to distribute power to ceiling-supported equipment. Read the limit in that sentence: this is one specific, engineered, listed system.
• The components, the connections and the loads are the system's own — they come with the listing, not from the parts shelf.
• The article is not permission to treat the ceiling grid as a raceway.
• It is not permission to use the grid as a support for ordinary wiring either.
Ordinary ceiling work does not move into this article. It stays under the general rules: securing and supporting under 300.11, and wiring in spaces used for environmental air under 300.22. Article 393 loosens neither one.
sections.on_the_job: Specialized commercial systems only. Ordinary ceiling work stays under 300.11 and 300.22 — this article does not loosen either. On a Florida office tenant job, if the space has a listed ceiling power system, Sharma works to that system's components and instructions, with no field substitutions. Everything else above the ceiling — the 20 A branch circuits for the lighting layout and the rest of the ordinary work — is installed the regular way under 300.11 and 300.22.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.

sections.why_it_exists: Ceiling grid is light structure, built to carry tiles and the fixtures made to sit in it — not to serve as a wiring method. Ordinary cable laid on grid or hung from it gets damaged, sags the grid, and sits in the ceiling plenum where fire and smoke rules are strict. A listed 393 system is engineered and tested for exactly this use, with defined components and loads. Field-invented 'grid power' has none of that behind it, and the failure shows up above a ceiling nobody watches.
inspection_fails: Ordinary branch-circuit wiring laid on the ceiling grid and called a 393 system.
Parts substituted into a listed ceiling power system that are not the system's components.
Loads connected to a ceiling power system beyond the system's own listed connections.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer says Article 393 lets you distribute ordinary branch power through the ceiling grid. It does not. Article 393 covers a listed low-voltage system with its own components, connections and loads. For everything else above the ceiling, 300.11 and 300.22 still apply in full — the article does not loosen either.

sections.title: Concealed knob-and-tube wiring
sections.plain_explanation:
Knob-and-tube is the oldest method in the chapter: single conductors run open on porcelain knobs and through porcelain tubes, found in older Florida houses. Article 394 governs its very limited permitted extensions and uses today. New knob-and-tube installations are effectively a closed door, and insulation contact with it is a known fire concern that other codes also address.
The prohibition that matters most on Florida re-insulation jobs sits in 394.12:
• Knob-and-tube is not permitted in the hollow spaces of walls, ceilings and attics where loose, rolled, or foamed-in-place insulation envelops the conductors.
Blowing insulation over live knob-and-tube buries a heat source the method was never designed for, and hides it. Where insulation work is planned over knob-and-tube, the wiring is replaced or the insulation plan changes — that conversation happens before the insulation truck, not after.
sections.on_the_job: On remodels in older houses, Sharma practice is identification and safe handling: document it, do not bury it in new insulation or extend it casually, and put replacement options in front of the customer. On a pre-war Tampa bungalow survey, that means photographs of every knob-and-tube run in the attic, a note on the estimate before any insulation line item, and the rewire conversation at the kitchen table — not after the insulation crew has been scheduled.
sections.florida_note: Older Florida housing stock — the pre-war bungalows of Tampa, Orlando, and Jacksonville — is where Sharma meets knob-and-tube, and it is exactly where blown-in attic insulation retrofits are sold hardest. Flag it on every survey.

sections.why_it_exists: Knob-and-tube was designed to shed heat into open air: single conductors, air space around them, porcelain between the wire and the wood. Wrap it in insulation and the heat has nowhere to go, on conductors whose own insulation is a century old. Buried, it also disappears — nobody can see the splice or the frayed covering cooking inside the blanket. Section 394.12 keeps the blanket off the wire.
inspection_fails: Blown-in attic insulation installed over live knob-and-tube — 394.12.
Foamed-in-place insulation sprayed around knob-and-tube inside a wall cavity — 394.12.
Knob-and-tube extended casually, with new NM spliced open in the attic — no box, no office decision.
Insulation crew scheduled before anyone surveyed the attic for knob-and-tube.
sections.exam_trap: 'It is grandfathered' is the trap. Existing knob-and-tube may stay in service, but 394.12 still forbids enveloping it in loose, rolled or foamed insulation in wall, ceiling and attic spaces. Grandfathered wiring does not grandfather the insulation job — the blown-in retrofit over live knob-and-tube is the violation.

sections.title: Messenger-supported wiring
sections.plain_explanation:
Messenger-supported wiring carries cables or conductors on a steel messenger strand strung between structures — overhead spans to outbuildings, site lighting and similar runs, using cable assemblies listed for the method. The messenger carries the load; the electrical cable is not its own support.
Article 396 recognizes four constructions (396.2):
• A messenger with rings and saddles supporting the conductors
• A messenger with field-installed lashing material
• Factory-assembled aerial cable
• Multiplex cables — duplex, triplex, quadruplex — twisted around a bare messenger
Only the cable types in Table 396.10(A) may ride a messenger: medium-voltage cable, Type MC, Type MI, Type SE, Type UF, tray cable, and other factory-assembled multiconductor cables identified for the use — each under its own article's conditions. In industrial establishments only, where qualified persons service the system, single conductors of the Table 310.4 types and MV cable are also permitted; outdoors they must be listed for wet locations and sunlight resistant.
The messenger is supported at dead ends and at intermediate points so the conductors carry no tension, and the conductors must not rest against the messenger supports, walls, pipes or the structure (396.30). The method is not permitted in hoistways or where subject to physical damage (396.12).
sections.on_the_job: Detached garage feeder, Marion County: a 60 ft span of quadruplex aerial cable on its bare messenger, house to garage. At final sag the span must still clear the residential driveway by 12 ft and the pedestrian-only parts of the yard by 10 ft (225.18) — string it on a cool morning and it will sit lower on a hot August afternoon. Overhead spans live outdoors and age outdoors: check the strand, attachments and clearances as one system at every service call.
sections.why_it_exists: A span of cable strung between buildings sags, swings in the wind and takes storm loads. If the cable carried its own weight, that tension would land on the terminations, and the insulation would chafe at every support until it failed. The steel messenger takes the mechanical load so the cable only carries current. The clearance rules then keep the whole span out of reach of trucks, ladders and pool poles.
inspection_fails: Messenger corroded through or broken, with the cable carrying its own weight and pulling on the terminations.
Span sagging below the required clearance at final sag — 12 ft over a residential driveway, 18 ft over a road (225.18).
Type NM or another unlisted cable type lashed to a messenger; Table 396.10(A) types only.
Conductors resting against messenger supports or the structure, insulation chafed through.
Messenger-supported wiring run where subject to physical damage (396.12).
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is that any cable can be lashed to a messenger — Type NM shows up on spans in the field. NM is not in Table 396.10(A), so the run fails no matter how neat the lashing looks. The messenger fixes the support problem; it does not widen the list of permitted cables.

sections.title: Open wiring on insulators
sections.plain_explanation:
Open wiring on insulators — individual conductors run exposed on insulators with set separations — is a legacy and specialized method (agricultural and industrial settings are its remaining home), governed by its own clearances and protection rules. It is not a shortcut version of knob-and-tube and not a method for new house work.
The gate is narrow (398.10): open wiring is permitted only in industrial or agricultural establishments, on systems of 1000 volts, nominal, or less — indoors or outdoors, in wet or dry locations, where subject to corrosive vapors, and for services. It is never permitted where concealed by the building structure (398.12).
The working rules are separation and protection:
• Conductors within 7 ft of the floor are considered exposed to physical damage and must be protected — guard strips, running boards, boxing, or conduit (398.15(C))
• In dry locations, conductors may be enclosed in flexible nonmetallic tubing in continuous lengths of 15 ft or less, strapped at intervals of 4½ ft or less (398.15(A))
• Conductors entering damp, wet or corrosive spaces get drip loops, then pass upward and inward through noncombustible, nonabsorbent insulating tubes (398.15(B))
• Conductors stay separated from each other — 2½ in — and pass through framing on insulating tubes or bushings (398.17, 398.30)
sections.on_the_job: Service call at a Marion County horse barn: an open-wiring feeder on porcelain insulators along the barn wall, installed decades ago and still legal where it stands. The check is the article in one pass — conductors below 7 ft boxed or in conduit, drip loops where the run enters the wash rack's wet area, spacers still holding the 2½ in separation on the long span, nothing concealed by the new ceiling in the tack room. Know it to recognize it. New Sharma work does not start here.

nec2023_change.change: Removed high-density polyethylene conduit (HDPE) as a permitted means to provide physical protection for open wiring on insulators in Section 398.15(C).
nec2023_change.source: Carosella/NFPA-based 2023 NEC change workbook: 398.15(C) Exposed to Physical Damage

sections.why_it_exists: There is no raceway and no cable jacket — each conductor hangs in the open with only its own insulation on it. Separation keeps conductors from touching each other or grounded surfaces, and the guards and boxing keep people, ladders, tools and livestock from reaching the low runs. Lose either one and the insulation is the only thing left between a fault and a fire.
inspection_fails: Open wiring concealed by a new wall or ceiling finish — 398.12 prohibits it outright.
Conductors within 7 ft of the floor with no guard strips, boxing or conduit protection (398.15(C)).
Conductors touching each other or lying against the wall — separation and spacers lost on the span (398.30).
Open wiring installed in a dwelling, retail or office occupancy — industrial and agricultural only (398.10).
No drip loops where conductors enter a wet or corrosive location (398.15(B)).
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating 398 as knob-and-tube with better PR. Knob-and-tube is Article 394, a different method with different rules — and 398.12 flatly prohibits concealing open wiring, the one thing remodelers most want to do with it. The second trap is the voltage: older books said 600 volts; the 2020 limit in 398.10 is 1000 volts, nominal.

sections.title: Outdoor overhead conductors over 1,000 volts
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 399 is the last article in Chapter 3. It covers outdoor overhead conductors that operate at over 1,000 volts and belong to the property owner — the campus- or plant-style medium-voltage distribution on a big site — not the serving utility's lines.
• What it is: a short, engineered article. It sets no prescriptive clearances of its own.
• Structures: 399.30 requires the supporting structures to be designed and documented by a licensed professional engineer.
• Clearances: the detailed clearance and construction rules live in the National Electrical Safety Code (NESC), not in the NEC.
• What it is not: utility installations under a utility's exclusive control sit outside the NEC altogether, under 90.2(B)(5).
• The number: in the 2020 NEC this article is 399, not 395 — the research draft's body text used 395 before its own index corrected it.
sections.on_the_job: This is not Sharma field work, and the field skill is knowing where our work stops. On a Central Florida industrial park or campus job, if the owner asks us to re-hang or extend an owner-owned overhead span over 1,000 volts, the answer is that the span belongs to the owner's engineer under 399.30 and the NESC — we document it, flag it to the owner in writing, and keep our scope on the premises wiring at 1,000 volts and under.

nec2023_change.change: Article 399 was renumbered as Article 395, Outdoor Overhead Conductors over 1000 Volts.
nec2023_change.source: ICC 2023 NEC Changes Educode (renumbered 315, 395, 495); Daily Reporter 2023 NEC changes

sections.why_it_exists: A span carrying thousands of volts over a parking lot or a walkway can kill without anyone touching it, and the failure is usually structural — a pole, a guy or a crossarm that was never engineered. That is why this article does not hand the installer a clearance table: it sends the design to a licensed engineer and the clearances to the NESC, the code written for overhead line construction.
inspection_fails: Owner-owned overhead span over 1,000 V with no engineered design or documentation for its supporting structures (399.30).
Premises span over 1,000 V laid out from the 225.18 / 230 clearance tables instead of the NESC.
Crew working on the utility's exclusive-control side of the service point as if it were premises wiring (90.2(B)(5)).
sections.exam_trap: The trap is answering from the familiar tables: 399 has no clearance table like 225.18, and its 2020 number is 399 — picking '395' imports the 2023 renumber into a 2020 permit. The other wrong answer is treating the owner's span like a utility drop; exclusive-control utility work is outside the NEC, but an owner-owned span is premises wiring with an engineered article.
